question: A girl chats with ChatGPT in plain English and asks her teacher what is answering her. He says it is a huge computer program trained on billions of pages of text, and the same kind of program sits under Claude. What is that kind of program called?
answer: A large language model
choices: A large language model
A web search engine
An expert system
A database program
context: LLM stands for Large Language Model. These are programs trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word in a sequence. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are all chatbots built on LLMs, and the term names the kind of system under every one of them.

question: A girl opens ChatGPT and stops at the capital letters at the end of its name. They are an acronym for words that describe what the model actually is, and the last word names the network design Google's team introduced in a famous 2017 paper. What do those letters stand for?
answer: Generative Pre-trained Transformer
choices: Generative Pre-trained Transformer
Google's Public Translator system
General Purpose Telephone helper
Graphic Processing Toolkit display
context: GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer. 'Generative' = produces new text. 'Pre-trained' = learned from huge amounts of text before you ever used it. 'Transformer' = the network architecture, introduced in a 2017 Google paper called 'Attention Is All You Need.'

question: A boy reads that the T in ChatGPT stands for Transformer and thinks of the toy robots from the movies. What kind of thing is a Transformer?
answer: Neural network architecture
choices: Neural network architecture
Robot from a movie series
A type of electrical device
A famous brand of laptop
context: In AI, 'Transformer' refers to a specific design (architecture) of neural network, introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need.' It became the foundation for almost every modern chatbot — GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama. The name is unrelated to the robot toys; the AI architecture came later.

question: A girl opens ChatGPT and types her first question. The company had already spent months and millions of dollars feeding it books, websites and articles, and by now it isn't studying anymore. The P in GPT stands for Pre-trained. Why does that word matter?
answer: It learns once, then just responds
choices: It learns once, then just responds
It rehearses for the singing show
It practices old guitar chords
It folds new origami cranes
context: Pre-training is a giant one-time computing job. The model studies huge amounts of text and adjusts its internal numbers (parameters). When you chat with the trained model, it's just running — not learning from your messages. Each new conversation starts fresh. This is why 'pre-trained' matters: training is past, response is present.

question: Suppose you want this morning's game score or a breaking story. Chatbots were often trained months ago and don't know today's events. Which of these is the best tool for looking up today's news?
answer: A search engine like Google
choices: A search engine like Google
A chatbot with no web search
A photo app on your phone
A calculator program
context: Search engines crawl the live web. Chatbots are pattern-completion programs trained months ago and don't know what happened today (unless given a search tool). For 'what just happened,' use search. For 'help me draft something,' a chatbot can help.

question: A nurse asks ChatGPT to work out a huge sum. Since 2023 it has been able to write a short program and run it. When the answer matters, what does that let the chatbot do?
answer: Compute the answer, not guess it
choices: Search the web for the answer
Ask a human to do the sum
Round the answer to look neat
Compute the answer, not guess it
context: OpenAI's Code Interpreter, launched for ChatGPT Plus in July 2023, runs Python code in a sandbox, so a real program does the arithmetic. Without a tool like that, the model only predicts a plausible-looking number.

question: A student asks a chatbot to summarize a famous novel. It confidently describes a whole chapter, with a scene and a character's speech, that isn't in the book at all. The chatbot did not lie on purpose; the model just filled in words that sounded plausible. What is a made-up fact from a chatbot usually called?
answer: Hallucination
choices: Hallucination
Overfitting
Jailbreak
Data drift
context: When an LLM confidently invents false information, people call it 'hallucination.' It happens because the model is predicting plausible-sounding text, not looking facts up. Watch out for invented book chapters, fake quotes, made-up court cases, and wrong dates.

question: A girl asks a chatbot how many r's are in 'strawberry,' and it says two, like many in 2024. Chatbots read text in chunks called tokens, like 'straw' and 'berry.' Why do they miscount?
answer: They don't see the single letters
choices: They don't see the single letters
They can't count above two
They ignore every vowel
They drop all double letters
context: A model receives 'strawberry' as a few token pieces, not ten letters, so counting the r's means reasoning about letters it never directly sees. Researchers quoted by TechCrunch said the problem is built into how these models read text.

question: Suppose you tell ChatGPT today that your favorite color is green. Tomorrow you open another conversation, memory off. Will it remember?
answer: No, each new chat starts fresh from blank
choices: No, each new chat starts fresh from blank
Yes, it remembers everything you ever said
Yes, but only for the next seven days
Only if you pay an extra monthly fee
context: LLMs don't remember between separate conversations by default. Each new chat starts blank. Some chat products bolt on a 'memory' feature that stores notes between sessions, but the underlying model itself has no built-in memory of you.

question: A boy asks a chatbot about a recent event, but the huge pile of books, articles and websites behind it was gathered only up to a specific date. Whatever happens after that date, the chatbot won't know unless it is connected to live search. What is that date called?
answer: The training cutoff
choices: The training cutoff
The expiration date
The opening line
The starter pack
context: Each model has a training cutoff — the date when training data collection stopped. The model has no information about events after that point. If you ask about something that happened last week, it either guesses or says it doesn't have that information. Many chatbots will report their cutoff if you ask.

question: A programmer tells a boy that ChatGPT and Claude run on a 'neural network,' and the boy asks what the word 'neural' is a hint about. She says it comes from a loose comparison. What is a neural network compared to?
answer: Cells in animal brains
choices: Cells in animal brains
Cables in a power grid
Stars in a galaxy
Roads in a city
context: Neural networks are layers of simple math units, loosely inspired by how brain cells (neurons) pass signals. They are NOT literal brains — they're math. The biology comparison is mostly historical naming; underneath, it's all numbers and equations.

question: A programmer looks inside a big chatbot like ChatGPT and finds billions of tiny numbers that decide how it answers. While the chatbot learns from books and websites, those numbers slowly change so it gets better at predicting words. What are those numbers usually called?
answer: Parameters
choices: Parameters
Passwords
Pictures
Pages
context: Parameters are the adjustable numbers (weights and biases) inside a model. GPT-3 had 175 billion of them. Training is the process of slowly tuning these numbers so the model produces better outputs. Bigger models often have more parameters — but bigger doesn't always mean better.

question: A team of programmers feeds a new chatbot huge piles of books, websites and articles so it can learn how words fit together. Only after that first big stage does it start answering people's questions. What is that first learning stage called?
answer: Training
choices: Training
Sleeping
Selling
Stopping
context: Training is the stage where the model adjusts its parameters by studying huge amounts of data. It's done once, in a giant computing job. The second stage — when you actually ask it questions — is called 'inference.' Training is expensive; inference is what you use every time you chat.

question: A girl asks ChatGPT for a poem and DALL-E for a picture of a dragon, and each makes something brand new. The filter on her email only sorts messages into spam or not spam. What is the kind of AI that makes new things called?
answer: Generative AI
choices: Generative AI
Discriminative AI
Symbolic AI
Reactive AI
context: Generative AI produces new outputs — text, images, audio, video. ChatGPT, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion are generative. Other AI just classifies — 'is this email spam?' — without producing anything new. The 2022 ChatGPT moment was about generative AI going mainstream.

question: A girl types a sentence into ChatGPT, and the program does not read whole words the way she does. It chops her text into little pieces, sometimes a short word, sometimes just part of a word, and it writes its reply the same way. What are these small pieces of text called?
answer: Tokens
choices: Tokens
Pixels
Folders
Pages
context: LLMs work with 'tokens,' which are subword pieces. 'Unbelievable' might be split into 'un,' 'believ,' and 'able.' This is why models sometimes spell words strangely or miscount letters — they aren't really seeing letters, they're seeing token chunks.

question: A boy keeps talking to ChatGPT, message after message, but the chatbot can hold only so much of any conversation at once. Programmers have a name for this limit on how much it can 'see' at one time. What is that limit called?
answer: Context window
choices: Context window
Quiet zone
Login screen
Hot key
context: The context window is the maximum chunk of text the model can consider in one go — usually measured in tokens. Modern chatbots have large windows but they aren't infinite. If a conversation gets very long, the model may lose track of what was said earlier.

question: Suppose you ask your phone, out loud, what the weather is today, or tell a smart speaker to play some music. The AI hears your voice as sound waves, not as words. Before it can work out what you want, it has one big first job to do. What is that job?
answer: Turn your speech into text
choices: Turn your speech into text
Charge its battery
Find your photos
Update its software
context: Voice assistants use speech-recognition AI to turn your spoken words into text. Then a separate system handles the request. Whisper (OpenAI), Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant all do this. The technology has gotten very good — but it also means the microphone has to be listening.

question: A programmer who spends all day typing code opens GitHub Copilot, the AI tool GitHub released in 2021. It sits in her editor, tries to guess what she will type next, and lets her take the guess with one key. What is Copilot's main job?
answer: Suggest code as she types
choices: Suggest code as she types
Back up her code online
Track her working hours
Check spelling in her emails
context: Code-assistant tools (Copilot, Cursor, others) read what a programmer is writing and suggest the next lines. They speed up routine work, but they can also suggest buggy or insecure code. The programmer still has to read and check what's offered.

question: A boy finishes a YouTube video, and 'Up Next' picks another one it thinks he will love. TikTok chooses the clips in his 'For You' feed, and Netflix rearranges its home page around what he has watched. All three use AI to decide what he sees next. What is the general name for this kind of AI?
answer: Recommendation systems
choices: Recommendation systems
Calendar reminders
Voice assistants
Spell checkers
context: Recommendation systems use AI to decide what content to put in front of you. They're trained on what you (and people like you) clicked on, watched, or shared. They're usually optimized for engagement — keeping you on the app — not for accuracy or your wellbeing.

question: A student downloads Meta's Llama to her laptop and runs it offline, with no internet. ChatGPT from OpenAI and Claude from Anthropic run only on their companies' servers, but a French startup called Mistral puts its models out for free download too. What is this kind of model called?
answer: Open-weight models
choices: Open-weight models
Proprietary models
Reasoning models
Cloud-only models
context: Open-weight models have their weights (the trained numbers) freely available. Anyone can download them, run them on a personal computer, study them, or build on them. Llama (Meta), Mistral, DeepSeek, and Qwen are major examples. Closed models like GPT-4 or Claude are only available through their company's website or API.

question: Suppose you ask a chatbot for a short school essay. A convincing draft arrives in seconds. Before you turn it in, whose job is it to check the claims?
answer: Yours — the chatbot can't tell what's true
choices: Yours — the chatbot can't tell what's true
The teacher's — grading catches mistakes
The company's — it built the chatbot
The chatbot's — it checks as it writes
context: Even when an LLM writes well, it can confidently include false claims, made-up dates, and invented quotes. The user is responsible for checking. Treat AI output as a draft from a clever friend who sometimes makes things up — useful, but never the final word.

question: A girl learns to stop at three habits on a page: one punctuation mark scattered everywhere, fancy stock phrases, and sentences that feel oddly even, all far beyond what a normal kid would write. What real-life skill is she building?
answer: Spotting AI-written text
choices: Spotting AI-written text
Spotting fake medicines
Spotting good handwriting
Spotting bird species
context: AI-generated text has subtle patterns: certain favored phrases, overuse of em-dashes, repetitive sentence structures. Spotting these is a useful skill — it tells you when something was likely written by AI rather than a person. The skill is recognition, not condemnation.

question: A hobbyist asks DALL-E for a gorgeous portrait, then looks closely at the hands: six fingers, two thumbs, and one hand melting into the other. What does this common mistake show about today's AI art?
answer: Even modern AI images often have flaws
choices: Even modern AI images often have flaws
Hands are always perfect in AI art
AI never makes images of hands
Photos always show six fingers
context: AI image generators (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney) often produce images with characteristic flaws: wrong finger counts, garbled text, jewelry blending into skin, asymmetric eye details. Learning to spot these flaws is a useful defense skill — you can tell a fake from a photo more often than you might think.

question: A cookbook company's engineers take a chatbot already trained on billions of pages of general text and train it a second time, using only recipes and food articles, to make it extra good at cooking questions. This narrow, extra round of training has a special name. What is it called?
answer: Fine-tuning
choices: Fine-tuning
Distillation
Quantization
Tokenization
context: Fine-tuning means taking a pre-trained model and giving it extra training on a specific task or in a specific style. The base model already knows English; fine-tuning teaches it to be a careful cooking helper, a polite customer-service bot, or whatever the company wants. It's cheaper than training a new model from scratch.

question: A boy types 'tell me about dogs' into a chatbot and gets a plain answer. His sister types 'write a fun poem about a dog named Rex who loves cheese' and gets something very different. What is the skill of careful wording called?
answer: Prompt engineering
choices: Prompt engineering
Keyword searching
Spell checking
Code debugging
context: Prompt engineering means writing your input in a way that's likely to get a useful output. Specific instructions, examples, and structure all matter. It isn't magic — it's just careful writing. The same model can give very different answers to a sloppy question versus a clear one.

question: A man chasing a lost parcel got the chatbot of DPD (a British parcel firm) to swear and write a poem mocking the firm in January 2024. What did the firm do next?
answer: Switched off the chatbot's AI part
choices: Switched off the chatbot's AI part
Kept the bot running unchanged
Sued the customer for libel
Reported the customer to police
context: Musician Ashley Beauchamp got the bot to swear and call DPD the worst delivery firm in the world, and his posts went viral. DPD blamed an error after a system update and disabled the AI element while it was fixed. A support bot can be pushed off its script.

question: A programmer feeds an AI tool a short recording of a real person talking. After that, the tool can say brand-new sentences that were never spoken, in that person's exact voice, tone and accent. What is this trick called?
answer: Voice cloning
choices: Voice cloning
Voice fasting
Voice exiting
Voice trimming
context: Voice-clone AI (ElevenLabs is a well-known company) can copy a voice from a small audio sample — a voicemail, a podcast clip, a social-media video. This is the technology behind 'grandparent scams,' where a caller sounds exactly like a relative. Knowing it exists is the first step in not being fooled.

question: A boy reads one of ChatGPT's impressive answers and asks how the program underneath learned to write it. The program was trained on one basic task, done over and over with billions of examples. In plain words, what was that task?
answer: Predict the next word in a text
choices: Predict the next word in a text
Look up answers in a database
Follow grammar rules it was given
Match questions to stored answers
context: An LLM is a program trained to predict the next word (or token) in a sequence of text. In a 'chat' it is predicting words one at a time, given the conversation so far. That single mechanism, guessing the next word, powers all modern chatbots.

question: A grandmother hears her grandson's voice crying for bail money, but scammers cloned it from his social-media videos. What habit at home, settled calmly before any such call, protects against this?
answer: Set up a family safe word
choices: Trust any familiar voice
Set up a family safe word
Pay urgent requests fast
Only speak in whispers
context: A family safe word is a short phrase only family members know. If someone calls sounding like a relative and asks for money or help, you ask for the word, and a voice clone cannot know it. The FBI recommends every family set one up.

question: Suppose you watch a grandmaster lose to a computer chess program. The commentators say the machine 'wanted' the victory, and to your eye it looks that way. Deep down, does the program actually want to win?
answer: No, it just plays high-scoring moves on the board
choices: No, it just plays high-scoring moves on the board
Yes, it gets excited like a person would feel
Yes, it cheers up right after every victory
Only when it is close to winning the game
context: A chess engine has no wanting, hoping, or feeling. It evaluates moves and picks high-scoring ones. The word 'wins' is just a label for what happened — the program didn't experience victory. Capability isn't the same as consciousness. This is the most basic distinction kids need to keep clear about AI.

question: The builders of GPT-3, the model that came before ChatGPT, fed it hundreds of billions of words of text. Most of that training mix came from one kind of source. What was the source?
answer: Pages copied from the open web
choices: Books from public libraries
Wikipedia's encyclopedia
Pages copied from the open web
Scripts of films and TV
context: In the GPT-3 paper, a filtered copy of Common Crawl, a giant archive of web pages, made up 60% of the training mix; books were 16% and Wikipedia just 3%. Much of how a model writes comes from the public web.

question: A girl says 'Alexa' to the smart speaker on the kitchen counter, and it jumps to attention. Only then does it start streaming her words to the cloud. On an iPhone, 'Hey Siri' is recognized right on the device before anything reaches Apple. What is such an activation phrase called in the AI industry?
answer: A wake word
choices: A wake word
A welcome bell
A start key
A boot button
context: Smart speakers and phones use a wake word — a short phrase the device listens for. The microphone is on, listening locally for that word. After the wake word, audio is sent to the cloud for processing. It's worth knowing that the device IS always listening, even if it's only supposed to act on the wake word.

question: A boy reading online meets four chatbot names. Three are real programs from real companies, and one is a made-up name that only sounds plausible. Which one is not real?
answer: ChatBuddy-X9 from a friendly lab
choices: ChatBuddy-X9 from a friendly lab
ChatGPT from the company OpenAI
Claude from the company Anthropic
Gemini from the company called Google
context: ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), and Gemini (Google) are the main chatbots from major US AI labs as of the 2020s. 'ChatBuddy-X9' is invented. When you see a chatbot name in the news, it's worth checking whether the model is real — confident articles sometimes cite chatbots that don't exist.

question: A student reading an article about AI art meets four names for tools that turn typed words into pictures. Three are real, and one is a made-up name that only sounds plausible. Which one is made up?
answer: PixelMaster-Z
choices: PixelMaster-Z
DALL-E
Midjourney
Stable Diffusion
context: DALL-E (OpenAI), Midjourney (a separate company), and Stable Diffusion (open-source) are the main text-to-image generators of the 2020s. 'PixelMaster-Z' is invented. Knowing real-tool names helps you spot fabrications — both human and AI-written articles sometimes invent plausible-sounding product names.

question: A girl asks a chatbot, 'What color is the sky?' It replies, 'I think the sky is blue.' What is the chatbot doing when it writes that reply?
answer: Using words it learned in training
choices: Checking a live weather map
Using words it learned in training
Copying a human's earlier reply
Following a rule about skies
context: Chatbots write phrases like 'I think' and 'I believe' because their training text is full of them; the model is predicting likely words. Whether anything like a thought lies behind such words is a question researchers still argue about.

question: A boy types his first message to a chatbot, but the company behind it has already slipped in hidden instructions on how the model should behave. Anthropic began publishing its own for Claude in 2024. What are these instructions called?
answer: A system prompt
choices: A model card
A system prompt
A user manual
A spam filter
context: A system prompt sets a chatbot's rules and tone before the conversation starts, and users usually never see it. In August 2024 Anthropic began publishing Claude's system prompts in its release notes, which most companies do not do.

question: A girl hears a radio ad call a chatbot 'the world's smartest friend.' It helps with her homework, but it does not remember her name the next day, and it would tell any stranger the same jokes. What part of that phrase is most misleading?
answer: It's a tool, not a friend
choices: It's a tool, not a friend
It's smart in every subject
It uses the internet to think
It is friends with other AIs
context: A chatbot isn't a friend. It has no skin in the game, no care for you, no memory of you across chats by default. It's a useful tool when you want a draft, a summary, or a starting point. Calling it a friend invites a kind of trust that the tool isn't built to deserve.

question: A visitor to Chatbot Arena, a popular leaderboard that began at Berkeley in 2023, types a question and reads two answers from unnamed models side by side. Then she does one thing. What?
answer: Votes for the better answer
choices: Votes for the better answer
Pays for the faster answer
Grades the models' spelling
Guesses which one is human
context: LMSYS's Chatbot Arena turns those blind votes into chess-style Elo ratings for each model. It measures which answers people prefer to read, which is useful but is not the same thing as being correct.

question: A parent asked a teacher, within weeks of the launch, who had built ChatGPT, the free chatbot that a small research lab in San Francisco released late in 2022. Which lab released it?
answer: OpenAI
choices: Google DeepMind
Meta AI
OpenAI
Anthropic
context: OpenAI released ChatGPT on November 30, 2022. Its growth was the fastest of any consumer product on record at the time, and the launch is widely treated as the moment the modern AI era went mainstream.

question: Sam Altman, Elon Musk and others founded OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, in 2015 to work on AI safety. What kind of group did OpenAI start as?
answer: A non-profit research lab
choices: A non-profit research lab
A for-profit software company
A government research agency
A university computer lab
context: OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a non-profit research lab with a stated mission of ensuring AGI benefits humanity. It later restructured to a 'capped-profit' company so it could raise the billions of dollars needed for the compute behind GPT-3 and GPT-4. ChatGPT was released on November 30, 2022.

question: A teenager tried to log in to ChatGPT late in 2022 and found the servers down, crashed by new users. The chatbot was smashing the record for reaching 100 million users, ahead of TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. About how long did it take?
answer: Two months
choices: Two months
Two weeks
Nine months
Two years
context: ChatGPT reached 100 million monthly active users in roughly two months after its November 30, 2022 launch — faster than TikTok, Instagram, or any prior internet product. The speed of adoption is part of why the moment felt seismic to so many.

question: A British mathematician asked in 1950 whether machines can think. He proposed a test in which a judge types to a hidden person and a hidden machine and tries to tell which is which. What is the test called?
answer: The Turing test
choices: The Turing test
The Wittgenstein test
The Hilbert test
The von Neumann test
context: Alan Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' opened with 'I propose to consider the question, can machines think?' He answered by proposing the imitation game, now called the Turing test. He didn't claim to have built such a machine; he argued for a way to settle the question if one ever appeared. Turing had broken the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during WWII and is considered a founder of computer science. Modern chatbots can sometimes pass simple versions of the test; whether that counts as 'intelligence' is still debated.

question: Four researchers wrote a funding letter for a small eight-week workshop at Dartmouth College, set for the summer of 1956, on whether machines could ever reason or learn like people. The young professor organizing the workshop needed a fresh name for this brand-new area of study to put on the letter. Who coined the name?
answer: John McCarthy
choices: John McCarthy
Marvin Minsky
Claude Shannon
Alan Turing
context: John McCarthy proposed the term 'artificial intelligence' for the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project. The term stuck. McCarthy went on to invent the LISP programming language in 1958. The Dartmouth workshop is widely treated as the founding moment of AI as an organized research field.

question: Ten researchers spent the summer of 1956 at Dartmouth College arguing about whether machines could reason, learn or use language like a person. The organizer had named the subject in his funding letter the year before. What was this brand-new field called?
answer: Artificial intelligence
choices: Artificial intelligence
Machine thinking
Cybernetics
Computer science
context: The 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence was held at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. John McCarthy organized it. Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester were among the attendees. They thought one summer would make significant progress on machine intelligence; it took decades.

question: A biologist looks at a long chain of amino acids folded into a tangled 3D shape, the kind of molecule at work in every living thing. For fifty years scientists could barely predict those shapes, until DeepMind's AlphaFold. What are these chains called?
answer: Proteins
choices: Proteins
Fats
Sugars
Vitamins
context: AlphaFold, built by DeepMind, predicts the 3D structure of proteins from their amino-acid sequences. It mapped roughly 200 million proteins — essentially every known protein in nature. Knowing a protein's shape is critical for drug design. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry honored this work.

question: Demis Hassabis's team at DeepMind in London built AlphaFold, which predicted the folded shape of nearly every known protein. The Nobel committee gave him and his teammate John Jumper a shared prize for it in 2024. In which field?
answer: Chemistry
choices: Chemistry
Physics
Medicine
Peace
context: Demis Hassabis shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Jumper (also DeepMind) and David Baker (University of Washington) for AlphaFold's protein-structure prediction work. Hassabis is a former chess prodigy who founded DeepMind in London in 2010; Google bought it in 2014.

question: The board of OpenAI, the lab behind ChatGPT, put out a short public statement on a quiet Friday afternoon in November 2023. Within hours employees were tweeting hearts, investors were calling emergency meetings, and reporters were racing to figure out what had just happened. What did the OpenAI board do that day?
answer: Fired CEO Sam Altman
choices: Fired CEO Sam Altman
Sold the lab to Microsoft
Shut ChatGPT down for a week
Paused all new AI research
context: On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's board fired Sam Altman, citing loss of confidence. Within five days, Altman was back as CEO and most of the board that fired him was gone. Microsoft (OpenAI's largest investor) and nearly every OpenAI employee had backed Altman. The episode showed how little outside control there is on the people building powerful AI.

question: OpenAI's directors suddenly fired their chief executive, Sam Altman, in November 2023, and everyone braced for a long shakeup. After a very public fight he was back in the job, under a new board. About how many days after the firing did Altman return?
answer: About five
choices: About five
About fifteen
About forty
About ninety
context: Sam Altman was fired Nov 17, 2023. Within days, Microsoft offered to hire Altman and the entire research team; nearly all OpenAI employees signed a letter demanding the board resign. Altman was back as CEO on Nov 22 — about five days. Most of the original board was out. It's a striking example of how fragile formal AI governance can be.

question: Geoffrey Hinton, a British-Canadian computer scientist many call a 'godfather of AI,' resigned in May 2023 from the big tech company he had worked at for over a decade, saying he wanted to speak freely about the dangers of powerful AI. Which company did he quit?
answer: Google
choices: Google
Meta
Microsoft
Amazon
context: Geoffrey Hinton resigned from Google in May 2023. He cited concerns about AI safety — mass-produced disinformation, job displacement, autonomous weapons. His concerns are different from Eliezer Yudkowsky's 'shut it all down' position. Hinton helped develop backpropagation (1986) and the AlexNet ImageNet breakthrough (2012).

question: Yann LeCun founded a new AI research lab at one of the biggest tech companies in the world in 2013, taking the title of Chief AI Scientist while he went on teaching at New York University. Which company was it?
answer: Meta
choices: Meta
FedEx
Tesla
Twitter
context: Yann LeCun is Chief AI Scientist at Meta (Facebook's parent company). He helped develop convolutional neural networks for image recognition. He shared the 2018 Turing Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio. He's one of the most prominent voices skeptical of 'AI doom' concerns — distinct from Hinton's middle-ground view.

question: Yoshua Bengio founded a big AI research lab called Mila and stayed in academia, while the two men who shared the 2018 Turing Award with him went to Big Tech. He teaches at a large university on the Saint Lawrence River, in a city that speaks French, and the lab stands there too. Which city is it?
answer: Montreal
choices: Montreal
Madrid
Manchester
Mumbai
context: Yoshua Bengio is a professor at the University of Montreal. He shared the 2018 Turing Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun for foundational deep-learning work. Unlike LeCun, Bengio has voiced concerns about advanced AI risk; unlike Hinton, he stayed in academia rather than leaving a big tech company.

question: Elon Musk, with ChatGPT everywhere and OpenAI enormously valuable, started a brand-new artificial intelligence company in 2023 to compete with the lab he had left. He gave it a very short name, just three letters, that plays on the word 'AI' itself. What is Musk's AI company called?
answer: xAI (Musk's lab)
choices: xAI (Musk's lab)
OpenAI (a different lab)
DeepMind (Google's lab)
Anthropic (Claude's maker)
context: Elon Musk founded xAI in 2023. Its chatbot is called Grok. Musk was a co-founder and early funder of OpenAI but left its board in 2018. He has been publicly critical of OpenAI's direction since. Grok is offered through X (formerly Twitter), which Musk bought in 2022.

question: Elon Musk released his AI company's own chatbot to compete with ChatGPT and Claude. The name is a slang word meaning 'to deeply understand,' borrowed from a famous 1961 science-fiction novel by Robert A. Heinlein, Stranger in a Strange Land. What is the chatbot called?
answer: Grok
choices: Grok
Bark
Squawk
Yawn
context: Grok is xAI's chatbot, integrated with X (formerly Twitter). The name is borrowed from Robert Heinlein's 1961 novel Stranger in a Strange Land, where 'to grok' means to deeply understand. Musk has marketed Grok as a 'rebellious' or 'anti-woke' alternative to ChatGPT, with mixed reviews on how that's actually played out.

question: Dario and Daniela Amodei and their colleagues had all worked together at a famous AI lab before they split off in 2021 to build a company more focused on AI safety. Their new San Francisco company became Anthropic. Which lab did the team leave?
answer: OpenAI
choices: OpenAI
Google DeepMind
Meta AI
IBM Research
context: Dario Amodei is CEO of Anthropic. His sister Daniela Amodei is President. Many Anthropic founders previously worked at OpenAI; they left in 2021 to start Anthropic with a focus on AI safety research. Claude is their main chatbot, competing with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok.

question: A student types a question into the chatbot from Anthropic, the San Francisco company Dario and Daniela Amodei helped start in 2021. Its friendly one-word name is a nod to the mathematician Shannon, who launched information theory in 1948. What is the chatbot called?
answer: Claude
choices: Claude
Carl
Carlos
Calvin
context: Claude is Anthropic's chatbot. The name is reportedly a nod to Claude Shannon, the mathematician who founded information theory in 1948 (and who attended the 1956 Dartmouth AI workshop). Claude competes with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok in the major-US-chatbot lineup.

question: Three University of Toronto researchers entered a giant picture-recognition contest called ImageNet in 2012 with a system later nicknamed AlexNet. It had to name what was in millions of photos. When the scores came in, the previous winning approaches had been left far behind. Why did this moment shock computer scientists?
answer: Neural networks beat older methods by a huge margin once they had enough data and computing power
choices: Neural networks beat older methods by a huge margin once they had enough data and computing power
A computer had named photos better than people for the first time, years ahead of forecasts
The winning system used no training data at all, only rules its three builders wrote by hand
No team had ever finished the contest before, so any winning entry at all was a surprise
context: AlexNet, named for Alex Krizhevsky (a graduate student in Hinton's lab, along with Ilya Sutskever), won the 2012 ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge with a top-5 error of about 15 percent, against about 26 percent for the next-best entry, using a deep neural network trained on GPUs. Year-on-year gains had been a point or two, so the leap convinced the field that deep learning worked at scale. It is often called the start of the modern deep-learning era.

question: A team of Google researchers published a short paper in June 2017 that would quietly change AI forever. It introduced a brand-new network design, the one that later powered ChatGPT, Claude and nearly every modern chatbot. Its title was a bold, catchy phrase. What was that title?
answer: Attention Is All You Need
choices: Attention Is All You Need
Try Faster, Lose Slower
The Future Is Big
Speak Up Now
context: 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the Transformer — a neural network design built around a 'self-attention' mechanism. Every major chatbot (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama) is built on Transformers. The paper is one of the most cited AI papers of all time.

question: Researchers gave GPT-3 jobs it was never trained for in 2020, like translating a phrase or unscrambling a word, and they did not retrain it. What did it need in the prompt to do each job?
answer: A few worked examples
choices: A few worked examples
Thousands of labeled pairs
A manual of the task's rules
A link to a finished answer
context: OpenAI's 2020 paper on GPT-3, 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners,' showed that the 175-billion-parameter model could do a new task from a handful of examples placed in the prompt, with no retraining. The ability is called few-shot learning; with no examples at all it is zero-shot. GPT-3 was not a polished chatbot: ChatGPT, built on a tuned GPT-3.5, brought the technology to non-experts in 2022.

question: ChatGPT users could start handing GPT-4 a photo or a homework screenshot in September 2023 and get an answer in words, and Google's Gemini and Anthropic's Claude accept pictures too. What do programmers call handling more than one kind of material like this?
answer: Multimodal input
choices: Multimodal input
Chain-of-thought
Fine-tuning
Tokenization
context: Handling more than one kind of input (text, images, sound) in a single model is called multimodal. OpenAI showed GPT-4's image input in March 2023 and opened it to ChatGPT users in September 2023; Google's Gemini (December 2023) and Anthropic's Claude 3 (March 2024) accept images too. GPT-4 was also a major upgrade on GPT-3.5 in reasoning and context length.

question: Joseph Weizenbaum, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), wrote one of the very first chat programs in 1966. It imitated a talk therapist, mostly by turning a user's sentences back into questions: 'my mom is angry' came back as 'why do you say your mom is angry?' What did he name this early chatbot?
answer: ELIZA
choices: ELIZA
PARRY
SHRDLU
BORIS
context: ELIZA, built by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT in 1966, was one of the earliest chatbots. It mostly reflected the user's input back as a question ('I'm sad' → 'Why do you say you're sad?'). Weizenbaum was disturbed by how readily people opened up to it — even though they knew it was a simple program. It's an early lesson about anthropomorphizing AI.

question: A professor locked up her AI lab in the mid-1970s after government funders in the US and UK pulled their money over hyped promises. The slump came again in the late 1980s. What seasonal name do historians give these long slumps?
answer: AI winters
choices: AI winters
AI autumns
AI summers
AI monsoons
context: An 'AI winter' is a period when AI funding and interest collapsed because progress fell short of grand promises. The first major winter started in the 1970s after the UK's Lighthill Report. A second hit in the late 1980s after the 'expert systems' boom went bust. The modern boom started after the 2012 deep-learning breakthrough.

question: International Business Machines (IBM) sent a room-sized machine onto a TV quiz show in February 2011 to face Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter, the show's two greatest human champions. It had to crack tricky word puzzles, buzz in and answer aloud in real time. What did IBM name that computer?
answer: Watson
choices: Watson
Deep Blue
BlueGene
Project Debater
context: IBM Watson defeated Jeopardy! champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter in February 2011. The win showed AI could handle complex natural-language puzzles, not just classical games like chess. IBM later tried to apply Watson to medicine and other industries, with much more mixed results.

question: OpenAI's chief executive released ChatGPT to the world in November 2022, sparking the chatbot boom almost overnight. He was one of the small group who had founded the San Francisco lab in 2015, wanting safe, open AI research. Who is he?
answer: Sam Altman
choices: Sam Altman
Demis Hassabis
Dario Amodei
Mark Zuckerberg
context: OpenAI was founded in December 2015 as a non-profit research lab. Co-founders included Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Ilya Sutskever, and others. It later restructured as a 'capped-profit' company. The mission as originally stated was to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity; whether the structure now matches that mission is a matter of ongoing debate.

question: A student downloads a chatbot model from Meta, owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, and runs it on his own computer. Meta has given away the trained weights of a whole family of these since 2023. What has Meta named this family?
answer: Llama
choices: Llama
Falcon
Mistral
BLOOM
context: Llama is Meta's open-weight model family: anyone can download the weights and run the model on a personal computer or server. Versions include Llama, Llama 2, Llama 3 and later releases. Other labs have since released open weights too, among them OpenAI with gpt-oss in 2025, and that year Mark Zuckerberg wrote that Meta would be careful about what it chose to open-source. Llama remains an important counterweight to closed-API-only models.

question: Lee Sedol, one of the greatest Go players alive, faced DeepMind's AlphaGo in Seoul in 2016. Millions watched live. Where did most of that audience sit?
answer: East Asia, where Go is huge
choices: East Asia, where Go is huge
Western Europe, where chess is huge
South America, where checkers is big
Northern Africa, where shogi is huge
context: AlphaGo's 4-1 victory over Lee Sedol in March 2016 was the most-watched AI breakthrough before ChatGPT. Hundreds of millions of viewers — especially in East Asia, where Go is a major game — followed the match. The win convinced many people that something fundamental had changed in machine learning.

question: OpenAI's leaders switched a few years after the lab's founding to an unusual setup they called 'capped-profit,' where outside backers could make money, but only up to a limit. Training modern AI models is enormously expensive: the biggest chatbots cost billions of dollars in computer time. What was the switch meant to do?
answer: Raise large amounts of investment
choices: Raise large amounts of investment
Pay its researchers less money
Cut its computing costs in half
Qualify for government grants
context: OpenAI restructured in 2019 to a 'capped-profit' model — investors can earn returns, but the returns are capped at a multiple of their investment. The move let OpenAI raise the billions needed for compute. Critics argue the change drifted the lab from its non-profit mission. The 2023 board drama partly turned on this tension.

question: Two friends from Poland, a programmer and a machine-learning researcher, founded ElevenLabs in 2022. Their best-known tool works from just a short sample. What does ElevenLabs do?
answer: Generates realistic voices
choices: Generates realistic voices
Makes paper notebooks
Sells flower bouquets
Designs nail polish
context: ElevenLabs is a voice-AI company that became prominent around 2022-23. Its technology can clone a voice from seconds of audio. The same tech that lets actors record once and dub many languages also powers the 'grandparent scam' wave — voice fakes that sound exactly like a real relative.

question: One very large investor pushed hard, in public, for Sam Altman's return after OpenAI's board fired him with almost no warning in November 2023. The investor, a tech giant, had already put more than ten billion dollars into OpenAI. Which company was it?
answer: Microsoft
choices: Microsoft
Amazon
Google
Nvidia
context: Microsoft, OpenAI's largest investor, immediately offered to hire Altman and the entire research team during the November 2023 board crisis. Nearly all OpenAI employees signed a letter demanding the board resign. Five days later, Altman was reinstated as CEO. The episode showed how fragile OpenAI's formal governance structure was against the economic pressure of its main backer.

question: Demis Hassabis and two friends founded DeepMind in 2010, the AI research lab that built AlphaGo, the program that beat human world champions at the ancient game of Go, and AlphaFold. In which city is DeepMind based?
answer: London
choices: London
Toronto
Zurich
Tel Aviv
context: DeepMind was founded in London in 2010 by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman. Google bought it in 2014 for an estimated $500 million. In 2023 Google merged it with Google Brain to form Google DeepMind, which leads Google's AI research and is still headquartered in London.

question: Computer scientists gave the 2018 Turing Award, often nicknamed the 'Nobel Prize of computing,' to a trio who had spent decades pushing deep learning, teaching computers to learn from huge piles of examples, through long years when almost no one believed in the idea. Which of these four famous AI names did not win it?
answer: Demis Hassabis (DeepMind founder)
choices: Demis Hassabis (DeepMind founder)
Geoffrey Hinton (Toronto/Google)
Yann LeCun (NYU/Meta)
Yoshua Bengio (Montreal)
context: The 2018 Turing Award went to Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio for foundational deep-learning work. Demis Hassabis founded DeepMind and later shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold — a different prize. Knowing who is recognized for what helps you read AI news critically.

question: A graduate student walked into Geoffrey Hinton's lab at a Canadian university, where Hinton taught and researched for decades, long before he began publicly warning the world about powerful AI. That school trained many of the students who later launched OpenAI, DeepMind and other big AI labs. Which Canadian school was it?
answer: University of Toronto
choices: University of Toronto
McGill University
University of British Columbia
University of Waterloo
context: Geoffrey Hinton was a professor at the University of Toronto for decades. His 2012 ImageNet team (Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever as graduate students) launched the deep-learning revolution from there. Hinton joined Google in 2013 and resigned in May 2023 to speak more freely about AI risks.

question: DeepMind's engineers fed AlphaGo famous human games, yet most of its real skill came from games inside the computer against one very particular opponent. Who did it mostly play?
answer: Itself, millions of times
choices: Itself, millions of times
Older Go programs from the 1990s
Top professional Go players
Random move generators
context: AlphaGo learned from a mix of human Go games and self-play — playing against copies of itself for millions of games. A later version, AlphaZero (2017), learned chess, shogi, and Go with NO human game data at all — purely self-play. Self-play turned out to be a powerful way to train game-playing AI past human level.

question: A lab technician opens DeepMind's giant public AlphaFold database and finds predicted 3D shapes for nearly every known protein on Earth, after decades when scientists could barely work out even a few. About how many is that?
answer: 200 million
choices: 200 million
200 thousand
200 billion
context: AlphaFold has predicted the 3D structure of roughly 200 million proteins — essentially every known protein in nature. The database is freely available. Knowing a protein's shape lets researchers design drugs that target it. The work won DeepMind's Demis Hassabis and John Jumper a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

question: A chemist studies a protein's curly 3D shape. A medicine slips into a spot on that protein like a key into a lock. Why does she need the exact shape?
answer: Drugs are designed to fit the shape
choices: Drugs are designed to fit the shape
Its shape sets how much it weighs
Its shape shows which animal made it
Its shape reveals how old it is
context: Proteins do almost all the work in living cells, and their shapes determine what they do. Drugs typically work by fitting precisely into a target protein, the way a key fits a lock. Knowing the shape upfront lets researchers design candidate drugs faster. AlphaFold made this once-slow lab work suddenly routine.

question: A radiologist opens a chest scan that an AI program has already read, with a faint shadow on a lung flagged for her. The AI is not allowed to diagnose a patient on its own; she still makes the final call. What role does the AI mostly play in that setup?
answer: Second reader catching missed details
choices: Second reader catching missed details
Trainee learning from her calls
Clerk filing the finished scans
Timer tracking how fast she reads
context: AI in radiology is most often used as a 'second reader' — the human radiologist reads the scan, then AI checks for things the human might have missed. The human stays responsible for the final read. This 'augment, don't replace' pattern is common across many domains where AI has been deployed in serious work.

question: A tourist in San Francisco climbs into a driverless taxi with no one in the front seat. One American company has been running such cars on real city streets in Phoenix, San Francisco and Los Angeles for years, using AI to read cameras, radar and lidar at once. What is that company called?
answer: Waymo
choices: Waymo
Cruise
Aurora
Mobileye
context: Waymo (a sister company to Google) operates self-driving taxi services in several US cities. Tesla offers driver-assistance software called Autopilot and a paid 'Full Self-Driving' option. Cruise (a GM subsidiary) ran similar services. Self-driving has made real progress but has also missed many predicted timelines.

question: Suppose you open YouTube and the home page fills with videos you never asked for, many of them exactly the kind of thing you like. An AI is choosing them for you, based on what you and millions of other viewers have clicked and watched. What is that system mostly trying to guess?
answer: What you'll watch next
choices: What you'll watch next
Where you live exactly
What you ate for dinner
Your shoe size in inches
context: YouTube's recommendation system predicts which videos you're likely to watch and watch for a long time. It's optimized for engagement — usually measured by watch time. It's NOT optimized for whether what you watch is true, useful, or good for you. Knowing what it's actually optimizing is the first step in choosing what to do about it.

question: A team called BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos won a prize from Netflix in 2009 for making its movie-recommendation system 10% more accurate. Netflix had offered the prize in 2006. How big was the prize?
answer: One million dollars
choices: One thousand dollars
Ten thousand dollars
One million dollars
One billion dollars
context: The Netflix Prize paid $1 million to BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos, whose entry beat Netflix's own Cinematch system by just over 10%; a rival team reportedly matched it but submitted 20 minutes later. Companies pay a fortune to predict your taste.

question: A boy's phone shows Grandma's name, and a crying voice begs for money. He has heard of a caller-ID trick called spoofing. What does the name on the screen prove?
answer: Nothing about who is calling
choices: That Grandma is the caller
That it is a family call
Nothing about who is calling
That the voice is real
context: The FCC defines caller ID spoofing as deliberately falsifying what your caller ID displays to disguise who is calling. A familiar name on the screen proves nothing, so hang up and call the person back on the number you already have.

question: A farmer looks out over fields too huge to walk every day. Now an AI model spots dry patches, pests and weak crops for him from far above, then tells him exactly where to water or spray. What does the AI use to watch his crops?
answer: Satellite images
choices: Satellite images
Old radios
Wooden spoons
Paper kites
context: Precision agriculture uses AI to analyze satellite and drone imagery, helping farmers spot drought stress, pest damage, and yield differences across fields. Combined with sensors and GPS-guided machinery, it has changed large-farm management. It also raises questions about who controls the data and whether small farms can compete on the same terms.

question: A forecaster waits hours for a giant physics simulation on a supercomputer to guess tomorrow's storms. In 2023 Google DeepMind's GraphCast, an AI model, matched such forecasts on a single computer. Compared with older tools, what do AI weather models often do?
answer: Run much faster
choices: Run much faster
Get sleepy in the rain
Need flat windless places
Smell coming storms
context: AI weather models (Google's GraphCast, Huawei's Pangu-Weather, others) can produce forecasts much faster than traditional physics-based numerical weather prediction. They're trained on decades of historical data. They don't replace traditional models entirely, but they've become a real complement — and faster forecasts mean more warning when severe weather is coming.

question: A chemist hunting a new drug faces a huge library of molecules that would take years to test by hand. An AI predicts which to build first. What is AI mainly used to do here?
answer: Speed up finding candidate compounds
choices: Speed up finding candidate compounds
Run the human clinical trials
Make the finished pills
Approve drugs for sale
context: AI in drug discovery is used to narrow the search for promising candidate compounds — sorting through billions of possibilities far faster than human chemists alone could. AlphaFold-style protein-structure prediction is one piece of this. Drug development still takes years and clinical trials, but the early-stage search has changed dramatically.

question: A student opens four giant AI chatbots side by side, ChatGPT and Claude among them. One of the four, built by Google, takes its name from the Latin word for twins. Which one is from Google?
answer: Gemini
choices: Gemini
Grok
Claude
ChatGPT
context: ChatGPT is from OpenAI, Claude from Anthropic, Gemini from Google and Grok from xAI (Elon Musk's company). Gemini is Latin for 'twins'; Google says the name nods to the two teams, Google Brain and DeepMind, that merged to build it. The four compete on different strengths: Gemini plugs into Google services, Claude is known for long context windows, ChatGPT had the biggest head start and Grok markets itself as less filtered.

question: Suppose you are stuck on a fractions problem with a chatbot like ChatGPT open beside you. It could hand you the final answer in a second. What is a productive way to use the chatbot for learning math?
answer: Ask it to walk through steps
choices: Ask it to walk through steps
Read its full solution twice
Have it do the hard ones
Copy its answer, then reread it
context: A chatbot is useful for learning when a student asks it to explain step by step, check the work and quiz him or her. Reading a finished solution, even twice, skips the practice, and so does handing it the hard problems. The line: AI for explanation and review helps; AI replacing the work a student should do makes him or her weaker.

question: A man asks his iPhone to set an alarm, send a text and search the web, all by voice, through an assistant Apple got by buying a small startup in 2011. Over a billion people now talk to that assistant every week. What is Apple's voice assistant called?
answer: Siri
choices: Siri
Bixby
Cortana
Sundar
context: Apple's voice assistant is Siri, launched in 2011 with the iPhone 4S. Amazon has Alexa (with Echo devices). Google has Google Assistant. Microsoft has Cortana. All of them rely on AI for speech recognition (turning your speech into text) and natural-language understanding (figuring out what you meant).

question: A family sets Amazon's new tabletop speaker, the Echo, on the kitchen counter in 2014. It waits for a spoken trigger, then answers questions, plays music and controls smart lights, all through a voice assistant with a woman's name. What is the assistant inside the Echo called?
answer: Alexa
choices: Alexa
Echo
Aria
Astra
context: Alexa is Amazon's voice assistant, built into Echo smart speakers and other devices. Like Siri and Google Assistant, it uses AI to recognize speech and process natural language. It's also a microphone in your house listening for the wake word 'Alexa' — worth being aware of when deciding where to put one.

question: A student lists four famous image generators, from OpenAI, Google, a private service and a British startup. Three keep the model locked inside company servers. One has open weights, free to download and run on a home computer. Which one is it?
answer: Stable Diffusion
choices: Stable Diffusion
DALL-E
Midjourney
Imagen
context: Stable Diffusion is open-source. Anyone can download the model and run it on a personal computer. DALL-E (OpenAI), Midjourney (its own company), and Stable Diffusion (Stability AI, image) are closed — you have to use the company's website or API. Open-source models are an important countervailing force to closed model companies.

question: Pandora's team built its music service on the Music Genome Project, begun in 2000. Instead of only watching what listeners played, Pandora described every song itself. Who did the describing?
answer: Trained musicians, by hand
choices: Random listeners, by vote
Trained musicians, by hand
The singers, by contract
Radio hosts, by phone
context: Founder Tim Westergren hired musicologists to analyze songs on hundreds of musical traits, so Pandora could suggest songs that sound alike. That is content-based recommendation; most big feeds lean on collaborative filtering instead, which matches you with people like you.

question: A small European team in Cologne, Germany, launched a translation tool called DeepL in 2017. It quickly became famous for translations that sound more natural than its bigger rivals, especially between European languages like German, French and English. Which big translation tool does DeepL compete with?
answer: Google Translate
choices: Google Translate
Duolingo
Rosetta Stone
Babbel
context: DeepL and Google Translate are the two best-known machine-translation services. DeepL is often praised for nuance with European languages, while Google Translate covers more languages overall. Both use deep neural networks trained on huge corpora of human-translated text. Both have moved the practical floor for cross-language communication.

question: A student sets out to have a computer search every legal position in Go, the game DeepMind's AlphaGo mastered in 2016. How does the number of positions compare with the atoms in the observable universe?
answer: Far more positions
choices: Far fewer positions
Far more positions
About the same
Exactly half as many
context: John Tromp calculated in 2016 that a Go board has about 2 x 10^170 legal positions, while the observable universe holds around 10^80 atoms. No computer could search all of that, which is why Go needed learned judgement rather than brute force.

question: A woman at home twists a protein on her computer screen into its best shape and scores points for it, using Foldit, which scientists at the University of Washington released in 2008. What kind of thing is Foldit?
answer: An online puzzle game
choices: A microscope camera
An online puzzle game
A lab robot arm
A DNA test kit
context: Foldit turned protein folding into a puzzle: players drag a molecule around on screen and score points for shapes that are physically likely. It came partly out of David Baker's lab, the scientist who later shared the 2024 Nobel Prize.

question: A teacher asks an AI image generator, trained on millions of photos, for a striking portrait and gets it in seconds, except that five fingers have become six and a thumb bends the wrong way. Why does this kind of mistake happen?
answer: The model doesn't truly understand hands
choices: The model doesn't truly understand hands
Hands are too small to draw at all
All cameras break around hands
Hands are illegal to depict by law
context: Image generators learn patterns of pixels that statistically appear together. They don't 'understand' that a hand has exactly five fingers — they just know what hands tend to look like. When the model isn't sure, it can produce six fingers, missing fingers, or impossible joints. Hands and text in images are the two classic giveaways.

question: A woman swipes her credit card at a store, and a statistical model at her bank checks the swipe in real time. AI fraud detection in banking is an example of what?
answer: Old AI that quietly works
choices: Old AI that quietly works
Brand-new AI from this year
AI built from chatbot tech
AI that talks like a person
context: Credit-card fraud detection has used machine learning since the 1990s. It is an example of older 'narrow' AI that quietly works every day, far from any chatbot drama. Much of the AI in daily life, from spam filtering and recommendations to fraud detection and voice transcription, has been working for years without fanfare.

question: A cyclist waiting beside a Waymo notices a tall, drum-shaped device spinning on the roof. It fires pulses in every direction and measures how long each one takes to bounce back, building a live 3D map of the road, the other cars and the pedestrians. What is this sensor technology called?
answer: Lidar (laser-based ranging)
choices: Lidar (laser-based ranging)
Sonar (sound-based ranging)
Radar (radio-based ranging)
Solar (sun-based ranging)
context: Lidar bounces laser pulses off objects and times the return to build a 3D map of the surroundings. Waymo and many other self-driving programs use it. Tesla famously chose to rely mostly on cameras and radar instead. Sonar uses sound, radar uses radio waves; lidar uses light. Each has different strengths for different conditions.

question: A famous actress asks an audiobook company to read a new novel aloud in an AI version of her own voice, so she need not sit in a recording studio for weeks reading every chapter. Before the AI can talk in her voice, the company needs one thing from her. What must she do?
answer: Give recorded samples for training
choices: Give recorded samples for training
Watch every chapter being read
Drive the audiobook truck
Pick the cover art color
context: AI voice cloning needs samples to train on. Legitimate uses (audiobooks, dubbing, accessibility) involve consent — the voice owner agrees and is usually paid. The same technology without consent powers voice-clone scams. The technology itself doesn't know the difference; that's why the law and personal habits both matter.

question: DeepMind's engineers released AlphaZero in 2017 as a follow-up to AlphaGo, which had studied recorded matches first. How did AlphaZero learn chess and Go?
answer: From scratch with no human games
choices: From scratch with no human games
By watching human players in person
From a printed book of moves
By copying older chess programs
context: AlphaZero learned chess, shogi, and Go using only the rules and self-play — no human game data at all. AlphaGo had used some human games. AlphaZero showed that pure self-play could match or exceed human-data-augmented training. It's a striking demonstration of how powerful self-play can be when the rules are clear and the system can play itself millions of times.

question: A web developer types 'make me a simple web page with a login button' into an AI coding tool like GitHub Copilot, and working code appears. Such tools learned from code that was sometimes buggy or insecure. Before she trusts the result, what must she still do?
answer: Read and test the suggested code
choices: Read and test the suggested code
Ask the tool if its code is safe
Check that the page loads once
Rewrite the comments in her words
context: AI coding tools speed up routine work but they can suggest buggy, insecure, or subtly wrong code. The programmer still has to read what's offered, test it, and decide whether to use it. 'Tool that drafts; human that reviews' is the discipline that keeps quality from sliding when AI is in the loop.

question: Suppose you open a short-video app like TikTok or YouTube Shorts, and its AI picks each next clip. The company says it measures one thing: engagement. That word doesn't mean you liked a video with a heart. It means two very specific numbers the app can actually count. What counts as engagement here?
answer: Watch time and shares
choices: Watch time and shares
How loud you cheer
Your shoe brand
Your last test grade
context: Engagement is usually measured by watch time, repeat visits, likes, comments, and shares. These are easy to count. They are NOT the same as 'did this help the user' or 'is the content true.' The system optimizes whatever it's measured by, so the metric shapes what gets shown. This is one of the most important facts to know about how these systems work.

question: Geoffrey Hinton, a famous AI researcher, told a 2016 conference in Toronto that the world should stop training radiologists, the doctors who read X-rays and scans, because within five years AI would do their job better. Nearly ten years later, what has happened to radiologist jobs?
answer: Radiologists are still in demand
choices: Radiologists are still in demand
Radiologists are rarely hired now
Most radiology jobs went to AI
Radiologists' pay has fallen by half
context: Hinton said in 2016 that people should stop training radiologists because deep learning would do better than them within five years. Nearly a decade later, radiologists are still in demand, and AI is used mostly as a second reader rather than a replacement; Hinton has since said he was too quick to predict it. The prediction is a famous cautionary tale: confident timelines for AI replacing a job have a poor track record.

question: A reviewer at the US Food and Drug Administration signed off on another AI medical device, one of more than 1,400 authorized by the end of 2025. About three in four of them did one kind of job. Which job?
answer: Reading medical scans
choices: Doing surgery
Reading medical scans
Mixing medicines
Booking appointments
context: Radiology, the specialty that reads X-rays, CT scans and MRIs, accounts for about 76 percent of the AI devices on the FDA's list. It is the medical field most crowded with AI, and also a field still short of doctors.

question: A grower flies a drone over her fields, and an AI program combs the pictures for tiny changes in the leaves: a plant that may be sick, a patch short of water, a place where bugs are chewing. What does the AI help her do?
answer: Spot crop problems early
choices: Spot crop problems early
Sing to the plants
Paint barns purple
Bake bread on the tractor
context: Precision agriculture uses AI on satellite imagery, drone footage, and ground sensors to spot drought stress, pest damage, nutrient deficiencies, and yield variation across a field. Farmers can then water, fertilize, or treat only where needed instead of treating the whole field uniformly. It's a quietly important application of AI to real-world problems.

question: Congresswoman Jennifer Wexton went to the House floor in 2024 after a brain disease took her speech. An AI company had built a model from her old speeches. What did that model let her do there?
answer: Speak in her own voice
choices: Speak in her own voice
Speak in an actor's voice
Vote without being there
Read speeches as text
context: Rep. Jennifer Wexton of Virginia has progressive supranuclear palsy, which damages speech. ElevenLabs cloned her voice from her earlier speeches, and in July 2024 she gave what is believed to be the first House floor speech in an AI-cloned voice.

question: A girl opens a chatbot the night before a biology exam. Psychologists find that one study habit makes an answer stick far better than reading it again. Which study habit is it?
answer: Self-testing
choices: Self-testing
Highlighting
Summarizing
Copying notes
context: Psychologists call it the testing effect, or retrieval practice. In a 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, students who tested themselves remembered far more a week later than students who reread. A chatbot that quizzes a student puts it to work.

question: Suppose you answer your phone and hear a voice exactly like your cousin's. He says he's in trouble and needs you to wire him money right away. AI can clone anyone's voice from a short recording, and scammers use such clones to fake calls from family. What's the smart first move before you send anything?
answer: Hang up and call your cousin back
choices: Hang up and call your cousin back
Wire the money right away
Whisper a secret family song
Tell him your address out loud
context: Voice clones can fool family members from just seconds of recorded audio. The single best defense is to hang up and call back on a number you already know. If it was really your cousin, he'll pick up. If it was a scammer, the call ends right there. Urgency is the scammer's tool; calling back is yours.

question: A scammer lifts a clip of a woman's voice from a podcast and feeds it to a cloning tool to fake a voice that sounds real. About how much recorded audio does modern AI need to clone a person?
answer: Just a few seconds
choices: Just a few seconds
Twenty years exactly
Half a lifetime
Several decades
context: Modern voice-cloning tools can produce a convincing imitation from just a few seconds of clean audio. The source can be a voicemail, a podcast, a social-media video, even a clip from a school play, so it is worth being careful about what audio of you is public.

question: A TikTok user called Ghostwriter posted the song 'Heart on My Sleeve' in April 2023, sung by AI copies of two stars who never recorded it. Streaming sites pulled it after the label complained. Whose voices were they?
answer: Drake and The Weeknd
choices: Eminem and Dr. Dre
Adele and Ed Sheeran
Drake and The Weeknd
Beyonce and Rihanna
context: The song used AI vocals imitating Drake and The Weeknd, neither of whom was involved. It drew millions of plays before Universal Music Group got Spotify, Apple Music and others to remove it. Famous voices are easy to clone because so much of their audio is online.

question: A big sister watches her brother chat with a free AI chatbot on his phone. If the company gets hacked, she warns, anything he pastes in might one day be read by another person. What does she tell him never to paste?
answer: His password
choices: His password
His essay draft
His math homework
His book report
context: Free chatbot services typically log conversations. The logs may be used to train future models, reviewed by employees, or reached under legal process. Passwords, full credit card numbers and sensitive medical or legal documents do not belong there. Anything sent to a free chatbot may one day be seen by someone else.

question: Suppose you tell a clinic your symptoms, and the US health-privacy law (HIPAA) guards them. You type them into a chatbot app. Does the law protect them there?
answer: No, it mostly covers doctors and insurers
choices: Yes, it covers every health app
Yes, once you click I agree
No, it mostly covers doctors and insurers
Only if the app is free to use
context: HIPAA applies to covered entities such as health providers and health plans, and to their business partners. A consumer app you download on your own generally falls outside it, so your health questions are governed mostly by the app's own privacy policy.

question: A boy scrolling online stops on a video of a famous politician saying something shocking. It looks totally real, but AI can fake a clip of anyone. Before he believes it or forwards it to friends, what is the smart first step?
answer: Check if trusted news outlets report it
choices: Check if trusted news outlets report it
Ask in the comments if it's real
Trust it because the clip is popular
Trust it because the face looks real
context: Deepfakes can put words in real people's mouths. Telltales (mouth-sync drift, weird blinking, voice mismatch) are useful but not foolproof. The bigger defense is: if something shocking happened, trusted news organizations are usually reporting it. If the only place you see a story is a viral clip on social media, treat it with extra suspicion.

question: A teenager scrolling online stops at a photo of a person holding up a big sign. Up close the letters are messy and jumbled: some are half-formed, others don't spell real words. What is a garbled sign like that a telltale clue of?
answer: An AI-generated image
choices: An AI-generated image
Bad camera focus only
Foreign-language script
Old vintage film
context: AI image generators (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney) often produce garbled, unreadable text in images — letters that look right at first glance but spell nothing. Real photos with real signs have real text. Garbled text on signs, labels, or storefronts in an image is a strong indicator that the image is AI-generated.

question: Mike Caulfield built a four-step habit for judging anything online, from a chatbot answer to a viral post, and named it SIFT (one letter for each step). What is the first step?
answer: Stop
choices: Share
Search
Screenshot
Stop
context: Caulfield's SIFT stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context. Stopping comes first because the urge to share is strongest in the moment, and a pause is when you ask whether you know what the source is at all.

question: A boy finds a strange bump on his skin and, instead of getting it looked at, types his symptoms into a chatbot. It gives him a confident-sounding diagnosis. But chatbots often 'hallucinate': they invent medical facts that sound authoritative. What should he do?
answer: See a real doctor, not the chatbot
choices: See a real doctor, not the chatbot
Ask the chatbot to double-check
Search online for photos of bumps
Wait a month to see if it fades
context: Chatbots can provide useful general information but they don't know your full medical history, they can't examine you, and they can be confidently wrong. For real symptoms, see a real doctor. Use the chatbot as a starting point for questions to ask, never as the final word. The same rule applies to legal advice — real lawyer for real legal issues.

question: A boy stuck on a homework math problem types it into a chatbot and gets a confident answer back. Chatbots are not always right at math. Before he turns it in, what is the smart step?
answer: Check it with a calculator
choices: Check it with a calculator
Ask the chatbot if it's sure
Trust it if it shows steps
Copy its working too
context: LLMs are bad at multi-step arithmetic. They predict text patterns, not numbers. They can be confidently wrong on big numbers, long chains of operations, or unusual calculations. Always verify chatbot math with an actual calculator. Some chatbot products bolt a calculator on — when they do, the math is reliable. Without it, don't trust it.

question: Suppose you close the tab on a free AI chatbot after a long talk, and the window vanishes from your screen. What does the company behind a typical free chatbot do with that chat?
answer: Logs it on its servers
choices: Logs it on its servers
Deletes it at once
Keeps it on your phone
Erases it in an hour
context: Most free chatbot services keep a log of conversations on the company's servers, and their terms of service say what the company may do with it. Closing the window only hides the chat from the screen. Reading the terms once for any heavily used service is worth a few minutes.

question: A student asks ChatGPT and Gemini the same question, and both give the same surprising fact. She is ready to call it settled. Does their agreement prove the fact is true?
answer: No — they may share training data
choices: Yes — two sources agree
Yes — they come from rival firms
Yes — if both sound certain
No — they may share training data
context: Two chatbots agreeing isn't independent confirmation. They were often trained on overlapping internet data and can share the same errors. Agreement can raise your confidence a little, but real verification needs a different kind of source, such as an encyclopedia or an official page.

question: A teacher plays a suspected deepfake for her class and asks the students to watch closely. At a glance it looks real, but a careful viewer can usually catch a small giveaway. Which of these signs is a typical tell?
answer: Mouth movement that doesn't quite match
choices: Mouth movement that doesn't quite match
A shaky handheld camera shot
Traffic noise in the background
A TV channel's logo in the corner
context: Deepfake video tells include: mouth movement that drifts slightly out of sync with the speech, weird blinking patterns, blurry or shifting hair or jewelry edges, voice that doesn't quite match the lip movement, and inconsistent lighting on the face. The technology keeps improving — so the tells keep getting subtler — but the general idea is to look for small mismatches.

question: A student's chatbot offers a beautiful, wise-sounding line it claims was written by Mark Twain or Albert Einstein. Chatbots often produce fake lines that sound real but were never actually said by that person. Before she uses it in an essay or shares it as real, what's the safe step?
answer: Search for the exact quote first
choices: Search for the exact quote first
Ask the chatbot if it's real
Check it matches his style
Reword it so it's not a quote
context: Chatbots invent confident-sounding quotes attributed to famous authors. The quote often sounds 'in style' but was never actually written by that author. Before using a quote in an essay, search for the exact phrase in quotation marks. If the only places it appears are AI outputs or scraped AI content, it's probably invented.

question: A teacher shows her class ChatGPT's Temporary Chat, which keeps a talk out of the saved history. OpenAI says it may still keep one thing for up to 30 days. What is it?
answer: A copy of the chat, for safety checks
choices: A card number, for billing
A voice recording, for ID
A location, for local ads
A copy of the chat, for safety checks
