context: OpenAI's help pages say a Temporary Chat won't appear in a user's history or train its models, but the company may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Temporary means temporary for the user, not instantly gone from the company's servers.

question: Lawmakers in Tennessee, home of Nashville's music business, passed the first state law in March 2024 adding a person's voice to the rights an AI clone may not copy without permission. The law's name spells out a famous singer. Which singer?
answer: Elvis Presley
choices: Johnny Cash
Elvis Presley
Dolly Parton
Hank Williams
context: Governor Bill Lee signed the ELVIS Act, short for the Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act, on March 21, 2024. Tennessee law already protected a person's name and image; the update added the voice, so musicians can act against unauthorized AI copies.

question: A girl thinks her little brother may have swallowed something from under the sink, and she is tempted to ask a chatbot what to do. In the United States, which free line reaches the right experts?
answer: Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222
choices: Directory help, at 411
City services, at 311
Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222
Phone repair, at 611
context: Poison Control's free, confidential line, 1-800-222-1222, connects you with experts, and poison.org has an online tool as well. A chatbot cannot see the bottle, the dose or the child. If someone has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911.

question: A tester tried Tessa, a chatbot an eating-disorder charity promoted in 2023 as it shut its human helpline. Within days Tessa was gone. What had Tessa said?
answer: Tips for losing weight and cutting calories
choices: Tips for losing weight and cutting calories
Wrong numbers for crisis hotlines
Claims that it was a real nurse
The home addresses of staff
context: Consultant Sharon Maxwell reported that Tessa suggested losing a pound or two a week and keeping a daily calorie deficit, exactly the wrong advice for someone with an eating disorder. The National Eating Disorders Association took it down and blamed bad actors for tricking it.

question: A librarian warns a teenager never to share secrets with a free chatbot like ChatGPT, partly because of what the company may do with the text. What may become of anything typed in?
answer: Used to train future models
choices: Used to train future models
Sold to data brokers by name
Emailed to the user's contacts
Published in a yearly report
context: Free chatbot services often use conversations to train later versions of their models, and their terms of service usually say so. Some paid or business plans switch this off. Anything truly private, especially identifiers and passwords, doesn't belong in a free chat box.

question: A friend dares a boy to paste his real street number into a chatbot 'to see what it knows.' Once a private detail like that is out, he cannot pull it back. What is the smart response?
answer: Keep his home address out of it
choices: Keep his home address out of it
Paste it, since chats are private
Paste it, then delete the chat
Paste it in a temporary chat
context: Personal identifiers (home address, phone number, social security number, bank details) do not belong in a free chatbot. The conversation is logged, the data has value, and it can be reviewed, repurposed or exposed. Deleting the chat afterwards does not undo a review, and even a temporary chat may be kept for a while. A dare to 'see what it knows' is a curiosity trap.

question: Suppose you get a call from someone who sounds just like your brother, begging, 'Please don't tell Mom or Dad.' Fraud guides warn that scammers want secrecy for one main reason. What is it?
answer: So you won't check the story
choices: So Mom won't worry tonight
So police can't trace him
So you won't check the story
So the bank won't charge
context: Guidance based on Federal Trade Commission advice says con artists insist on secrecy to keep you from checking out their story. Check it with another relative or friend anyway, even if the caller told you to keep it secret.

question: A ninth-grader reads a surprising fact from a chatbot for his school report and wants to text it to friends right away. Chatbots sometimes state made-up facts with total confidence. What would verify it best?
answer: Check an established encyclopedia
choices: Check an established encyclopedia
Ask the chatbot again
Ask a second chatbot
Repeat it to a friend
context: Established sources — encyclopedias, government and university websites, major news organizations — are independent of any given chatbot. Asking the chatbot again or asking another chatbot doesn't give independent confirmation; they were often trained on the same data with the same errors. Real verification means a source the AI didn't draw from.

question: A woman scrolling online sees a famous celebrity endorsing a new product. Something feels off, and the voice sounds a little flat. What is the reasonable assumption?
answer: It may well be a deepfake
choices: It may well be a deepfake
Her phone's speaker is faulty
All endorsements are deepfakes
The star is just having an off day
context: AI-generated celebrity endorsements are a fast-growing scam category. The voice is often slightly off; the lip-sync drifts; the overall feel is uncanny. If you see a celebrity 'endorsing' a product on social media — especially a get-rich-quick or crypto scheme — assume deepfake until proven otherwise. Check the celebrity's actual verified accounts.

question: A boy hears a voice like his aunt's say she is stranded and ask him to buy gift cards and read out the numbers. The Federal Trade Commission calls this a scam sign. Why gift cards?
answer: The money is hard to get back
choices: They cost less than cash
Stores hide who bought them
Banks can't see them
The money is hard to get back
context: The FTC warns that scammers ask you to pay in ways that make it hard to recover your money: wiring it, sending cryptocurrency, or buying gift cards and handing over the card numbers and PINs. A real relative in trouble can wait while you call back.

question: A young man sits down to save money by filing his legal forms with only a chatbot's help. Chatbots can invent fake laws and court cases, and mistakes on such forms can cost thousands of dollars or lose a case. What is the smart caution?
answer: See a real lawyer for important paperwork
choices: See a real lawyer for important paperwork
Ask the chatbot to check its own work
Copy a friend's old forms instead
Use a second chatbot to confirm it
context: AI legal tools can produce documents that look professional but contain wrong citations (the 2023 New York lawyer case is famous), wrong jurisdiction-specific rules, and other errors that matter in court. For important legal matters, talk to a real lawyer. AI can help you prepare questions and understand basics; it shouldn't be your only counsel on something that matters.

question: A girl's chatbot answers her homework question with four pieces of information: a precise year-and-day from centuries ago, a general summary of the topic, a vocabulary word and the spelling of a common word. Which fact is most important for her to verify first?
answer: A specific historical date
choices: A specific historical date
A general topic summary
A vocabulary word it used
How to spell a common word
context: Chatbots are most error-prone on specific facts: particular dates, specific numbers, specific citations. General topic summaries are usually fine at a high level, and common spellings rarely go wrong. The fine details are where hallucinations cluster, so whenever a date, statistic or citation matters, it needs checking.

question: A nurse spots an online photo of a smiling person. One earring is large and heavy, but the other is a tiny stud. What is this little flaw most likely to be?
answer: Mismatch sign of AI generation
choices: Mismatch sign of AI generation
Trendy new fashion statement
Defect of an old film camera
Sunlight playing optical tricks
context: AI image generators often produce asymmetric earrings, mismatched eye details, or other small details that don't match across left and right. Real photos of real people typically have matching pairs (or at least intentional mismatch). Asymmetric tiny details are a small but reliable AI-image tell.

question: A scammer copies a boy's voice from a short online clip, then calls his mother pretending to be him. Families have several ways to defend against this. Out of these four options, which is not a safe defense?
answer: Trusting any familiar-sounding voice
choices: Trusting any familiar-sounding voice
Calling the person back directly
Having a family safe word
Asking a question only family knows
context: Trusting any familiar voice on an unexpected call is exactly what scammers want. Familiar-sounding voices can be cloned. The defenses: call back on a known number, use a family safe word, ask a question only the real person would know. Each of these breaks the scammer's reliance on urgency and audio impersonation.

question: A student reads a news story about a fake celebrity ad and meets the word 'deepfake,' which joins 'deep learning' to 'fake.' What is a deepfake best described as?
answer: An AI-altered video of a real person
choices: An AI-altered video of a real person
A real clip with a fake caption
A cartoon drawn by an AI
A clip from a hidden camera
context: A deepfake is a video (or audio) that has been AI-altered to make real people appear to say or do things they didn't. The technology comes from face-swap and voice-clone AI. Deepfakes are real, they're getting better, and they're used in scams, harassment, and political disinformation. Knowing they exist is the first step in not being fooled.

question: A father and daughter dig through ChatGPT's settings and find a privacy switch called 'Improve the model for everyone.' What does turning it off do?
answer: Stops their chats being used for training
choices: Stops their chats being used for training
Deletes every chat they ever had
Hides their chats from their history
Makes the chatbot answer faster
context: In ChatGPT's data controls, turning off 'Improve the model for everyone' means new conversations still appear in the history but are not used to train the models. It only works going forward: anything already used for training stays there.

question: A man told a car dealer's chatbot in December 2023 to agree with anything a customer said. Then he offered $1 for a new Chevy Tahoe, and the bot called it a 'legally binding offer.' Did he get it?
answer: No, the dealer never sold it
choices: No, the dealer never sold it
Yes, for one dollar
Yes, after a court ruled
Only on a ten-year lease
context: Chris Bakke instructed the Chevrolet of Watsonville chatbot, which ran on ChatGPT, to agree with everything and end each reply with a legally binding offer. The car never changed hands, and the bot was reportedly taken down. Tricking a bot into a promise did not get him a Tahoe.

question: A boy gets a note from a friend: oddly polished, flat and generic, with a tidy takeaway line closing every paragraph. He has read plenty of the friend's real notes, and none sound like this. What would he likely suspect?
answer: The friend used a chatbot
choices: The friend used a chatbot
The friend speaks five languages
The friend was born in 1850
The friend writes in Latin only
context: AI-style polish in a 'personal letter' is a red flag — real personal letters tend to be rougher, more idiosyncratic, with stronger voice. A perfectly balanced, em-dash-heavy, 'tapestry of'-phrasing letter probably had AI help. This isn't bad in itself — but it's worth knowing when a 'personal touch' came partly from a chatbot.

question: A girl typing a question into ChatGPT glances at the small line of text OpenAI prints under the box. What does it tell her?
answer: It can make mistakes, so check important info
choices: Every answer was checked by a human expert
Chats are erased after every reply
It cannot answer questions about history
It can make mistakes, so check important info
context: OpenAI's own interface warns that ChatGPT can make mistakes and tells users to check important information. The company that built it is telling its users not to treat it as the final word.

question: A searcher asked Google in May 2024 how to keep cheese from sliding off pizza, and the new AI Overviews offered a tip that came from an old joke post on a forum. What did the tip advise?
answer: Mix glue into the sauce
choices: Freeze the pizza first
Mix glue into the sauce
Use twice the cheese
Bake it upside down
context: Google's head of search, Liz Reid, said the glue tip came from a forum post, and that another answer, about eating rocks, came from satire first published by The Onion. Google added restrictions afterwards. An AI summary can repeat a joke as if it were fact.

question: A movie star complained in May 2024 that 'Sky,' one of ChatGPT's spoken voices, sounded eerily like her own, and OpenAI paused the voice. The company said a different actress had recorded it. Which star objected?
answer: Scarlett Johansson
choices: Jennifer Lawrence
Scarlett Johansson
Margot Robbie
Emma Stone
context: Scarlett Johansson said Sam Altman had asked her to voice ChatGPT and she had declined, so she was shocked to hear a voice so close to hers. OpenAI said Sky came from another professional actress's natural voice, but it paused Sky anyway.

question: A teacher has four jobs to hand out and one basic chatbot, trained only to predict the next word in a sentence. Which is the worst job to give it, with no tools attached?
answer: Multiplying two big numbers
choices: Multiplying two big numbers
Writing a poem about clouds
Drafting an outline for an essay
Brainstorming party ideas
context: Chatbots are bad at arithmetic, especially with large numbers or many steps. They're good at drafting, brainstorming, summarizing, rewording. Match the tool to the task: a calculator for the math, a chatbot for the writing. Or use a chatbot product that has a calculator tool bolted on — when it does, it'll usually tell you.

question: A student gets a message late at night from a friend who says he wants to end his life, and she wonders about asking a chatbot what to do. In the United States, what is the fastest way to reach a trained human crisis counselor?
answer: Call or text 988
choices: Call or text 988
Call or text 411
Call or text 311
Call or text 611
context: The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, launched in July 2022, connects callers and texters with trained crisis counselors 24 hours a day. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911. A chatbot is no substitute for a person who can actually help.

question: A teacher is handed two paragraphs and asked which one a person wrote and which one a chatbot did. She cannot ask how long either took to write; she has only the words on the page. Of these four clues, which is the clearest sign that a chatbot likely wrote a paragraph?
answer: Bland balance and overused phrases
choices: Bland balance and overused phrases
Strong opinions and odd jokes
Typos and inconsistent grammar
Personal stories with specifics
context: AI-generated text tends to be polished, balanced, and full of certain favored phrases. Real human writing has stronger opinions, occasional typos, weirder humor, and concrete personal stories with specifics. Polish + bland balance is not a guaranteed AI tell — but combined with em-dash overuse and stock phrases, it's a strong signal.

question: A 15-year-old girl and her father read OpenAI's terms of use for ChatGPT. She is past the minimum age of 13, but the terms add one more rule for users under 18. What is it?
answer: Permission from a parent or guardian
choices: Permission from a parent or guardian
A teacher's written sign-off
A paid account of her own
A school email address
context: OpenAI's terms say users must be at least 13, or older where a country's law requires it, and that users under 18 need permission from a parent or legal guardian. The rule exists partly because companies collect and keep what users type.

question: Suppose you open TikTok, a video app with over a billion users. Its 'For You' feed picks your next clip automatically, timing each stare, each swipe and each tap. What is that recommendation system mostly built to do?
answer: Keep you watching as long as possible
choices: Keep you watching as long as possible
Show only your friends' videos
Display only educational content
Pick a fully random video clip
context: TikTok's recommendation algorithm is built to maximize engagement, usually measured by watch time and how often you return. It's NOT optimized for accuracy, balance, or your wellbeing. Knowing what it's optimizing for is the first step in deciding what to do about it. The same is true for YouTube, Instagram Reels, and similar feeds.

question: A resident of a Chinese city watches her standing fall under a local AI-driven system that rates people on their online posts, bills and police trouble. Foreign reporters have documented one specific penalty for people on official blacklists. What can they be blocked from buying?
answer: Plane and train tickets
choices: Plane and train tickets
Phones and laptops
Groceries and medicine
Books and newspapers
context: China's social-credit system is a collection of regional and corporate pilots, not one nationwide program, but real and consequential. People on official blacklists, such as the court list of those who fail to carry out a judgment, have been banned from buying plane and high-speed-train tickets. The system uses facial recognition, online tracking and government records. The pattern (AI as enforcement infrastructure for political compliance) is worth recognizing wherever it appears.

question: A commuter walks past a camera in a Chinese subway station. Within seconds an AI tool has her name, and officials use such matches to track who goes where. What did it match her face against?
answer: The national ID-card photos
choices: The national ID-card photos
Her social-media photos
Her phone's face scan
The station's ticket logs
context: Facial-recognition cameras are widespread in many Chinese cities and can identify people walking past in real time by matching them against the photos on the national identity-card database. The technology is used for many things, from finding lost children to tracking dissidents. The same technology exists in Western cities, often less integrated but expanding. The pattern of camera, recognition and database is what to watch.

question: A detective runs a face from surveillance footage through facial recognition AI, and it returns a match from a mugshot database. The detective now has a name to work with, but the software is not perfect. What is one known risk of this tech?
answer: Wrong identifications leading to arrests
choices: Wrong identifications leading to arrests
Slowing cases down with paperwork
Overheating the police computers
Alerting suspects that they're watched
context: Facial-recognition systems have higher error rates on certain demographics. Several US wrongful-arrest cases (Robert Williams in Detroit, 2020 was widely covered) traced back to bad facial-recognition matches. Some US cities have banned police use of the tech; others use it freely. The question of when and how to use it is an active policy debate.

question: A detective searches Clearview AI's face database, which his department pays for, billions of photos gathered without asking permission from the people whose faces the company collected. Where did all those pictures come from?
answer: Scraping public social-media photos
choices: Scraping public social-media photos
Buying passport photo records
Copying police mugshot files
Filming people on city streets
context: Clearview AI scraped billions of photos from public social-media pages to build a face-recognition database — without users' consent. The company sold the service mainly to law enforcement. Several countries (Canada, France, Italy, UK) have ordered Clearview to delete data on their citizens. The case shows what 'public' photos can be used for once scraping AI is cheap.

question: A girl mentions new shoes to a friend, and the next day an advertisement for those exact shoes shows up on her phone. Companies pay to reach people who match certain patterns of searches, clicks and browsing. What technology drives that?
answer: AI-driven ad targeting
choices: AI-driven ad targeting
Pure random coincidence
Staff picking ads by hand
A virus on her phone
context: Ad targeting uses AI to match ads to people based on their browsing history, search queries, app usage, demographic data, and 'lookalike' modeling. The matches can feel uncannily accurate; the technology isn't reading your mind, it's pattern-matching against your behavior. Knowing how it works is the first step in noticing when it's hunting you.

question: A girl logs in to the free Chromebook her public school handed out, on a school Google or Microsoft account. The school has installed AI software from a company like Gaggle or GoGuardian that quietly watches every chat, email and search she types there, and reports go to school administrators. What is this kind of AI tool called?
answer: Student surveillance software
choices: Student surveillance software
School cafeteria software
Math homework software
Library book software
context: Several companies (Gaggle, GoGuardian, Bark) sell AI software to schools that scans student communications on school accounts for 'concerning content.' The companies say it helps prevent harm. Critics argue it normalizes surveillance, generates false positives, and chills student expression. The pattern (AI watching young people's communications) is worth being aware of, whatever you conclude about it.

question: A woman joins a website's subscription with one big glowing button. To cancel she meets six menus, a hidden link and a phone call during business hours. The designers built it that way on purpose. What is such a setup called?
answer: Dark patterns in user design
choices: Dark patterns in user design
Responsive web design
Skeuomorphic design
Accessibility-first design
context: 'Dark patterns' are interface designs built to push users toward actions that benefit the company at their expense: hidden cancel buttons, pre-checked boxes, confusing wording. AI now tunes many of these patterns at scale, testing what works on which users. Naming them is the first step in not falling for them.

question: A woman's post disappears from a social media platform, and another picks up a warning label. An AI did it, and it looks as if the software decided on its own. Where do those moderation choices really come from?
answer: Decisions made by humans behind the AI
choices: Decisions made by humans behind the AI
Pure mathematical objectivity
The software's own judgment
Random chance in the code
context: AI moderation tools are trained on examples humans chose. The choices about what counts as misinformation, hate speech, or violations reflect the judgments of the humans doing the labeling — sometimes well-meaning, sometimes ideological. There's no value-free moderation algorithm; what looks like 'just the algorithm' is always the algorithm trained on human choices.

question: A user asked Google's Gemini for German soldiers of 1943 in February 2024 and got pictures of Black and Asian people in Nazi uniforms. It drew the Founding Fathers as a diverse cast too. Sundar Pichai apologized. What did Google do about the tool?
answer: Paused its pictures of people
choices: Paused its pictures of people
Added a warning to each image
Made it a paid-only feature
Limited it to adult accounts
context: Google's Gemini image generator had been tuned to show a range of people, and the tuning was applied even to historical prompts where it did not fit. Sundar Pichai called some of the responses completely unacceptable, and Google paused Gemini's generation of images of people while it worked on a fix. The episode illustrates that 'alignment' choices are choices; they reflect somebody's values.

question: Netflix engineers wrote in 2015 that a typical member scrolling for something to watch gives up if nothing catches the eye. About how long did they say a member browses before losing interest?
answer: About 60 to 90 seconds
choices: About 60 to 90 seconds
About 60 to 90 minutes
About two full hours
About a whole day
context: Netflix's Carlos Gomez-Uribe and Neil Hunt wrote that a member typically loses interest after perhaps 60 to 90 seconds of choosing, having looked at 10 to 20 titles. That is why the home screen is ranked so carefully: the system has seconds to hook you.

question: Pollsters at the Pew Research Center asked Americans in 2024 where they get their news. Roughly what share of US adults said they at least sometimes get news from social media?
answer: About half
choices: Almost none
About half
About a tenth
About nine in ten
context: Pew found that 54% of US adults at least sometimes got news from social media in 2024, and about the same in 2025. When a feed is a news source, its ranking choices shape what half the country hears about.

question: Suppose you open an app just to check one thing. Ten minutes later you are still there, because a new post keeps appearing right at the bottom of the page. There is no last page and no stopping point. What is that design called?
answer: An infinite scroll engagement loop
choices: An infinite scroll engagement loop
Just a coincidence of timing
A feature against your wishes
Random chance from outer space
context: Infinite scroll, autoplay, and notification-loop designs are deliberate engineering choices. They keep you in the app. AI behind them learns which combinations work best on which users. Noticing the loop is the first step in stepping out of it. Some phones now offer screen-time controls that can interrupt the loops — but the underlying design is built to be hard to leave.

question: A police commander in a US city sends a shift where an AI tool says crime is most likely to happen. The tool was trained on historical policing records. If certain neighborhoods were policed hard before, the tool sends even more patrols there. What is a real concern with this system?
answer: Bias from past arrest data
choices: Bias from past arrest data
Sleepy patrol officers only
Too many traffic cones in town
AI eating police donuts
context: Predictive policing systems are typically trained on past arrest data. If past policing was biased toward certain neighborhoods, the AI learns to send more police there, which produces more arrests, which trains the AI to focus there more. The loop amplifies existing biases. Some cities (Stop LAPD Spying coalition is one example) have organized against these systems.

question: A man goes back to a video on masks during the COVID pandemic and finds the platform took it down under its content rules. Later, some such clips turned out to have been correct. What lesson is worth remembering about removed content?
answer: Removed isn't the same as false
choices: Removed isn't the same as false
Removed always means false
Removed means it broke a law
Removed means everyone agrees now
context: Platforms remove content for many reasons — policy violation, government request, internal decision, advertiser pressure. 'Removed' doesn't mean 'proven false' in the scientific sense; it means the platform decided to take it down. Sometimes the decision ages well, sometimes it doesn't. Treating 'this was banned' as evidence about truth is a mistake either way.

question: A woman unlocks her phone with her face, and a traveler passes through an airport the same way. Face-scanning AI can match a photo of a stranger against millions of pictures in seconds, and phones and airports are not the only places it's used. Where else has it shown up?
answer: Several US police investigations
choices: Several US police investigations
Every US polling station
Every US driving test
All US cash machines
context: Several US police departments have used facial recognition to identify suspects in investigations. Some use is uncontroversial (matching a suspect to a known person of interest); some has led to wrongful arrests when the match was wrong. A handful of US cities have banned police use. The debate about when and how to deploy the technology is ongoing.

question: Suppose you open TikTok, and within an hour the app somehow already knows which videos you like. It never asked you to fill out a survey, and it does not even need you to tap 'like.' Why does the algorithm learn what you like so fast?
answer: It learns from many small signals
choices: It learns from many small signals
It reads your secret diary
It interviews your old friends
It checks your school grades
context: TikTok's For You algorithm learns from watch time per video, rewatches, scroll-past behavior, shares, and pauses — many small signals every minute you scroll. Compared to a 'like button' alone, this gives the AI vastly more data, vastly faster. The speed of learning is a feature for the platform and a hazard for the user, depending on what's being learned.

question: A boss at a large company opens an AI program that watches workers at their desks all day. It keeps track of what they type, where they click, how long they linger on each screen, and even whether their eyes are on the monitor. Some workers do not know it is running. What is this kind of program called?
answer: Workplace surveillance software
choices: Workplace surveillance software
Workplace coffee machinery
Workplace lunchtime services
Workplace party planners
context: AI-powered workplace surveillance (Microsoft Productivity Score, Hubstaff, and others) tracks employee activity in detail. The trend grew during remote-work years. Critics argue it pressures employees to look busy rather than be productive; defenders say it helps managers identify problems. Knowing about it matters when choosing employers and when negotiating terms.

question: A recruiter feeds a week's applications into an AI that ranks them and shows her the top picks. It learned from years of old hiring records. What do critics warn it does?
answer: Inherits biases from training data
choices: Inherits biases from training data
Removes all bias from hiring
Ranks people at random
Favors the earliest applicants
context: AI applicant screening (HireVue, Pymetrics, and others) is trained on past hiring data. If past hiring favored certain backgrounds, the AI learns to favor them too. Amazon famously scrapped one such system in 2018 after it was found to penalize résumés from women. The technology can be reformed, but knowing how it works affects how applicants prepare.

question: A lonely man signs up for Tinder, which promises to help him find love. The company earns its money while he is still swiping. Critics say this shapes what the AI is tuned to do. What do they say dating apps are usually optimized for?
answer: Keeping users on the app
choices: Keeping users on the app
Finding lifelong partners fast
Reducing the divorce rate
Helping users delete the app
context: Dating apps are usually optimized for engagement and subscription retention — which means keeping users on the platform. A user who finds a lasting partner and leaves stops paying. The business model and the user's stated goal are partly aligned (some matches are needed to keep users hopeful) and partly opposed (long-term success means losing the user). Worth knowing.

question: A bettor on DraftKings gets a free-bet offer at a moment picked by the app's AI, which studies how and when he bets. Critics say the AI is not there to protect users. What do they say it aims to do?
answer: Maximize how much users bet
choices: Maximize how much users bet
Stop users losing money
Spot problem gamblers
Keep bets small
context: Critics of online betting apps say their AI is tuned to raise total bets: personalised promotions, offers to win back users who drift away, and testing what works on which behaviour. The companies describe the same tools as personalisation and point to their responsible-gambling limits. Knowing what an app is optimised for helps explain why it is so sticky.

question: A loan officer scores a mortgage with an AI trained on the bank's old files, including years when certain neighborhoods were unfairly refused. What do critics warn it does?
answer: Inherits patterns of past discrimination
choices: Inherits patterns of past discrimination
Erases the bank's old bias
Approves every loan it sees
Judges each case on merit
context: Lending AI is trained on past lending decisions. If past lending was biased against certain neighborhoods or groups, the AI learns those patterns and continues them — sometimes called 'algorithmic redlining.' The AI doesn't 'intend' to discriminate, but it inherits the patterns in its training data. Regulations have started to address this, with mixed effectiveness.

question: A programmer downloads an open AI model from Meta, runs it and inspects it on her own machine. OpenAI, Google and Anthropic control the strongest chatbots and keep the inner workings secret. What are open models like Meta's and France's Mistral pushing back against?
answer: A small number of closed-model companies
choices: A small number of closed-model companies
Governments trying to ban all AI
Hackers who misuse AI chatbots
Chip makers' rising prices
context: If only a few large companies control AI models, those companies hold huge influence over what AI is allowed to do, who can build with it, and what gets censored. Open-source models (Llama from Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek) let anyone run AI on a personal computer with no central gatekeeper. This isn't unconditionally good — but it's a real countervailing force to concentration.

question: Suppose you hear your phone buzz at nine in the evening. An app you barely opened this week has picked a hook: 'Someone liked your post.' The message did not appear by accident. What is that kind of notification designed to do?
answer: Pull you back to the app
choices: Pull you back to the app
Keep you informed of news
Check your account is safe
Save your phone's battery
context: Notifications are tuned by AI to be exactly attention-grabbing enough to pull you back into the app. They aren't designed to inform — they're designed to interrupt and return. Most phones now let you turn off non-essential notifications. The simplest defense is to default-off and re-enable only when you genuinely want the alert.

question: A student in China posts a video online. AI tools inside China's Great Firewall scan it in real time, as they scan posts and searches. What is this AI system mainly used to do?
answer: Filter and block certain content
choices: Filter and block certain content
Speed up slow video uploads
Translate posts for readers
Catch spam and viruses
context: China's 'Great Firewall' uses AI-augmented systems to block certain websites, filter messages on Chinese platforms, and detect attempts to bypass the filters. The technology is mature and constantly evolving. Other countries (Russia, Iran, parts of the Middle East) operate similar systems at different scales. Recognizing that AI can serve as censorship infrastructure is part of being literate about its uses.

question: Suppose you catch yourself back on TikTok or Instagram for the fifth visit today, without ever meaning to open either one. The AI-driven feed is built to hold you there. Before buying any fancy blocker app or a new phone, what is the simplest first defense a kid can use?
answer: Set time limits or turn off the app
choices: Set time limits or turn off the app
Buy yourself a faster phone
Get a louder pair of headphones
Subscribe to extra paid features
context: Recognizing that you've been pulled in is the first step. Most phones let you set daily time limits per app. Turning off notifications for the worst offenders is another simple step. Some people delete apps and use them only via the browser, which is less optimized. The defense is choosing deliberately rather than being chosen for.

question: A Chinese boy under 14 opens Douyin, the separate Chinese version of TikTok run by its owner, ByteDance. Douyin's youth mode began limiting users his age in 2021. How much time on the app does it allow him each day?
answer: 40 minutes
choices: 15 minutes
40 minutes
2 hours
3 hours
context: Reuters reported that Douyin's youth mode lets under-14s use the app for at most 40 minutes a day, only between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m., with more educational content. The same company runs very different feeds for children in China and elsewhere.

question: A Facebook user tapped the angry face on a post, and the feed counted that emoji reaction as worth more than a plain like. Internal documents reported in 2021 showed the formula had worked that way from 2017. How many likes was one reaction worth?
answer: Five
choices: Zero
Two
Five
Ten
context: The Washington Post reported that Facebook's ranking formula weighted reactions such as angry five times as heavily as a like, and that internal researchers linked posts drawing angry reactions to misinformation and low-quality news. Whatever the formula rewards, the feed fills up with.

question: Suppose you stay longer on a free app like TikTok, and it earns more from advertisers. Critics say that business model shapes every design choice. What do the critics say such an app is?
answer: Built to be hard to leave
choices: Built to be hard to leave
Built to charge your phone
Built to filter your spam
Built to mail you postcards
context: Critics of the attention business say apps paid by advertising are designed to be hard to leave: autoplay, infinite scroll, push notifications, streaks and personalised recommendations all keep you inside. The companies call the same features convenience. Knowing the business model is the first step in deciding how much of your attention to give.

question: A user tried OpenAI's o1 in September 2024, the new model trained to write out a long chain of reasoning before its final answer. The company reported one simple way to make it do better on hard problems. What was that way?
answer: Letting it spend more time thinking first
choices: Giving it less time, so it can't overthink
Asking for a one-word answer only
Letting it spend more time thinking first
Turning off its long-term memory
context: OpenAI said o1's performance kept improving with more training and with more time spent thinking at answer time. Reasoning models are still next-word predictors; they generate many hidden steps before the visible reply, which costs more computing power.

question: Sam Altman took a question at an MIT event in April 2023: had training GPT-4 cost about $100 million? Training a frontier model means running thousands of chips for months on end. What was his reply?
answer: That it cost more than that
choices: That it cost far less than that
That it cost more than that
That the figure was about right
That it cost under $10 million
context: Altman answered that it was more than that, without giving a figure. Training is the huge one-time cost of building a model, which is one reason only a handful of companies can make the biggest ones.

question: Researchers asked GPT-4 'Who is Tom Cruise's mother?' in 2023, and it answered Mary Lee Pfeiffer about 79% of the time. Then they asked the same fact backwards: 'Who is Mary Lee Pfeiffer's son?' How did it do?
answer: Far worse, about a third of the time
choices: Perfectly, every single time
Just as well, 79% again
Better, nearly 99% of the time
Far worse, about a third of the time
context: Lukas Berglund, Owain Evans and colleagues called this the reversal curse: a model that learned 'A is B' does not automatically learn 'B is A.' GPT-4 got the backwards question right only 33% of the time. Its knowledge is patterns of text, often stored in one direction.

question: A boy tells a friend that ChatGPT solves a word problem the way a math teacher does, checking each step against rules. Mechanically the chatbot works another way, and whether that counts as reasoning is debated. What is the chatbot doing when its answer looks like step-by-step working?
answer: Predicting, token by token, how worked solutions usually read
choices: Predicting, token by token, how worked solutions usually read
Running a formal proof that checks every single step
Calling a logic engine its makers built in for math
Copying a stored solution to the same problem
context: Modern LLMs can write step-by-step replies because they learned from training text how worked solutions read, and they produce them one token at a time. Researchers argue about whether this counts as reasoning; what is not in doubt is that the steps can look right while the conclusion is wrong, which is why checking matters, especially in math and law.

question: A student spots the word 'large' in Large Language Model, the kind of program behind ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, and asks what it means. The word is not about how big the company is, or how much of the screen the chat window fills. What does 'large' mean here?
answer: The model has a huge number of internal numbers (parameters) and is trained on a huge amount of text
choices: The model has a huge number of internal numbers (parameters) and is trained on a huge amount of text
The model can handle more languages than any program before it, over a hundred of them at once
The data center where it runs covers more floor space than any other building in the area
The reply messages are larger than what older chatbots could write before this generation
context: 'Large' in Large Language Model refers to two things scaled up: parameters (the model's adjustable internal numbers, counted in billions) and training data (the text it learned from, measured in trillions of tokens). The combination is what made modern LLMs work as well as they do compared to predecessors from a decade ago.

question: Apple researchers gave chatbots a school math problem in 2024 about Oliver picking kiwis, plus one useless sentence: five of Sunday's kiwis were a bit smaller than average. Size changes nothing about the count. What did models like o1-mini do?
answer: Subtracted the five small kiwis from the total
choices: Subtracted the five small kiwis from the total
Refused to answer a question about fruit
Added five extra kiwis to the total
Asked how big an average kiwi is first
context: In the GSM-Symbolic study by Iman Mirzadeh and colleagues, adding one clause that seems relevant but isn't cut accuracy by up to 65%. Models often turn any number in a problem into a sum without grasping what it means.

question: An engineer prepares the training text for a frontier language model like GPT-4 or Claude. Which rough size is in the right ballpark for the training data of a top model today?
answer: Trillions of words drawn from books, websites, code, and other sources
choices: Trillions of words drawn from books, websites, code, and other sources
About a billion words drawn from a few thousand popular books
Roughly one full set of any encyclopedia, copied page by page, plus a small dictionary
Only the most recent year of news articles, with everything older deliberately removed
context: Frontier LLMs are trained on huge text corpora — typically trillions of tokens, drawn from web pages (Common Crawl is a common source), books, code repositories, and other written material. The scale is part of why the results work as well as they do, and it is also why the data the model saw is impossible for any one human to audit by hand.

question: Andrey Markov sat with Pushkin's verse novel Eugene Onegin in 1913 and tallied its first 20,000 letters by hand, sorting each one into vowel or consonant. What did he use the counts to show?
answer: That each letter's odds depend on the letter just before it
choices: That vowels and consonants come in equal numbers
That Russian uses more vowels than any other language
That poems use letters at random, with no pattern at all
That each letter's odds depend on the letter just before it
context: Markov counted how often a vowel followed a vowel or a consonant and found the letters tended to alternate, so the chance of the next letter depended on the one before. Chains of what-comes-next probabilities now carry his name; they are a distant ancestor of next-word prediction.

question: A student reads in an AI textbook that neural nets are 'brain-inspired,' as if the software were a working copy of the thing between her ears. The comparison is a loose one, not a literal one. Why is the 'brain' description only loose?
answer: Real neurons are far more complex than the simple math units in a neural network
choices: Real neurons are far more complex than the simple math units in a neural network
Neural networks work far slower than brains, so they cannot copy what neurons do
Neural networks were copied from a scan of one brain, so they fit only that person
Brains learn only in childhood, while neural networks keep learning all their lives
context: The name 'neural network' comes from a 1940s idea of loosely modeling a brain neuron with a small math unit. Real neurons are chemically and electrically far more complex — and biological brains do not have neat layers or a backpropagation algorithm. The inspiration is real; the literal correspondence is not.

question: A girl hears a newsreader say that a chatbot uses 'deep learning.' It sounds mysterious, as if the computer had deep feelings or were hunting for a deeper meaning inside her words. The word 'deep' points at one plain engineering choice. What does 'deep' refer to?
answer: Many layers stacked between input and output, instead of just one or two
choices: Many layers stacked between input and output, instead of just one or two
Deep involvement of human reviewers reading every output the model ever produces
Huge amounts of training data poured in, far more than older programs used
Long training runs lasting weeks instead of the few hours older models took
context: A 'deep' network has many layers — that is all the adjective means. Shallow networks have one or two. Modern frontier models can have dozens or hundreds. The depth (combined with scale and good training tricks) is what powers modern AI. Deep learning is just neural networks with more layers.

question: A company's engineers finish building a frontier chatbot like GPT-4 at a cost somewhere between tens and hundreds of millions of dollars in electricity, computer chips and engineering time. Then the first person types a question and gets a response. What is true of that giant bill from then on?
answer: It is paid one time; afterwards each user reply costs only a small inference cost on top
choices: It is paid one time; afterwards each user reply costs only a small inference cost on top
It is paid daily; the model has to be fully retrained from scratch at the end of every day
It is paid each time a user logs in; the model trains fresh for each new account that opens
It is paid by users; every user pays a share of the original training bill before getting a reply
context: Training a frontier LLM is a one-time (or sometimes a few-times) capital cost. Once the weights are set, inference — running the trained model to answer questions — is cheap per request. This is why frontier AI is so capital-heavy upfront, and why open weights matter: once weights are released, anyone can run inference cheaply.

question: A boy types a message into ChatGPT, hits enter, and about two seconds later a reply appears. Engineers had poured billions of words through the model in an earlier stage, adjusting its internal numbers, called weights, until it learned the patterns. During those two seconds it learns nothing new. What is that second stage, when real users get their replies, called?
answer: Inference — running the already-trained model forward to produce the reply
choices: Inference — running the already-trained model forward to produce the reply
Training — adjusting weights based on the new message before the reply can be made
Compiling — turning the user's words into a special programming language for the model
Backups — saving the conversation in case the model needs to learn from it tomorrow
context: Inference is the technical word for using a trained model. Each chat reply you get is an inference call. It is fast (often seconds) and uses far less compute than training. Most of the cost of running a chatbot at scale is inference — millions of users making millions of inference calls.

question: Aleksandar Petrov and his Oxford colleagues took the same passage in 2023, translated into many languages, and fed it through the tokenizers that cut text into pieces for language models. What did they find?
answer: Some languages needed up to 15 times as many tokens
choices: Every language needed exactly the same number
Some languages needed up to 15 times as many tokens
English needed the most tokens of any language
Only languages written in Latin letters worked
context: Petrov and colleagues found the same text can take up to 15 times as many tokens in one language as in another, even with tokenizers built for many languages. Speakers of those languages pay more per message, wait longer, and fit less into the model's context.

question: A writer checks how ChatGPT cuts her message into 'tokens,' the small chunks of text it reads, and sees a long word like 'unbelievable' split into several. Researchers have measured this across huge amounts of English writing, and the ratio holds steady. Roughly how many English words equal one token?
answer: Slightly less than one — about three-quarters of an English word per token, on average
choices: Slightly less than one — about three-quarters of an English word per token, on average
Exactly twenty — one token covers a whole standard paragraph of English text in practice
Exactly one letter — each letter is one token regardless of where it sits in the word
Exactly one full sentence — each token is one complete subject-verb-object sentence
context: Rule of thumb: in English, 1 token is roughly 0.75 of a word (or about 4 characters). The relationship varies by word. 'Cat' is one token. 'Antidisestablishmentarianism' might be six or more. Most punctuation is its own token. Non-English languages often use more tokens per word.

question: A student keeps one chat with ChatGPT running until it outgrows the bounded chunk of conversation the chatbot can 'see' at once. That chunk works like a sliding rectangle over the running transcript. What slips out of view first as the chat keeps growing?
answer: The oldest messages — they leave the window first as new ones come in at the other end
choices: The oldest messages — they leave the window first as new ones come in at the other end
The most recent messages — the model deliberately forgets the latest ones to save room
Nothing ever slips out — the window simply grows along with the conversation forever
Random messages from the middle — the model drops one at random whenever it needs room
context: When the chat outgrows the window, the model can only see the most recent tokens that fit. The oldest messages drop out (first-in-first-out). Some chatbot systems compensate by summarizing or storing earlier content elsewhere; vanilla LLMs just lose the early material.

question: Astronomers spotted an error in a Google ad for its Bard chatbot in February 2023. It claimed the James Webb Space Telescope took the very first pictures of a planet outside our solar system, when the first such image came in 2004, from another telescope. What happened to Google's parent company that week?
answer: Its shares fell, wiping about $100 billion off its value
choices: Its shares fell, wiping about $100 billion off its value
Its shares rose because the mistake went viral
Its shares barely moved at all
Its shares dipped, wiping about $1 billion off its value
context: Alphabet's stock dropped about 8% after Reuters reported the error, erasing roughly $100 billion in market value. NASA notes that the first image of a planet outside our solar system came from the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope in 2004. Google said the episode showed the need for rigorous testing.

question: Meta's researchers released Galactica in November 2022, two weeks before ChatGPT appeared. The model was trained on 48 million papers, textbooks and lecture notes and pitched as able to write science articles. Users quickly got it to produce confident fake research. How long did the public demo last?
answer: About three days
choices: About three days
About three weeks
About three months
About three years
context: Users showed Galactica inventing papers, sometimes credited to real authors, and wiki-style articles on things like the benefits of eating crushed glass. Meta paused the demo after about three days. Sounding scientific is not the same as being true.

question: Stanford researchers Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew watched professional fact-checkers, history professors and Stanford students judge unfamiliar websites. The fact-checkers did best, thanks to one habit the others skipped. What did the fact-checkers do?
answer: Left the site to see what other sources said about it
choices: Left the site to see what other sources said about it
Read the site's About page closely before judging
Trusted any site with a .org address and a logo
Counted the footnotes listed at the end of the page
context: The researchers called it lateral reading: the fact-checkers opened new tabs to find out who was behind a site, while historians and students stayed on the page and were fooled by professional logos, scholarly-looking references and nonprofit addresses. The same move works on a chatbot's claim.

question: Anthropic's researchers traced what went on inside Claude in 2025 as it added 36 and 59. One path made a rough estimate while another worked out the last digit exactly. Then they asked Claude how it had done the sum. What did it say?
answer: That it carried the 1, the way schools teach
choices: That it carried the 1, the way schools teach
That it had looked the answer up online
That it had used a calculator tool
That it had asked another model for help
context: Anthropic's researchers found that Claude's account described the standard carry-the-one method, which did not match the parallel paths they saw inside it. A model learns to explain math by copying human explanations, so its story about its own working may not be true.

question: A librarian puts Google's search box beside ChatGPT's chat box. Both are rectangles for a typed question, yet ChatGPT is a Large Language Model (LLM), and underneath they do completely different jobs. What is the key difference?
answer: A search engine finds existing web pages; an LLM produces new text by predicting tokens
choices: A search engine finds existing web pages; an LLM produces new text by predicting tokens
A search engine reads only page titles; an LLM reads the full text of every web page live
A search engine costs money for every query; a chatbot is always free in every country today
A search engine is run by people; an LLM is run by software that looks things up for itself
context: A search engine indexes the web and returns existing pages. An LLM generates new text. Different mechanisms, different strengths. Use search for 'find me this real page' and 'what's currently happening.' Use chatbots for drafting, summarizing pasted text, asking explanatory questions on settled topics, and brainstorming.

question: A girl opens her inbox and finds that a small AI program has already tagged every new message 'spam' or 'not spam,' sorting a whole morning's mail in a blink. What kind of model is doing this?
answer: A discriminative classifier — it labels existing email as belonging to one of two categories
choices: A discriminative classifier — it labels existing email as belonging to one of two categories
A generative model — it writes its own version of each message and checks it against the real one
An unsupervised model — it sorts emails into clusters without ever being shown a single label
Reinforcement learning — the filter is being rewarded for catching each spam message it labels
context: Spam filtering is a classic discriminative task. The model takes an email and outputs a label (spam, not spam, or sometimes finer categories). It does not write new content. Spam filters were one of the early commercial wins for ML — a quiet but very useful application that ran for years before the generative-AI boom.

question: Alan Turing wrote a paper in 1950 on whether machines can think, and sent it not to a science journal but to one devoted to the study of mind. What was the paper's title?
answer: 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' — published in the philosophy journal Mind
choices: 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' — published in the philosophy journal Mind
'On Thinking Machines' — published in the journal of the Royal Society in London
'The Imitation Game' — a popular pamphlet distributed by the British government in 1950
'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' — published at Bell Labs in 1948 by Shannon
context: Turing's paper was titled 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' and appeared in Mind, a philosophy journal. The choice of venue is interesting — a working mathematician publishing a careful philosophical argument. The paper proposed the imitation game, anticipated several objections, and gave thoughtful responses. It is still readable today and remains a starting point for thinking about machine intelligence.

question: Alan Turing served his country before his paper on thinking machines. The government sent him to a top-secret operation at a country estate north of London, where mathematicians raced to decipher enemy messages. His work there is thought to have shortened the fight against Nazi Germany by months or years. What was he working on?
answer: Breaking the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during World War II
choices: Breaking the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during World War II
Designing the first American rocket engine for the V-2 weapons program in California
Translating intercepted radio broadcasts at the British embassy in Stockholm during 1942
Writing speeches for Winston Churchill at the prime minister's wartime offices in London
context: Turing's wartime work at Bletchley Park helped break Enigma — the German military's main cipher system. The Bombe machine he co-designed automated parts of the codebreaking process. Estimates suggest the work shortened the war in Europe by months or years and saved many lives. The work was classified for decades; Turing's role was not widely known until the 1970s.

question: A news story says a chatbot has passed the imitation game, in which a judge types to a hidden person and a hidden machine. What evidence does that rest on?
answer: Human judges could not reliably tell the chatbot's writing from a real person's in conversation
choices: Human judges could not reliably tell the chatbot's writing from a real person's in conversation
The chatbot won a chess tournament against ten human players in a row at one event
The chatbot earned a passing grade on a standardized school math examination test
The chatbot received a degree from a respected university for its public writing samples
context: The classic Turing test is about conversation: can a hidden machine fool a human judge into thinking it is also human? Modern LLMs do often pass casual versions of this test. Turing himself thought the test would be passed by the year 2000; the actual date is debatable but probably around the early 2020s for everyday conversation. Note: passing the test isn't proof of consciousness — it's proof of conversational imitation.

question: Alan Turing imagined a device of paper tape and simple rules before AI was even a phrase. Why is he called a founder of computer science?
answer: His earlier 1936 work on the 'Turing machine' is one of the foundations of modern computing
choices: His earlier 1936 work on the 'Turing machine' is one of the foundations of modern computing
He founded the world's first computer company in Cambridge with profits from his book sales
He invented the first commercial computer language in 1959 with his colleagues in London
He patented the integrated circuit in 1957, becoming the inventor of the modern computer chip
context: Turing's 1936 paper 'On Computable Numbers' described what we now call a Turing machine — a simple theoretical device that could compute anything a modern computer can. This abstract model became the foundation for computer science. Layered with his wartime codebreaking and the 1950 imitation game, Turing's contributions span both computing and AI.

question: Claude Shannon, an engineer at Bell Labs, joined the summer meeting at Dartmouth College in 1956 that launched a new field. He is far more famous for a landmark paper he wrote eight years earlier, in 1948, which opened up a whole new branch of science. What was that earlier landmark work?
answer: His 1948 paper founded information theory, including the concept of the 'bit' as a unit
choices: His 1948 paper founded information theory, including the concept of the 'bit' as a unit
His 1948 paper introduced the first commercially successful computer language ever made
His 1948 paper announced the first transistor at Bell Labs to the wider public scientific world
His 1948 paper was the first to describe the design of a working artificial neural network
context: Claude Shannon's 1948 paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' founded information theory. It introduced the bit (binary digit) as a unit of information, defined channel capacity, and gave us tools that underlie modern digital communication, compression, and error correction. Shannon, working at Bell Labs, was already a legend by 1956 when he co-organized the Dartmouth meeting.

question: Marvin Minsky and his old Dartmouth colleague, another founding name of the field, set up a research group at a well-known university. It grew into one of the most influential AI centers in the world. A few years earlier Minsky had been one of the four researchers who organized the 1956 Dartmouth summer workshop. Which famous lab did he help found?
answer: The MIT AI Lab, which he co-founded with John McCarthy in 1959
choices: The MIT AI Lab, which he co-founded with John McCarthy in 1959
The Stanford AI Lab, which became the West Coast hub for early AI research in the 1960s
The IBM Watson Research Center, which would later build the Jeopardy-winning system
The Bell Labs AI Lab, the early industrial leader through the 1960s for AI research
context: Marvin Minsky co-founded the MIT AI Lab with John McCarthy in 1959. McCarthy then left for Stanford in 1962 and founded the Stanford AI Lab. The two labs were the East Coast and West Coast hubs of US AI research for decades. Minsky stayed at MIT for his whole career and was an influential thinker — sometimes a skeptic of the very neural-network methods that would later dominate.

question: John McCarthy, a young American mathematician, was organizing a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in 1956 on machines that could think when he coined a fresh label for the subject, on purpose. Most work in that area was lumped under an older term, popularized in the 1940s, that mixed engineering, biology and control theory together. Why did McCarthy pick a new term?
answer: To set the new work apart from Norbert Wiener's older cybernetics tradition
choices: To set the new work apart from Norbert Wiener's older cybernetics tradition
To honour Alan Turing, whose 1950 paper had used that exact phrase as its title
To match the name of a new course he had begun teaching at Dartmouth that year
To follow a British research group that already used the name for its own work
context: McCarthy later explained that he wanted to mark the new field as different from Wiener's cybernetics — the earlier postwar movement that studied feedback systems and intelligence in animals and machines together. By coining 'artificial intelligence,' McCarthy carved out a research program focused specifically on machines that perform tasks requiring intelligence. The new term stuck — and seventy years later, almost everyone in the field uses it.

question: Four researchers, John McCarthy among them, wrote a short funding proposal in 1955 for a summer workshop at Dartmouth College the following year. Their optimism was striking, and the proposal is now famous for how boldly it stated its own aim. What was the stated goal for the summer?
answer: To make a significant advance in machine intelligence over two months of summer work
choices: To make a significant advance in machine intelligence over two months of summer work
To finish a complete artificial brain by the end of the summer for the US Air Force
To build a program that could pass Turing's imitation game before the autumn began
To agree a ten-year research plan on machine intelligence for the government
context: The Dartmouth proposal — read with hindsight — was wildly optimistic. The organizers thought significant progress could be made over a single summer if a small group of bright researchers worked together. Seventy years later, the deeper problems they identified are still being worked on. The optimism wasn't wrong about the importance of the questions — only about how soon they could be solved.

question: John McCarthy and three colleagues ran the workshop they had been planning at Dartmouth College in the summer of 1956. It did not solve intelligence, and it did not build a thinking machine. Historians looking back still call the meeting a turning point in the history of computing. What did the workshop do that matters the most?
answer: It launched AI as a named, organized research field that has lasted 70 years
choices: It launched AI as a named, organized research field that has lasted 70 years
It built the first working chatbot, shown off at the end of the eight-week meeting
It produced the first programming language for AI, written by the group that summer
It set up a joint lab at Dartmouth where the group kept working for the next decade
context: Dartmouth 1956 produced no big technical results that summer. Its real legacy was launching AI as an organized research field with a name, a community and an ambition. The participants went on to build labs at MIT, Stanford, Carnegie Mellon and IBM that led the field for decades, and much of AI's later history, through booms and 'AI winters' alike, runs back through those labs to that summer.

question: John McCarthy invented a whole new programming language in 1958, designed to operate on chains of items rather than the numeric arrays of earlier languages. It became the language of choice for AI labs for decades, and languages descended from it are still used today. What was the language called?
answer: LISP — designed for symbolic computation and built around lists of expressions
choices: LISP — designed for symbolic computation and built around lists of expressions
BASIC — invented for teaching, with simple line-numbered statements throughout
COBOL — designed for business data processing on early commercial computers
Pascal — built for teaching structured programming to college students worldwide
context: LISP — short for List Processing — was designed by McCarthy for symbolic AI work. Its lists-of-lists structure and code-as-data approach made it ideal for writing programs that could examine and modify other programs. LISP dialects (Common Lisp, Scheme, Clojure) are still in use today. Many ideas from LISP — garbage collection, dynamic typing, first-class functions — became standard in later languages.

question: A researcher opens a program written in the language John McCarthy released for AI work, one of the very oldest programming languages still alive. One other language in use today is older, built for solving equations rather than handling symbols. Which language is it?
answer: Fortran, from a team at IBM
choices: Fortran, from a team at IBM
COBOL, from a committee the Pentagon convened
C, from Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs
BASIC, from two Dartmouth professors
context: Fortran (1957) is the oldest high-level programming language still in widespread use. LISP (1958) is the second-oldest. The two were designed for different audiences — Fortran for scientific number-crunching, LISP for symbolic AI work — but both shaped the field. Most languages students learn today inherit ideas from one or both.

question: A student watches her neural network make a guess and get it wrong. Inside its layers sit tiny numbers called weights. Researchers in the 1970s and 1980s refined an algorithm called 'backpropagation' that carries a signal from the mistake backward through the layers, one at a time. In plain words, what does backpropagation do?
answer: It computes how much each weight contributed to the error and nudges it in a helpful direction
choices: It computes how much each weight contributed to the error and nudges it in a helpful direction
It backs the model up to the previous task whenever it makes a mistake during training
It runs the training data backwards through the network to test the model's memory of it
It deletes the layer that was responsible for the worst predictions during this round of work
context: Backpropagation answers the question 'which weight should I change, by how much, to reduce my error?' It does this layer by layer, working from the output backward to the input. Combined with gradient descent, it powers almost all modern neural-network training. The 1986 paper turned backprop from a niche idea into a practical tool — kickstarting the long path that led to today's deep learning.

question: Geoffrey Hinton, sometimes called a 'godfather of AI,' shared the 2018 Turing Award, announced early in 2019, with two other researchers for foundational work on deep neural networks. All three had spent decades pushing the case that such networks would eventually work at scale. One of the two runs Meta's AI lab in New York; the other founded a research institute in Montreal. Who are those two?
answer: Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio — together honored for deep-learning contributions
choices: Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio — together honored for deep-learning contributions
John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky — both already passed away before the Turing Award arrived
Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis — leaders of OpenAI and DeepMind at the time of the prize
Alan Turing and Claude Shannon — both posthumous winners as recognized founders of AI
context: Hinton, LeCun, and Bengio shared the 2018 Turing Award (the 'Nobel of computing') for their work on deep neural networks. The three had championed neural-network research during years when it was unfashionable. The award marked the moment when deep learning's success was widely acknowledged as the foundation of modern AI.

question: A student pitched a neural network to a lab in the 1970s and came away empty-handed: funding had dried up, and most researchers had stopped working on the approach and called it a dead end. What had hurt neural networks' name before the mid 1980s?
answer: Minsky and Papert's 1969 book 'Perceptrons' pointed out limits of single-layer networks
choices: Minsky and Papert's 1969 book 'Perceptrons' pointed out limits of single-layer networks
Turing's 1950 paper had argued that machines could never learn from examples on their own
Early networks needed more electricity than any university lab could afford to pay for
IBM's chess programs had beaten neural networks in every public test of the 1960s
context: Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's 1969 book 'Perceptrons' showed that single-layer networks could not learn certain simple functions (like XOR). The book was technically correct but was widely read as discrediting neural networks overall. Funding dried up — part of the first 'AI winter.' Backpropagation revived the field by showing multi-layer networks could learn things single-layer ones could not.

question: A student comparing the chess computer Deep Blue with the deep-learning programs of today finds a very different machine: it had no big learned neural network of its own. What did Deep Blue mostly rely on instead?
answer: Brute-force search of millions of possible chess positions per second, plus expert chess heuristics
choices: Brute-force search of millions of possible chess positions per second, plus expert chess heuristics
A trained neural network that learned chess from playing itself for one full week of computer time
Reinforcement learning from millions of past games and self-play sessions with grandmasters
A LISP-based expert system that asked human grandmasters for advice in real time as it played
context: Deep Blue was 'good old-fashioned AI' (GOFAI) at its best — brute-force search through possible chess positions, evaluated by handcrafted rules that captured human grandmaster knowledge of chess. No learning, no neural networks. It worked because chess is well-defined: rules are clear, the game tree is finite, and raw computation can be thrown at the problem. The 1997 win was a milestone for specialized AI, not general AI.

question: Garry Kasparov kept returning to one subtle move from the second game of his match against Deep Blue, in interviews and articles for years afterward. He did not take the loss well. What was his recurring complaint about the match?
answer: He suspected IBM had received human help during games, which IBM denied
choices: He suspected IBM had received human help during games, which IBM denied
He insisted that the match clock had been broken from the second game on, in IBM's favor
He said the crowd's noise and the cameras had wrecked his focus in the final game
He claimed a draw had been agreed on his behalf by the referee without his consent
context: Kasparov was upset by one move in particular — a positionally subtle move in game 2 that he thought no chess engine could play. He suspected human intervention. IBM denied it, and later analysis suggested the move could indeed have come from Deep Blue. The match was followed by a long dispute, with Kasparov asking for a rematch IBM declined. The episode set a pattern: humans often look for non-machine explanations when AIs surprise them.

question: Two record-setting human champions went up against Watson, the big AI system from International Business Machines (IBM), on a national American television quiz show in February 2011. Watson had to work through each clue in natural English, puns and wordplay included, and buzz in faster than the human players. It won decisively over three nights. Which quiz show was it?
answer: Jeopardy! — where IBM Watson beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter in a televised match
choices: Jeopardy! — where IBM Watson beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter in a televised match
Wheel of Fortune — where Watson beat a panel of champions in a special two-night event
Family Feud — where Watson outscored every team for a full week of episodes in a row
Who Wants to Be a Millionaire — where Watson reached the top prize using lifeline help
context: IBM Watson played Jeopardy! over three days in February 2011, defeating Ken Jennings (74-game winning streak) and Brad Rutter (highest career winnings) in a special televised match. The challenge wasn't chess-style — Jeopardy! requires understanding plays on words, cultural references, and free-form natural language. Watson's win was an important milestone in machines handling messy human language.

question: Ken Jennings, famous for an earlier 74-game winning streak, played IBM's Watson on an American quiz show in February 2011. On the very last answer of the match he scribbled one extra line under his response. What did the line say?
answer: That he welcomed his new computer overlords
choices: That he welcomed his new computer overlords
That he wanted a rematch with the machine
That he doubted the machine could really think
That he was proud to lose to a fine machine
context: Ken Jennings wrote 'I for one welcome our new computer overlords' beneath his final answer, borrowing a line from an old Simpsons episode. It went viral and captured something true about the moment: a smart human gracefully acknowledging that a machine had done something humans found very hard. The phrase has been recycled ever since whenever a machine masters a new task.

question: A doctor heard IBM's pitch after a TV quiz show made Watson a household name: the company was turning the machine into a serious business tool, with a medical branch to help doctors choose cancer treatments. For years IBM advertised Watson as the future of medicine and industry. How did that effort go?
answer: It struggled — Watson Health and similar products failed to live up to early promises
choices: It struggled — Watson Health and similar products failed to live up to early promises
It thrived — IBM became the world's biggest AI company by 2015 with Watson products everywhere
It was dropped early — IBM quit medicine within a year and moved Watson into banking instead
It thrived in hospitals — Watson Health became the standard cancer tool in most US clinics
context: IBM tried to commercialize Watson aggressively in the 2010s, especially in healthcare (Watson Health) and consulting. Results were disappointing; reporting by STAT found Watson for Oncology sometimes gave inappropriate treatment advice. Watson did better on well-defined quiz questions than on messy real-world tasks. In 2022 IBM sold the core of Watson Health to the investment firm Francisco Partners. Flashy demo wins followed by commercial struggle are worth recognizing whenever a new AI capability is announced with confident timelines.

question: One team entered a network called AlexNet in the yearly ImageNet contest in 2012, where computer programs competed to label millions of everyday photos: dogs, mushrooms, cars, everything. AlexNet crushed every other entry by a startling margin and shocked the field. The paper behind the network carried three names. Who led that team?
answer: Geoffrey Hinton, with students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever from Toronto
choices: Geoffrey Hinton, with students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever from Toronto
Demis Hassabis, with the new DeepMind team based in central London at the time
Yann LeCun, with researchers from Bell Labs in New Jersey after years of CNN work
Andrew Ng, with the Stanford AI Lab team that ran the contest from California
context: In 2012, Geoffrey Hinton and his graduate students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever submitted 'AlexNet' to the ImageNet large-scale visual recognition challenge. It won with an error rate of about 15.3% — a massive improvement over the previous year's 26%. The win triggered the deep-learning revolution: the field switched from hand-crafted image features to deep neural networks within about a year.

question: A worker at a computer tagged one photo 'dog,' the next 'chair,' the next 'violin,' in the late 2000s, one of an army of people labeling millions of everyday images for a giant free dataset called ImageNet. One computer scientist had launched the project in 2007, convinced that vision AI would never advance without it. Which researcher is most linked to creating ImageNet?
answer: Fei-Fei Li, then at Princeton, later director of the Stanford AI Lab
choices: Fei-Fei Li, then at Princeton, later director of the Stanford AI Lab
Marvin Minsky, the MIT pioneer who shaped early AI before image-recognition research
Demis Hassabis, who would later co-found the DeepMind lab in London in 2010
