question: A fact-checker zooms in on the ears in a suspicious portrait. Ears may seem a strange body part to focus on, but they are one of the sharpest giveaways in an AI-generated photo of a person. Why do ears often give away an AI-made photo?
answer: Ears have complex folds that AI tools often render asymmetrically or with wrong details
choices: Ears have complex folds that AI tools often render asymmetrically or with wrong details
Ears are larger in real photos than in AI photos by exactly twenty percent
AI tools refuse to draw ears and always cover them with hair
Ears glow in AI photos because the model adds light to every face
context: Ears have intricate folds and ridges that vary subtly between people. AI image models often slip on them — ears that don't match each other (asymmetric), missing folds, fused edges, or unusual shapes. Plus, jewelry, hair, and earrings interact with ears in ways that confuse the model. Photographers' tip: zoom in on the ears of any suspicious image. It's a low-glamour but reliable tell.

question: A teacher stops at two phrases in a student's paper, phrases many readers now recognize at a glance as chatbot writing. What about phrases like these is the actual giveaway?
answer: They appear too often, in the wrong contexts, like a tic
choices: They appear too often, in the wrong contexts, like a tic
They are words that don't actually exist in any English dictionary
They are spelled wrong every time an AI model uses them
They are translated from a language no human speaker uses today
context: 'Delve into' and 'tapestry of' are real English phrases. Humans use them. The tell is overuse — they show up at the start of paragraphs, in conclusions, in casual contexts where a human would just say 'look at' or 'mix of.' The frequency and contexts are the signal, not the phrases themselves. Same with 'navigate the landscape,' 'in the realm of,' 'multifaceted.'

question: Suppose you try a chatbot service for a few weeks and decide you don't want an account anymore. The company still holds your email address and the files you uploaded, and closing the tab or uninstalling the app removes none of it from its servers. What is a reasonable next step?
answer: Request account deletion through the service's settings or contact form
choices: Request account deletion through the service's settings or contact form
Delete each chat one by one, which closes the whole account as well
Log out on every device, which wipes the account after thirty days
Wait for the service to notice you've left and delete you on its own
context: EU users have a legal right to deletion under GDPR, and California residents have similar rights under CCPA. Most services now offer account deletion in settings, though they may keep some data for legal reasons. Deleting single chats or logging out does not close an account. Deletion is a partial defense: a model already trained on the data keeps whatever it learned.

question: Suppose you sit through a whole class period while your teacher explains a topic in careful detail. That evening you ask a chatbot about the same topic, and it gives a confident answer that flatly contradicts your teacher. Either one can be wrong. Whose judgment should win in the end?
answer: Yours, after thinking carefully, and probably your teacher's first
choices: Yours, after thinking carefully, and probably your teacher's first
The AI's, because computers are more accurate than human teachers
Your teacher's, always, because teachers are trained and checked
The AI's, as long as it can name a source for what it says
context: AI is a tool, not an authority. A chatbot can be wrong even when it sounds confident, and can invent a source to back itself up; a teacher can be wrong even when certain. The student's job is to think it through. In subjects with established consensus (math, science, history dates), textbooks and primary sources settle it. In contested topics, AI and teacher are both inputs. Disagreement between authorities is an invitation to think, not a tie-break by who has more letters after the name.

question: Chris Rudge, a researcher at the University of Sydney, found in 2025 that a 237-page report the consulting giant Deloitte had written for the Australian government cited papers that did not exist and included a made-up quote from a court judgment. The corrected version admitted AI had been used. What did Deloitte agree to do?
answer: Refund the final payment of its fee
choices: Refund the final payment of its fee
Refund the entire fee, plus a fine
Pay a fine set by a regulator
Stop using AI on government work
context: The government said Deloitte would repay the last installment of the roughly A$440,000 contract, and the revised report disclosed that Azure OpenAI had been used. Deloitte said the matter was resolved with the client and did not say whether AI caused the errors. Professionals fall into the same trap as students.

question: Carlos Gomez-Uribe and Neil Hunt, Netflix engineers, reported in a 2015 paper that the service's recommendations influenced the choice behind about 80% of the hours members streamed. Where did most of the remaining fifth of viewing come from?
answer: Members searching for a title
choices: Members searching for a title
Shows a friend sent by text
Ads seen on other websites
Titles picked at random by staff
context: Their paper said the recommender system influences choice for about 80% of hours streamed at Netflix, with the remaining 20% coming from search. Most of what people end up watching is what the system put in front of them.

question: A girl opens a social app and sees a video that makes her angry, then another, then another. The app judges itself by clicks and by how long people stop on each post. Angry posts get more clicks than calm ones, and the AI notices within hours. Nothing tells it to prefer kindness over rage. What does an app that chases clicks learn from that?
answer: To surface more outrage because that's what the metric rewards
choices: To surface more outrage because that's what the metric rewards
To show every user a balanced mix so that no one gets bored
To keep posts in the order they arrived, the newest first
To favour posts from close friends, since people trust those most
context: Optimization systems do exactly what they measure. If outrage holds attention longer than agreement, the system learns to feed you outrage. If fear is more sticky than reassurance, fear wins. The effects are documented at scale — Frances Haugen's 2021 Facebook disclosures, Jonathan Haidt's research on adolescent mental health. The fix isn't 'better AI'; it's recognizing what the system is doing and choosing not to be optimized.

question: A man in Shenzhen stops at a spot where a swipe card or a ticket used to be enough. Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen have put millions of cameras on the street, and in places a camera check of a person's face now decides who passes. What daily thing has such a check controlled?
answer: Entering subway stations, schools, or apartment buildings
choices: Entering subway stations, schools, or apartment buildings
Starting a car parked in its owner's own garage
Making a call from a home landline telephone
Buying a newspaper at a street kiosk with cash
context: China has deployed facial recognition at enormous scale. Documented use cases include subway entry, school check-in, residential access in some compounds, store payments, and policing. Cameras are integrated with government identity databases. The build-out is uneven across regions and has met some resistance. Recognition: surveillance infrastructure is a deployment decision, not a property of AI itself — the same tools can be built and not deployed, or restricted by law.

question: Kashmir Hill exposed Clearview AI in January 2020 with a story titled 'The Secretive Company That Might End Privacy as We Know It.' The startup had been selling its face-search app to police in near-secret. Which newspaper ran her story?
answer: The New York Times
choices: The Wall Street Journal
The New York Times
The Washington Post
The Guardian
context: Kashmir Hill's January 2020 article in The New York Times revealed that Clearview had scraped billions of photos and that hundreds of police agencies were using its app. Lawsuits and regulators followed within weeks.

question: Testers at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) ran Amazon's face-recognition service, Rekognition, at its default settings against 25,000 public arrest photos in July 2018. The software wrongly flagged 28 people from one famous group as matches for people who had been arrested. Who were they?
answer: Members of the US Congress
choices: Players in the NFL
Amazon's top executives
Members of the US Congress
Hollywood film stars
context: Rekognition wrongly matched 28 lawmakers from both parties with arrest photos, and people of color were overrepresented among the false matches. Amazon replied that its default 80 percent confidence setting suited photos of things like hot dogs and chairs, not identifying people. A default setting is a choice someone made.

question: Suppose you open a free app and see an ad that seems weirdly perfect: the exact hobby you searched for last night, or a store you visited once last month. No charity runs the app, and the company behind it has to make money somewhere. What is the basic mechanism behind such ads?
answer: The platform tracks your behavior and sells access to people who match a profile
choices: The platform tracks your behavior and sells access to people who match a profile
The platform hands your name and phone number to any advertiser who pays
The platform asks every advertiser to guess what each user might want
The platform shows the same three ads to every user in the world
context: Targeted advertising is built on behavior tracking — apps used, searches made, locations visited, items bought. Platforms build profiles and sell advertisers the ability to target by combinations: 'parents in this zip code who bought baby food this month.' The level of targeting can be uncannily specific. The deal is that the service is 'free' because you are the product. Recognizing this is the first step toward making it a choice.

question: A shop owner uploads her list of buyers to Facebook and asks for a 'lookalike audience.' The platform combs through billions of profiles and comes back with a fresh group of people to show her advertisement to. Who exactly is in that group?
answer: People whose behavior looks similar to the advertiser's existing customers
choices: People whose behavior looks similar to the advertiser's existing customers
People who have already bought from the advertiser at least once before
People who live in the same towns and zip codes as the existing buyers
People who chose in their settings to see ads from shops like hers
context: 'Lookalike audiences' are an advertising tool offered by Facebook, Google, TikTok, and others. The advertiser uploads their existing customer list; the platform finds users whose behavior pattern resembles those customers and serves them ads. It's effective for the advertiser and uncanny for the user — you start seeing ads for things you didn't know you'd want. Behind the magic: tracking + statistical similarity, scaled across billions of profiles.

question: A reporter checks the top of every benchmark in 2025 to see who builds the AI models that write, reason and code best, and she finds the same small handful of large American companies. Reporters call them 'frontier labs.' Which five companies are usually named as the leaders of that group?
answer: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft
choices: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft
IBM, Intel, Oracle, Cisco, and Dell
Nvidia, Apple, Tesla, Netflix, and Uber
Salesforce, Adobe, Zoom, Slack, and Dropbox
context: The frontier-AI 'big five' commonly listed in 2025 are OpenAI (ChatGPT), Anthropic (Claude), Google DeepMind (Gemini), Meta (Llama), and Microsoft (heavily invested in OpenAI, also building Phi). All US-based. The compute, data, and capital required to train frontier models has produced concentration. Open-source releases from Meta, Mistral (France), DeepSeek (China), and others provide a countervailing force. Recognizing concentration is half the politics of AI.

question: Former researchers from Google DeepMind and Meta founded Mistral in Paris in 2023, and it became the flagship European entry against the big American AI labs. Rather than hide its technology behind a paid interface, the company let developers around the world take its work home. What kind of models does Mistral ship?
answer: Open-weight large language models that anyone can run locally
choices: Open-weight large language models that anyone can run locally
Television sets with built-in AI for European cable customers
Robot vacuum cleaners that translate languages in real time
Wireless routers that block all AI traffic by default everywhere
context: Mistral, founded 2023 in Paris by former Meta and DeepMind researchers, ships open-weight LLMs that anyone can download and run. Mixtral (a mixture-of-experts variant) and Mistral Large are widely used. Mistral is one of Europe's two best-known frontier-AI labs (along with the UK's DeepMind, owned by Google). Their open-weight approach makes them an important counterweight to closed American labs.

question: Investors dumped AI-related stocks after a Chinese lab called DeepSeek released its V3 and R1 models in late 2024 and early 2025. Western researchers had assumed that only a handful of American labs, spending hundreds of millions of dollars on huge computer farms, could reach the top of the AI benchmarks. What was the surprise?
answer: Its open-weight models matched leading Western models at much lower training cost
choices: Its open-weight models matched leading Western models at much lower training cost
Its models ran only on Chinese-made chips, with no American hardware at all
Its chatbot drew more users in one week than ChatGPT had in two years
Its model was the first AI ever to pass the bar exam and the medical boards
context: DeepSeek's V3 and R1 models, released 2024-25, performed competitively with US frontier models at a fraction of the reported training cost. V3 was trained on Nvidia H800s, a slower chip Nvidia made for China to meet US export rules, which the US then banned in October 2023. The team released open weights, letting anyone download and test the models. The release rattled US AI markets, partly on cost and partly because it broke the assumption that frontier AI requires the very newest chips.

question: US officials raised the alarm, from 2020 on, that American teens' viewing habits on TikTok could end up on a Beijing server. Tens of millions of Americans used the short-video app, whose parent company was ByteDance. Why did TikTok face political pressure in the US?
answer: ByteDance is based in China, where laws can require data sharing with the government
choices: ByteDance is based in China, where laws can require data sharing with the government
ByteDance paid no US taxes on the money its app earned from Americans
ByteDance broke US antitrust law by buying up rival video apps
ByteDance hid its ads so users could not tell posts from paid ones
context: ByteDance, TikTok's parent, is headquartered in Beijing. Chinese national security laws (notably the 2017 National Intelligence Law) require Chinese companies to assist intelligence work when asked. US officials worried that data on well over a hundred million American users, and the algorithm shaping what they saw, could be reachable by Chinese authorities. ByteDance disputed this. Congress passed a sell-or-ban law in 2024, and in January 2026 TikTok's US app passed to a joint venture in which ByteDance keeps 19.9 percent. Who owns the algorithm matters, especially across jurisdictions.

question: Elon Musk handed Twitter's old internal Slack messages and emails to a few reporters in December 2022, after buying the company. The first batch dug into a news story Twitter had stopped users from sharing in October 2020, weeks before the US presidential election. Which story was it?
answer: The New York Post's reporting on Hunter Biden's laptop, blocked under a 'hacked materials' rule
choices: The New York Post's reporting on Hunter Biden's laptop, blocked under a 'hacked materials' rule
The New York Times's reporting on Donald Trump's tax returns, blocked under a privacy rule
A leaked tape of a candidate's private fundraiser speech, blocked under a privacy rule
A leaked memo from a campaign's own staff, blocked under a rule against private documents
context: After Musk bought Twitter in October 2022, he gave journalists internal documents. The first release (December 2, 2022) by Matt Taibbi showed how Twitter blocked the New York Post's Hunter Biden laptop story in October 2020 — locking accounts that shared the link. Taibbi found no evidence the government ordered that specific block; later releases documented other government-platform contacts.

question: A nurse scrolling Twitter during the COVID pandemic finds a 'misinformation' label on a post about vaccine side effects. Over the next few years, several claims that Twitter, Facebook and YouTube had labeled turned out to be defensible or even correct. What does this pattern suggest about the labels?
answer: Labels that look neutral can in practice silence views that later prove valid
choices: Labels that look neutral can in practice silence views that later prove valid
Labels never affect what users see or share on social media at all
Labels are applied randomly by computer with no human review involved
Labels were always applied by outside fact-checkers, never by the platforms
context: During COVID, several claims were labeled 'misinformation' on major platforms that later gained mainstream credence — including discussion of the lab-leak hypothesis (later treated seriously by the FBI and Department of Energy) and certain vaccine side-effect discussions. The pattern matters for AI literacy: content-moderation labels are not neutral verdicts; they're decisions made by a team using a policy at a moment in time. Recognition: the label shapes what users see. Question the label.

question: A user asked the new image generator inside Google's Gemini AI for medieval English kings in February 2024, and others asked for American Founding Fathers or Nazi soldiers. Gemini drew them as many different races, and the pictures were historically wrong. Who decided the tool should draw people this way?
answer: Google's product and alignment teams — through deliberate tuning choices
choices: Google's product and alignment teams — through deliberate tuning choices
The image generator itself — through choices the model made on its own
An outside hacker group — through prompt injection that bypassed safeguards
United States federal regulators — through a rule requiring diverse outputs
context: Google's Gemini image generator was tuned to show a range of people by default, apparently to counter bias in its training data. Applied to historical and specific requests, it produced anachronisms such as diverse Nazi soldiers and Founding Fathers. Sundar Pichai apologized, and Google paused Gemini's pictures of people. The episode shows that 'alignment' is not value-neutral; it is a series of choices made by people. Recognizing alignment as a carrier of values is core AI literacy.

question: Sam Altman learned he had lost his job as OpenAI's chief executive at about noon on Friday, November 17, 2023. Board member Ilya Sutskever, the company's chief scientist, had reached out to him that morning. How did the board deliver the news?
answer: On a Google Meet video call
choices: In a letter left on his desk
By text message at midnight
On a Google Meet video call
At a public press conference
context: Altman joined a Google Meet with nearly the whole board and was told he was fired; the public announcement followed within the half hour. The leader of the world's best-known AI lab was removed by video call, by four directors.

question: Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX billionaire, abruptly split from OpenAI in 2018 and left the board of the San Francisco nonprofit he had helped fund from its founding in 2015. He and the rest of the founding team, Sam Altman among them, told different versions of what happened. What is the main reason reported since?
answer: He wanted to take charge of OpenAI directly, and the other founders refused to hand him control
choices: He wanted to take charge of OpenAI directly, and the other founders refused to hand him control
He sold OpenAI to a Japanese game studio to focus on flying car prototypes that year
OpenAI dissolved itself in 2018 and was relaunched two years later by a different team
He left because the lab refused to relocate from California to Mars before launch
context: In early 2018, Musk reportedly proposed either taking a majority stake in OpenAI or folding it into Tesla. The other co-founders, including Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, and Ilya Sutskever, refused — they did not want one person controlling the lab. Musk left the board in February 2018, publicly citing a Tesla conflict of interest. He later sued Altman in 2024 over the lab's shift toward for-profit work.

question: Guillaume Chaslot built a website, AlgoTransparency, in 2018 to track what YouTube's recommendation system suggested. He had worked on that system himself before leaving Google in 2013. What did he report the system steered viewers toward for searches like 'global warming'?
answer: Conspiracy-theory and anti-science videos
choices: Conspiracy-theory and anti-science videos
Only videos from official science agencies
Videos from mainstream TV news channels
Climate lectures from university scientists
context: Chaslot said that, for some searches, YouTube's recommendations favored conspiracy-theory, anti-science or anti-media videos, and seemed to favor divisive speakers. Critics said his early project cherry-picked a handful of search terms. YouTube later changed its systems, though by how much is debated.

question: Officials at the US Department of Homeland Security announced a new 'Disinformation Governance Board' in April 2022, to advise the government on what counts as false information online, and put the researcher Nina Jankowicz in charge. What happened the next month?
answer: The board was paused after huge public backlash, and Jankowicz resigned three weeks in
choices: The board was paused after huge public backlash, and Jankowicz resigned three weeks in
The board expanded into a full federal department with thousands of staff by that fall
The board began work and published its first list of false claims online
The board was moved to the State Department and quietly kept running there
context: DHS announced the board April 27, 2022. Critics on the right called it a 'Ministry of Truth,' echoing Orwell's 1984. Jankowicz received death threats. The board was paused May 18, 2022 — three weeks in — and formally disbanded by August. The episode showed how quickly content-moderation infrastructure can attract bipartisan distrust depending on who runs it.

question: A boy opens the free Chromebook and Google email account his US public school gave him. Software from a company like Gaggle or GoGuardian runs quietly on that school account, and parents and students often don't realize it is watching. What do these tools do?
answer: Scan student emails, documents, and chats for flagged keywords using AI
choices: Scan student emails, documents, and chats for flagged keywords using AI
Lock students out of school accounts after exactly five hours each day
Translate student work into Spanish without anyone asking them to
Show students cartoon clips during free periods on Fridays
context: Tools like Gaggle, GoGuardian, and Bark scan content created on school accounts — Google Docs, school email, browser activity — looking for flags like self-harm keywords, threats, or 'inappropriate' content. Schools defend the tools as safety measures; critics argue they normalize surveillance and produce false positives. The wider recognition: AI-powered content scanning is increasingly built into platforms used by minors. Students and parents may not know what's monitored.

question: Joy Buolamwini, a graduate student at the MIT Media Lab, built a project that needed face-tracking software to see her face. It would not detect her dark-skinned face at all. What did she have to do before the software noticed her?
answer: Put on a white mask
choices: Shave her head
Wear thick glasses
Stand in sunlight
Put on a white mask
context: The software tracked Buolamwini only when she wore a white mask. That moment led to her 2018 Gender Shades study with Timnit Gebru, which found commercial systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ misjudged darker-skinned women up to 34.7 percent of the time, against under 1 percent for lighter-skinned men.

question: Apple's team sent a rare 'threat notification' to iPhone users in 92 countries in April 2024, warning that their phones were being targeted by extremely powerful spy software, the kind that can silently read messages, listen to microphones and track location. Reporters asked which company made the spyware most named in the alerts, a firm that sells its tools to governments. Which firm was it, and which product?
answer: NSO Group, makers of the Pegasus spyware that targets phones of journalists and activists
choices: NSO Group, makers of the Pegasus spyware that targets phones of journalists and activists
Apple itself, which had quietly built spyware into iOS and then warned users about it
Google, which had been sold the spyware by Apple in a secret deal earlier that year
The United Nations, which runs a global phone-monitoring program from a Geneva office
context: Pegasus is spyware sold by Israel-based NSO Group to governments. It can silently turn on a phone's microphone and camera and read messages. Apple has sent 'mercenary spyware' alerts to users in over 150 countries since 2021, mostly targeting journalists, activists, and politicians. The April 2024 wave reached 92 countries in a single day.

question: Loren Brichter invented a gesture for his Twitter app, Tweetie, in 2009: drag the feed down with a thumb, let go, and fresh posts appear. Twitter bought the app, and the gesture spread to almost every phone. Looking back in 2017, what did Brichter say about his invention?
answer: That it is addictive, and he regretted it
choices: That it is addictive, and he regretted it
That it was his proudest moment
That Apple had stolen it from him
That it saved phone batteries
context: Brichter told The Guardian in 2017 that pull-to-refresh is addictive, like Twitter itself, and that he had not been mature enough to think about that when he built it. He added that apps can refresh on their own, comparing the gesture to an elevator's close-door button that people simply like to push.

question: Justin McLeod rebuilt his dating app around serious relationships, though most dating apps earn money while users keep swiping. Its ads then destroyed the app's own mascot each time two users paired off. What was the app, and its slogan?
answer: Hinge: Designed to be deleted
choices: Tinder: It starts with a swipe
Bumble: Make the first move
OkCupid: Dating deserves better
Hinge: Designed to be deleted
context: Hinge's founder Justin McLeod redesigned the app for people who want lasting relationships and adopted the tagline designed to be deleted; its ads killed off the mascot, Hingie, whenever a couple matched. Hinge is now owned by Match Group, which also owns Tinder.

question: A graduate sends a company like Amazon her resume, one of thousands for a single job. The company runs the pile through an AI that ranks it and cuts most of it. What is a typical concern with this system?
answer: The AI can reject good applicants for opaque reasons that no human reviewed
choices: The AI can reject good applicants for opaque reasons that no human reviewed
The AI reads every resume more fairly than a tired human recruiter can
The AI is too slow to sort thousands of resumes in time for the deadline
The AI shares each resume with rival companies hiring for similar jobs
context: AI-based applicant screening (HireVue, Pymetrics, and many in-house systems) sifts resumes and sometimes scores video interviews. Concerns include opacity (rejected candidates often get no explanation), shifting criteria the model learned from past hires (which may encode past bias), and difficulty of appeal. Some jurisdictions now require disclosure when AI is used in hiring. The recognition: when you apply for a job, a model may decide whether a human ever sees you.

question: Reporters at 'Wired' and 'The 74 Million' investigated how Gaggle actually behaves. The monitoring software, used in about 1,500 US school districts, scans everything students type into their school accounts and flags words like 'gun,' 'suicide' or 'drugs.' It cannot tell a horror-story class assignment from a real warning sign. Why have these tools drawn heavy criticism?
answer: They generate huge numbers of false alarms on jokes and homework, and chill ordinary student speech
choices: They generate huge numbers of false alarms on jokes and homework, and chill ordinary student speech
They refuse to run on any school computer manufactured before the year 2015 by Apple
They make every student type in Latin during exam weeks to slow down rapid cheating
They reward students who write the longest essays with extra recess each Friday afternoon
context: Gaggle, GoGuardian, and Bark scan student email, search, and writing on school accounts for words like 'gun' or 'kill.' One Kansas district found almost two-thirds of over 1,200 alerts were false (homework, photo assignments, jokes). A student joking about guns in a school document was reported to police in one case. Critics warn students self-censor when they know everything they type is read.

question: Suppose you run an open-weight model like Meta's Llama or China's DeepSeek offline on a high-end gaming laptop, using software like Ollama. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini run on faraway company servers, and every message travels there over the internet. Why is your setup significant?
answer: Your prompts never leave your computer, so no company logs them
choices: Your prompts never leave your computer, so no company logs them
The model can fly between countries to find new information for you
The model erases all data on your hard drive when you start it up
The model invents new languages each time you ask it a question
context: Open-weight models — Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen, Phi — can be downloaded and run locally with tools like Ollama or LM Studio. A modern laptop can run a competent model. Local models mean prompts never leave your machine: no logging, no training on your conversations, no cloud bill. The trade-off is that local models lag the latest frontier in capability. For privacy-sensitive work, that trade is often worth it.

question: President Biden signed a federal law in April 2024 that named TikTok specifically: the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act (PAFACA). TikTok was then owned by ByteDance, a company headquartered in Beijing, China. What did the law require ByteDance to do?
answer: ByteDance had to sell TikTok's US business within roughly 270 days or US app stores must drop the app
choices: ByteDance had to sell TikTok's US business within roughly 270 days or US app stores must drop the app
ByteDance had to move all US user data to American servers while keeping full ownership
ByteDance had to hand TikTok's algorithm to a US regulator for a yearly review
ByteDance had to pay the US Treasury a yearly fee for every American using the app
context: PAFACA (Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act) was signed April 24, 2024. It applied to apps controlled by foreign adversaries and named TikTok's parent ByteDance specifically. Concerns centered on China's 2017 National Intelligence Law, which requires Chinese organizations to assist intelligence work. The Supreme Court upheld PAFACA in January 2025.

question: A father shared a post about COVID on Facebook in 2021 and watched a 'misinformation' warning appear on it. Facebook, Twitter and YouTube labeled millions of posts that way in 2020 and 2021, and sometimes deleted them. Internal documents and later court filings showed how the labels were decided. Who got to decide what counted?
answer: Platform trust-and-safety teams, often consulting government and outside health authorities
choices: Platform trust-and-safety teams, often consulting government and outside health authorities
Outside fact-checking groups alone, with the platforms barred from any say
A federal agency, which issued binding orders on each post to the platforms
Computer programs alone, with no person ever reviewing a single label
context: Each major platform had its own trust-and-safety team making labeling decisions, often in consultation with public-health authorities (WHO, CDC) and government agencies. The Twitter Files (2022-23) documented some of this coordination during COVID and the 2020 election. The general recognition: 'misinformation' labels are not neutral verdicts from above. They're decisions made by people, under pressure, on contested topics, in real time.

question: The Supreme Court's justices decided TikTok v. Garland on January 17, 2025. TikTok had challenged the 2024 American law that ordered its Chinese owner to sell TikTok's US business or face a ban. How did the justices rule?
answer: Unanimously, upholding the law
choices: Five to four, striking it down
They refused to hear the case
Unanimously, upholding the law
Unanimously, striking it down
context: The Supreme Court upheld the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act without dissent, in an unsigned opinion. It accepted the government's national-security concern about a company in China controlling the app's data and algorithm.

question: Mark Zuckerberg spent tens of billions of dollars on AI at Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, and the company released its main model, Llama, with 'open weights' anyone can download for free. OpenAI's GPT-4 and Anthropic's Claude stayed private. What did Meta say it gained?
answer: Wider adoption, faster outside improvement, and a counterweight to closed competitors
choices: Wider adoption, faster outside improvement, and a counterweight to closed competitors
A licensing fee from each of the startups that build their products on its models
A tax credit for sharing research under the US government's open-science rules
Free advertising for Facebook, with its logo shown wherever the models are run
context: Meta's open-weight strategy with the Llama family has several rationales: wider adoption means more people building on Meta's stack; outside researchers improve the models for free; an open ecosystem checks the market power of closed competitors like OpenAI. Mark Zuckerberg has framed it as similar to Meta's earlier open-source contributions (React, PyTorch). Taken together, open weights are a major counterweight to concentration, and worth defending.

question: Matt Taibbi and Bari Weiss got a delivery in December 2022: a social network's old internal Slack messages, emails and moderation notes, handed over by Elon Musk, who had bought the company that October for about $44 billion. They published the material as a long series of online threads. What was this stack of releases called?
answer: The Twitter Files
choices: The Twitter Files
The Facebook Files
The Musk Memos
The Slack Papers
context: The 'Twitter Files,' published December 2022 through 2023, were a series of releases by journalists including Matt Taibbi, Bari Weiss, and Michael Shellenberger. They drew on internal Twitter documents to describe content-moderation decisions, government coordination, and trust-and-safety practices during the Trump era and COVID. Different observers read them differently — but the underlying documents are public. The recognition: platform moderation is not always the platform alone deciding.

question: Customers rushed to pull their deposits from the crypto site FTX in November 2022, and the run brought it down almost overnight with billions of dollars missing. Sam Bankman-Fried, who built it, was arrested for fraud. He had publicly joined the cause of Effective Altruism and given away hundreds of millions of dollars. Why did that crash matter for AI policy fights?
answer: Its founder had funded many AI-safety nonprofits, so funding for that movement was tied to him
choices: Its founder had funded many AI-safety nonprofits, so funding for that movement was tied to him
The exchange was secretly developing the world's largest language model
FTX was the only company that hosted the OpenAI website on its servers
The crash made everyone forget about AI for the entire next decade
context: Sam Bankman-Fried built FTX into one of the largest crypto exchanges before its November 2022 collapse. He had publicly tied himself to Effective Altruism and longtermist AI-safety advocacy, funding nonprofits in that space. The implosion revealed that a substantial portion of AI-doomer advocacy had been funded by a fraud-built fortune. SBF was convicted of fraud in November 2023. The recognition: follow the money, even on 'safety' causes.

question: A teen opens YouTube and gets intense political videos one after another. The site's recommendation AI learned from his past viewing that he'll click those clips, so it keeps offering more of the same. He wants the feed to calm down. What is the simplest first counter-move?
answer: Clear watch history or use a fresh session to break the recommendation pattern
choices: Clear watch history or use a fresh session to break the recommendation pattern
Watch the same video on a louder speaker for several extra hours
Send the videos to ten friends so they share the same recommendations
Send the YouTube CEO an email asking for a personal change
context: The recommendation system learns from your watch history. If you've been pulled into a rabbit hole, clearing history (or switching to incognito) resets the model's picture of you. Conscious choice from a fresh start lets you set new patterns. Other moves: subscribe explicitly to channels you trust so subscribed-content competes with recommendations, use 'not interested' on intense clips, watch on a schedule, or take a few days off the platform entirely.

question: A teenager pays real money for a loot box in a video game, a sealed crate of random items, and learns what he bought only after he opens it. Belgium's Gaming Commission examined the paid loot boxes in Overwatch, Counter-Strike and a best-selling soccer game in April 2018. What did it rule they were?
answer: Illegal gambling
choices: Harmless collectible toys
Prizes of pure skill
Ordinary in-game gifts
Illegal gambling
context: Belgium's Gaming Commission ruled that the paid loot boxes in those games were games of chance that broke its gambling law, and the justice minister, Koen Geens, warned publishers they faced criminal penalties unless they removed them. Paying for a random reward is the same bargain a slot machine offers.

question: Suppose you run an open-weight AI model on your laptop. Its makers publish its trained numbers, the weights, so anyone can download it and run it offline. A closed application programming interface (API) model like ChatGPT or Claude runs only on the company's servers, and you pay per question. Compared to a top closed-API model, what is one common downside of the model on your laptop?
answer: Capabilities tend to lag the very latest frontier model by some margin
choices: Capabilities tend to lag the very latest frontier model by some margin
Open-weight models charge fees per question, unlike closed models
Open-weight models can only respond in Latin or Ancient Greek
Open-weight models share every answer with your internet provider
context: Open-weight models you can run locally are powerful but typically trail the absolute frontier in capability. The frontier labs invest enormous compute in their newest closed models. Open releases (Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen) often lag by 6-12 months — sometimes less. For many tasks, that lag doesn't matter. For privacy-sensitive use, the trade is often worth it. The picture is fluid; capability gaps close and open as new releases ship.

question: Two Stanford students sit down with one laptop in 2025 to build a model in the league of GPT-4, Claude or Gemini, and they simply cannot compete. Why is it so hard to start a brand-new frontier-AI company?
answer: Training a leading model needs huge compute, huge data, and huge capital
choices: Training a leading model needs huge compute, huge data, and huge capital
Federal law requires a license before anyone can train a new model
Cloud companies refuse to rent their computer chips to new startups
The big labs have patented every method for training language models
context: Training a frontier model takes tens of thousands of high-end chips, massive curated datasets, energy, and engineering talent — typically hundreds of millions to billions of dollars per training run. Only a handful of companies and governments have the resources. The result is concentration. Open-weight releases lower the barrier to using a strong model but don't change the cost of training a new frontier one. Recognition: cost shapes who builds the technology and whose interests it serves first.

question: YouTube's staff announced in January 2019 that the site would start recommending fewer 'borderline' videos, such as ones selling phony miracle cures or claiming the Earth is flat, without removing them. How much of the content on YouTube did they say the change would touch?
answer: Less than one percent
choices: Less than one percent
About half of it
Nearly all of it
Exactly a third of it
context: YouTube's blog said it would reduce recommendations of borderline content and content that could misinform users in harmful ways, and that the change applied to less than one percent of videos. Recommending less is a powerful lever: it shapes what millions see without deleting anything.

question: A moderator at a social-media platform looks at a post she thinks is wrong and has two choices. She can add a 'misinformation' label and let people see the post with a warning, or she can delete it entirely. Deletion sounds cleaner, but it carries a real risk that labeling avoids. Why is deleting risky?
answer: Some 'misinformation' calls turn out to be wrong, and deletion erases the record
choices: Some 'misinformation' calls turn out to be wrong, and deletion erases the record
Deletion breaks US law, since platforms must keep every post for public records
Deletion costs far more server power than adding a label to the post does
Deletion lets the author sue the platform for breach of free-speech law
context: Permanent removal forecloses debate. If a 'misinformation' label later proves wrong — as happened with several COVID-era claims, including the lab-leak hypothesis — labeled posts can at least be re-examined. Deleted posts vanish from the record, and the wrong call can't easily be revisited. The general lesson for AI-augmented moderation: errors will happen at scale; design systems so errors can be corrected, not buried. Transparency over erasure.

question: San Francisco's lawmakers passed a law in 2019 restricting how police may use facial recognition, which pairs cameras with AI to match a face in a crowd against a database of names. Boston, Portland and other US cities followed. Supporters of these bans point to two problems that together make the technology risky. What is the usual concern?
answer: False matches plus the chill effect on protest and public life
choices: False matches plus the chill effect on protest and public life
High costs plus the slow speed of matching faces in crowds
Hacked cameras plus footage leaking to criminal gangs
Lost police jobs plus the price of all the new cameras
context: San Francisco (2019), Boston, Portland, and other US cities have passed laws restricting government facial recognition. The two main concerns: documented false-match errors (Robert Williams Detroit 2020 and other cases) plus the broader chilling effect on lawful public activity — protest, assembly, attending a place of worship. The recognition isn't anti-AI; it's that deployment decisions are political, and 'we have the technology' is not the same as 'we should use it everywhere.'

question: A US critic of TikTok looks over 'Project Texas,' the app's public answer to fears about China's government. The plan stores all US user data on servers in Texas, operated by the American firm Oracle. Critics say this is not a full answer to the worry. Why don't they consider Project Texas enough?
answer: Where data is stored is only one of several access pathways the company controls
choices: Where data is stored is only one of several access pathways the company controls
Oracle may sell the data, since US law makes stored data the property of its host
Texas law lets any state agency read whatever data is stored inside the state
Storage location doesn't matter at all on any social media platform
context: TikTok's 'Project Texas' moved US user data storage to Oracle servers in the US, with claimed restrictions on access. Critics pointed out that storage location was only part of the picture: engineering, model training, content recommendation and corporate ownership remained with ByteDance, and internal investigations surfaced cases of mainland-China-based ByteDance staff accessing US data. In January 2026 a joint venture in which ByteDance keeps 19.9 percent took over the US app. Privacy promises must be weighed against the full system, not just the storage server's address.

question: Suppose you compare two feeds on an app like Facebook, Instagram or TikTok. The first, an older style, shows what your friends recently posted, newest first, with no algorithm mixed in. The second, a modern algorithmic feed, shows whatever a machine-learning model picks, even if none of your friends ever made it. What is the important difference between these two feeds?
answer: The second one optimizes for your attention, not for your social circle
choices: The second one optimizes for your attention, not for your social circle
The two feeds are identical because they show the same friends always
The first feed is illegal in all countries under privacy regulations
The second feed shows only old posts from many years in the past
context: Early social media was chronological — what your friends posted, newest first. Modern feeds are algorithmic — what a recommendation system thinks will hold you. The shift made the platforms more addictive and lower-cost (the platform doesn't depend on your friends being interesting). Most platforms now offer chronological or 'following' modes as an option you have to find. Switching back is one of the simplest counter-moves available.

question: An American user opened TikTok on the night of January 18, 2025, just before the sell-or-ban law took effect, and found the app doing something it had never done to its American users before. What was it?
answer: Went dark, then came back the next day
choices: Doubled its ads, then removed them all
Changed its name to a new brand
Went dark, then came back the next day
Banned every video about politics
context: TikTok shut itself off for American users late on January 18, 2025, with a message appealing to President-elect Trump, and was back by the afternoon of January 19 after he promised to delay enforcement. Once in office he ordered the law not to be enforced for 75 days, the first of several delays. In January 2026 a joint venture majority-owned by American and other non-Chinese investors took over TikTok's US app, with ByteDance keeping 19.9 percent.

question: A student writes a phrase that mentions self-harm in an essay, and the monitoring software her school runs on every essay alerts a counselor or school administrator at once. The school says the tool has one specific stated purpose. What is the school's claim about why the tool exists?
answer: To intervene early when a student may be in danger
choices: To intervene early when a student may be in danger
To embarrass the student in front of classmates by default
To delete all writing the school does not personally agree with
To grade the essay automatically and notify the parent of a low score
context: Schools defend tools like Gaggle, Bark, and GoGuardian as safety measures — automated scanning for self-harm signals, threats, or signs of abuse. The defense is real: in some cases the tools have flagged students in crisis. Critics raise three issues: false positives that scar the student, normalization of surveillance, and the trade-off between safety and privacy. The recognition: 'for your safety' framings cover real cases and real costs. Worth being precise about both.

question: Suppose you are about to overspend, and a budgeting app's AI nudges you to move money into savings instead. Then you are about to log off a casino-style betting app, and its AI nudges you to place one more bet before you go. What is the same and what is different between the two apps?
answer: Same technique with opposite goals, where one serves your interest and the other serves the platform's
choices: Same technique with opposite goals, where one serves your interest and the other serves the platform's
Different techniques with the same goal, since both apps really want you to keep spending money
Same technique with the same goal, since every nudge serves only the company that wrote it
Opposite techniques with one shared goal, since both are built to keep you opening the app daily
context: The technology is morally neutral. The deployment is not. Personalized nudges from a budgeting app, fitness app, or medication reminder can serve the user well. The same technique inside a gambling app, dark-pattern checkout, or attention-maximizing feed serves the platform at the user's expense. Recognition: every nudge has a beneficiary. Ask, feature by feature, who actually benefits. Same tools, different ethics.

question: YouTube's engineers changed what the recommendation system aimed for in March 2012. They said the old target was a weak sign that viewers actually valued a video, and that it had encouraged misleading thumbnails and titles. What had the old system mainly rewarded?
answer: Clicks on a video
choices: Likes from subscribers
Comments from viewers
Uploads by news outlets
Clicks on a video
context: Before 2012 YouTube's system favored videos that got clicked, so misleading thumbnails and titles paid off. YouTube's creator blog said it would focus more on time watched instead, and the company later said it had moved further, toward measures of viewer satisfaction.

question: Reporters went through Twitter's internal documents in late 2022 and found messages from officials at the FBI, White House and CDC asking Twitter to remove posts on COVID and elections. Emails like these, gathered in court, sat at the core of the lawsuit Murthy v. Missouri. What did the plaintiffs say the officials were doing?
answer: Officials had been 'jawboning' — pressuring platforms to delete posts the government could not lawfully ban itself
choices: Officials had been 'jawboning' — pressuring platforms to delete posts the government could not lawfully ban itself
Officials had been 'astroturfing' — paying fake accounts to flood the platforms with friendly posts
Officials had been 'doxxing' — publishing the home addresses of critics who posted online
Officials had been 'wiretapping' — reading users' private messages without any court warrant
context: Murthy v. Missouri reached the Supreme Court in 2024. Plaintiffs argued the federal government had pressured platforms through 'trust-and-safety' channels — informal requests with implicit consequences. The Court dismissed the case in June 2024, ruling plaintiffs lacked standing, without resolving the underlying First Amendment question. 'Jawboning' is the legal term for this kind of indirect pressure on private speech.

question: A police technician plugs a locked phone into a Cellebrite kit, and the Israeli company's tool cracks the passcode, pulls out the messages and downloads the photos. Cellebrite sells these tools to police forces around the world, including in countries with harsh governments that jail dissidents and journalists. What does that show about a tool like this?
answer: Once a tool to break into phones exists and is sold, the buyer list is hard to control
choices: Once a tool to break into phones exists and is sold, the buyer list is hard to control
The tools only work on phones made before 2010 and cannot reach any modern devices
Cellebrite tools are required by law to be reviewed by the United Nations before any sale
Phone unlocking tools always fail on encrypted messages and are useless against any chat app
context: Cellebrite sells UFED kits that extract data from locked phones. Customers include US police but also Belarus, Saudi Arabia, and other governments accused of targeting dissidents. Once a capability is built and sold, it tends to spread; tools sold for one purpose under one government become available for other purposes under the next. This is a general pattern for surveillance technology.

question: Claude Shannon built fake English with no computer at all in his 1948 paper. To pick each next word, he opened a book at random, found the word he had just written, and copied down the word that followed it there. What did the method show?
answer: Text built only from which word tends to follow which already reads like English for short stretches
choices: Words chosen this way read as pure nonsense, since a word gives no clue to the one after it
Copying words this way rebuilds the original book exactly, page after page, every time
Text built only from which word tends to follow which already reads like English for short stretches
English sentences can only be produced by a machine after grammar rules are programmed in
context: Shannon's word-by-word approximation produced lines like 'attack on an English writer that the character of this,' which reads like English a few words at a time. A language model does the same job at vast scale: it predicts what comes next from the statistics of real text.

question: A New York lawyer asked ChatGPT for help with a brief in a real case, Mata v. Avianca, and got back precise-sounding citations such as 'Varghese v. China Southern Airlines, 925 F.3d 1339 (11th Cir. 2019),' formatted just as real federal case law is. The brief was filed, and neither Avianca's lawyers nor the judge could find that case or five others like it. What mechanism made this happen?
answer: The model produced text that looks statistically like real legal citations and never checked anything against a real database.
choices: The model produced text that looks statistically like real legal citations and never checked anything against a real database.
The model deliberately fabricated a citation to test whether the user would catch it before submitting.
The model copied a real citation but accidentally typed one digit wrong while transcribing it.
The model was hacked by an attacker who injected fake legal references into its response stream.
context: Citations have a predictable shape — 'Name v. Name, NUMBER F.Nd PAGE (CIRCUIT YEAR).' An LLM trained on legal text learns that pattern. When asked for a citation, it generates text matching the pattern. The pattern looks right; the case may not exist. This is the same mechanism behind made-up book titles, fake URLs, and invented quotes. The defensive habit: any specific reference an LLM gives you must be verified against a real source before you use it.

question: A girl watches ChatGPT write a reply to her message, one token at a time; a token is a word or a piece of a word. Halfway down the paragraph the chatbot seems to change its mind and heads off in another direction. Why can a chatbot do that?
answer: Each token is chosen based on the text so far, not a fixed answer the model committed to at the start.
choices: Each token is chosen based on the text so far, not a fixed answer the model committed to at the start.
The model has a long-term goal and adjusts the goal whenever a new sentence begins in the paragraph.
A second model checks the first model's answer halfway through and forces a correction at that point.
The chatbot service routes the conversation to a different backend after every two or three sentences.
context: A language model generates one token, adds it to the text, and is then asked again for the next. Nothing locks in the whole answer at the start, though interpretability research at Anthropic in 2025 found that models can plan a few words ahead, for instance a rhyme. A mid-paragraph change of course is the predictor following a different path now that more words are in front of it. Newer 'reasoning' models add explicit steps that look more like planning, but underneath the basic mechanism is still token-by-token generation.

question: A bookkeeper types 'What's 23,847 times 6,019?' into a Large Language Model (LLM), and it confidently answers '143,571,693.' A one-dollar calculator app proves that wrong in a blink. Why does an LLM, trained on billions of words of internet text, fail at this?
answer: It predicts a number that looks plausible from training text, instead of running the actual multiplication algorithm.
choices: It predicts a number that looks plausible from training text, instead of running the actual multiplication algorithm.
It rounds the answer to the nearest hundred million by default to save processing time on big numbers.
It runs out of memory partway through a long multiplication and guesses the final digits instead.
It returns the answer to an unrelated multiplication problem because the question used unfamiliar digits.
context: An LLM has no built-in arithmetic engine. When it sees '23,847 × 6,019 =' it generates a number that looks statistically plausible — usually right magnitude, often right last digit, almost never exactly right. Modern chatbots get around this by handing math problems to a calculator tool when one is available. The recognition habit: never trust an LLM for arithmetic; verify with a calculator, or ask the model to write code that does the math.

question: A boy asks a chatbot with no web search what time tonight's football game starts, and it replies at once with a precise, real-looking kickoff time. The text it was trained on stops months before today's date. What probably happened?
answer: The model produced a plausible-sounding time based on training-text patterns about football schedules, and that guess is almost certainly wrong.
choices: The model produced a plausible-sounding time based on training-text patterns about football schedules, and that guess is almost certainly wrong.
The model recalled the time from another user who asked earlier that evening, so the answer should be right.
The model checked a built-in sports calendar its makers refresh each morning, so the time is up to date.
The model worked the time out from the teams' usual kickoff slots in past seasons, and that answer is very likely right.
context: Without a web-search tool, a language model cannot know today's date or tonight's schedule, and it keeps nothing from other users' chats. It still answers, because it is built to produce a likely continuation, and the continuation looks factual. It is almost certainly wrong. For current events, a search engine or a chatbot with live web access is the tool, and that needs checking too.

question: Emily Bender and her co-authors coined a nickname in a 2021 paper for language models of the kind behind ChatGPT: 'stochastic parrot.' A parrot repeats words it heard without knowing what they mean; 'stochastic' means picking by chance from a probability distribution. Some AI researchers say the picture is too harsh; others find the nickname useful even though it leaves things out. What makes the nickname useful to them?
answer: It captures the core mechanic of repeating statistical patterns from training data, with no claim of understanding behind the words.
choices: It captures the core mechanic of repeating statistical patterns from training data, with no claim of understanding behind the words.
It captures that chatbots copy whole passages word for word from the pages they were trained on.
It captures that chatbots give a random answer each time, with no link to what was asked of them.
It captures that chatbots only repeat what their users have just said, the way a pet parrot does.
context: Emily Bender, Timnit Gebru and co-authors used the 'stochastic parrot' label in a 2021 paper to push back on hype that framed language models as thinking. The metaphor leaves out useful work the models can do (translation, code, brainstorming); in the authors' view it names what a language model is not, a system that understands what it says. Other researchers argue the models do more than the metaphor allows. A reader impressed by a chatbot can ask whether the work needed understanding or only the right kind of text.

question: A teacher watches ChatGPT write an essay one word at a time: it picks the next word, adds it to the text, then picks the word after that, with no plan and no outline. Yet the long paragraphs stay on topic. Why do next-word-at-a-time models produce writing that stays coherent?
answer: The model attends to every earlier word when picking the next one, so each prediction is shaped by the whole conversation so far.
choices: The model attends to every earlier word when picking the next one, so each prediction is shaped by the whole conversation so far.
The model writes a complete essay plan internally before it produces a single output word for the user.
The model has a long-term memory module that stores key points across multiple chat sessions over time.
The model rewrites its earlier sentences silently as it goes, keeping later paragraphs lined up with them.
context: The transformer architecture's self-attention is why LLM output reads coherently. Every new token's prediction looks at all the earlier tokens at once. Stay on topic at word 200 is downstream of attending to words 1 through 199. There is no separate planning module in a vanilla LLM. The coherence is an emergent property of attention plus next-token prediction at scale.

question: Suppose you type 'Once upon a time, there was a' into ChatGPT and ask it to continue. It writes 'dragon.' You clear the chat and type the exact same prompt again, and this time it writes 'farmer.' Nothing about the model itself has changed between the two tries. Why did the word change?
answer: The model samples from a probability distribution over possible next tokens, so high-probability words can each be chosen on different runs.
choices: The model samples from a probability distribution over possible next tokens, so high-probability words can each be chosen on different runs.
Other users' prompts contaminate yours when traffic is high, changing which word the model selects.
The chatbot keeps a hidden list of words it has given you and avoids repeating any of them.
The chatbot spreads its picks evenly, counting how often each word has gone to every user.
context: An LLM predicts a probability for every possible next token, then samples from that distribution. With a 'temperature' setting above zero, sampling is random: high-probability tokens are likely, low-probability ones still possible. Set temperature to zero and the model picks the single most likely token, giving nearly the same output every time. This is also why creative-writing tasks usually run at higher temperature than fact-lookup tasks.

question: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer and their colleagues at Google Brain, eight authors in all, published a short paper with a bold title in June 2017. Within a few years, almost every modern chatbot, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA among them, was built on the design that paper proposed. What did the paper propose?
answer: The transformer — a network architecture built around self-attention instead of older sequence-step approaches.
choices: The transformer — a network architecture built around self-attention instead of older sequence-step approaches.
The convolutional neural network — image-style sliding filters scaled up for processing word sequences.
The recurrent neural network — looping cells that pass a hidden state from one word to the next one.
The decision tree ensemble — a stack of branching rules trained with gradient-boosted optimization.
context: The 2017 paper introduced the transformer. The key idea: instead of processing words one at a time and passing a hidden state forward (the older RNN/LSTM approach), let every word attend to every other word in parallel. The result was faster training and better long-range coherence. Within five years, transformers became the foundation of virtually every leading language model. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama — all transformers.

question: A researcher types the classic ambiguity sentence into a transformer, the neural network design behind ChatGPT: 'The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big.' A mechanism called self-attention lets each word work out which other words matter to it, and the pronoun could point back to either noun. Which word matters most for working out what 'it' refers to?
answer: 'Trophy' — without that link the model can't tell whether 'it' is the trophy or the suitcase.
choices: 'Trophy' — without that link the model can't tell whether 'it' is the trophy or the suitcase.
'Suitcase' — every pronoun in English defaults back to whichever noun came most recently.
'Because' — the word 'because' tells the model exactly which earlier noun a pronoun refers to.
'Fit' — verbs control all pronoun reference, and 'fit' is the controlling verb in the sentence.
context: Pronoun resolution — figuring out what 'it' refers to — is exactly what self-attention is good at. The mechanism lets the model compute, for every word in the sentence, a score against every other word, and route attention to the ones that matter. If 'it' attends strongly to 'trophy,' the model treats it as referring to the trophy. Change the sentence to 'because it was too small' and the right answer flips to 'suitcase' — and a well-trained transformer flips with it.

question: An engineer training an older language model watched it read a sentence one step at a time, passing a hidden 'state' forward, so word two had to wait for word one to finish. The transformer replaced that step-by-step design with attention. Why was the switch such a big win for training?
answer: Every word could be processed at once on a GPU, making training on huge datasets dramatically faster.
choices: Every word could be processed at once on a GPU, making training on huge datasets dramatically faster.
Transformers automatically translate every language pair without any training data being needed at all.
Transformers used less computer memory because they discarded earlier words once they were processed.
Transformers stopped needing electricity to train, so labs could run them on simple laptops.
context: Recurrent networks were inherently sequential — word N had to be processed before word N+1. That made it hard to use the parallel computation that GPUs are good at. Transformers process all the words in a block at once. The result: bigger training runs at the same wall-clock time. Combined with the larger datasets that became available in the late 2010s, this is the technical change that enabled the scale-up to today's LLMs.

question: Google researchers proposed a neural-network design called the transformer in a June 2017 paper, 'Attention Is All You Need.' Late in 2022 the public met that design inside ChatGPT, the work of a different, smaller lab. What makes that an odd turn in the story of the idea?
answer: Google invented the architecture; OpenAI was the company that scaled it up into ChatGPT and brought it mainstream.
choices: Google invented the architecture; OpenAI was the company that scaled it up into ChatGPT and brought it mainstream.
Google had kept the design secret for years and published it only after OpenAI's first GPT model.
Google had sold the transformer outright to OpenAI, along with the whole team that invented it.
Google had never used the transformer itself, keeping to older designs for all of its products.
context: Google Brain (later folded into Google DeepMind) introduced the transformer in 2017. Google then used it internally — BERT in 2018, PaLM, Gemini. But OpenAI used it to build the GPT line, and ChatGPT (Nov 2022) was the product that made the public notice. A common pattern in tech: the lab that publishes a key idea is not always the company that captures the consumer market built on it.

question: An engineer cuts text into tokens for a language model. 'Hello' might stay one token, 'unbelievable' might split into three ('un,' 'believ' and 'able'), and 'antidisestablishmentarianism' might become six. Why design the model around these subword pieces rather than whole words?
answer: Subword pieces let the model handle rare words, made-up words, and other languages without exploding its vocabulary.
choices: Subword pieces let the model handle rare words, made-up words, and other languages without exploding its vocabulary.
Subword pieces let the model see the future of each word by predicting endings before beginnings.
Subword pieces let the model compress training data into smaller files for storage on company hard drives.
Subword pieces let the model output text in any color or font the user requests at any given moment.
context: A whole-word vocabulary would be unmanageable — there are millions of words in English alone, plus typos, names, slang, code, and every other language. Tokenizing into subword pieces gives a smaller vocabulary (often 50K-100K tokens) that still covers everything: rare words like 'pterodactyl' get split into pieces the model has seen. A side effect: 'token count' is the standard unit for billing API usage and measuring context limits.

question: An engineer feeds a transformer, the neural network design behind ChatGPT, a sentence of exactly 100 words. Self-attention lets every word in the sentence attend to every other word in it, and that makes a lot of word-pairs to compute. Roughly how many attention pairs does the model have to consider?
answer: About 10,000 — every word attends to every word, so the work grows with the square of the length.
choices: About 10,000 — every word attends to every word, so the work grows with the square of the length.
About 100 — one attention computation for each word, processed once in a single pass.
About 200 — each word attends to itself once and to one other word it picks at random.
About 1,000,000 — the model attends to every word in every order, including all reversed sequences.
context: Self-attention is O(N²) in sequence length — for N words, that's N×N pairwise comparisons. For 100 words it's 10,000 pair-scores. For 100,000 words, it's 10 billion. This is why long context windows are expensive and why research on more efficient attention variants — sparse attention, sliding windows, state-space models — is an active area. The quadratic cost is the headline technical limit of the basic transformer.

question: A search engineer stores the word 'king' as an embedding: a long row of numbers, [0.21, -0.44, 0.87, ...], maybe 1,024 of them. 'Queen' becomes a different row of the same length, and a sentence or an image can get one too. Why represent meaning as a big row of numbers instead of just storing the word itself?
answer: Numbers let the model measure how similar two words are, by checking how close their lists are in space.
choices: Numbers let the model measure how similar two words are, by checking how close their lists are in space.
Numbers let the model translate every word into ancient Greek before processing it for analysis.
Numbers let the model compress every word into a single digit between zero and nine for fast lookup.
Numbers let the model avoid using any letters at all, which saves on font-rendering time for output.
context: An embedding turns a word into a point in a high-dimensional space. Words with similar meanings sit close together — 'king' and 'queen' end up near each other, 'king' and 'rutabaga' do not. The model can then do math on meaning: famously, the embedding for 'king' minus 'man' plus 'woman' ends up near 'queen.' Embeddings are also how modern search 'understands' queries — both query and document get embedded, then the closest documents are returned.

question: Google researchers behind a model called word2vec took the embedding for 'king' in 2013, the long list of numbers standing for that word, subtracted the one for 'man' and added the one for 'woman.' The answer landed right next to the embedding for 'queen.' What does that result reveal about how the model stores such ideas?
answer: Concepts like gender and royalty live as directions in the number-space, so adding and subtracting them shifts meaning predictably.
choices: Concepts like gender and royalty live as directions in the number-space, so adding and subtracting them shifts meaning predictably.
The model has memorized every dictionary entry and is simply returning the word with the closest definition.
The model can solve linguistic puzzles only when the words involved start with the same letter of the alphabet.
The model invented the relationship between king, queen, man, and woman after a developer typed it in by hand.
context: This 'king − man + woman ≈ queen' result, popularized by the word2vec paper (Mikolov et al. 2013), was a striking early demonstration that embeddings capture structured meaning, not just word identity. Directions in embedding space correspond to attributes — gender, royalty, country-of-origin, plural-vs-singular. Modern LLM embeddings are larger and more entangled, but the same idea drives them: meaning lives as geometry.

question: A dog owner types 'how do I get a dog to stop barking' into a search engine and gets back a document titled 'training your puppy to be quiet.' The engine, like the vector databases inside chatbots such as ChatGPT, turned her query into an embedding, a list of numbers, and compared it with the numbers for each document. Why does that beat plain keyword matching?
answer: Two texts can mean nearly the same thing without sharing any words, and embeddings catch the meaning overlap anyway.
choices: Two texts can mean nearly the same thing without sharing any words, and embeddings catch the meaning overlap anyway.
Embeddings let the search engine skip reading the documents and just check their file size for relevance.
Embeddings turn every search query into a single English sentence the engine answers from a list of replies.
Embeddings let the search engine sort documents alphabetically while looking for relevant matches in order.
context: Classical search (keyword matching) misses paraphrases. 'How do I fix a leaky faucet' and 'plumbing repair for a dripping tap' share no key content words yet mean almost the same thing. Embedding-based search puts both queries near each other in the number-space, so a document that matches one will be retrieved for the other. This is the technical backbone of modern semantic search and is also how RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) systems pick relevant documents to feed into an LLM.

question: A researcher opens a trained chatbot and looks at the embedding for one input token, a list of several hundred numbers. Nobody wrote those numbers by hand; training set them from scratch, inside a transformer, the architecture behind ChatGPT and other Large Language Models (LLMs). What do those numbers represent, once training is done?
answer: Different features the model has learned to track, with no single number mapping cleanly to a human-readable concept.
choices: Different features the model has learned to track, with no single number mapping cleanly to a human-readable concept.
One number per letter of the alphabet, with extra slots for punctuation and uppercase versus lowercase use.
Phoneme codes copied from the International Phonetic Alphabet so the model can pronounce every word.
Dictionary definitions encoded so each number stands for one word in the explanation of the original token.
context: An embedding's individual numbers don't usually correspond to clean human concepts like 'is plural' or 'is a verb.' They're learned features — the result of training adjusting the numbers until the model predicts well. Some research tries to find interpretable directions inside the embedding (mechanistic interpretability), but in general, each individual number isn't readable on its own. The structure shows up at the level of relationships between embeddings, not inside any single one.

question: A writer tried GPT-3, released by OpenAI in 2020, and got fluent essays and stories. But it happily followed rude prompts, made up fake facts on command and often ignored polite requests to stop. OpenAI then added a step in which paid humans rate model outputs and the model learns to prefer highly-rated ones. In plain words, what does that step fix?
answer: It makes the model behave like a helpful assistant instead of a raw text-predictor that completes anything.
choices: It makes the model behave like a helpful assistant instead of a raw text-predictor that completes anything.
It teaches the model new facts that were missing from its original pre-training run on the dataset.
It lets the model run twice as fast at chat time by pre-computing answers to common user questions.
It connects the model to a live internet feed for the first time after pre-training has finished entirely.
context: Pre-trained text models are 'completion' engines — they continue whatever pattern they see, including offensive or unhelpful patterns. RLHF realigns the model toward what humans want from a helpful assistant: answer the question, refuse genuinely harmful requests, write in a steady tone. RLHF doesn't add facts and doesn't make the model faster. It changes which of the many possible continuations the model prefers — toward the ones humans ranked high.

question: A paid rater looks over a pair of chatbot answers and picks the one she likes better, and the model then learns to give more answers like the winners. Critics, including some AI-alignment researchers, point out that this does not make the model 'truthful.' It makes the model give answers raters liked. Why is that difference important?
answer: Raters can be misled by confident-sounding wrong answers, so the training can reward output that sounds right rather than is right.
choices: Raters can be misled by confident-sounding wrong answers, so the training can reward output that sounds right rather than is right.
Raters check each answer against an encyclopedia, so the model learns to repeat encyclopedia wording word for word.
Raters are paid by the answer, so the model learns to give the shortest replies a rater can score in seconds.
Raters' choices last only until the next update, so the model forgets each round of feedback within weeks.
