question: The prompt engineer Riley Goodside showed a new hiding place for secret orders to a chatbot in January 2024. Unicode, the standard that lists every character computers can display, includes a block of 'tag' characters that mirror ordinary letters. Text written in them can be pasted into a message, a webpage or a file. Why is this such an effective trick against chatbots?
answer: The model reads the hidden letters while a person sees only blank space
choices: The letters crash the chatbot and wipe out its safety rules
The model reads the hidden letters while a person sees only blank space
The letters are a secret password that unlocks an admin mode
The letters only work on phones that are set to airplane mode
context: Goodside showed ChatGPT reading and following instructions written in Unicode tag characters, which most screens display as nothing at all; Johann Rehberger built a tool to encode them, and the trick became known as ASCII smuggling. A person checking the text sees nothing suspicious. Defenders now strip invisible characters out before text reaches the model.

question: A developer gave an AI agent 'tool access,' letting it browse the web, run code on a computer or call APIs (Application Programming Interfaces that let one program command another). The agent stopped being a chatbot and started being an actor in the real world. A webpage the agent read might contain a hidden instruction, and the agent already had permission to send email or move money. What practical principle for deploying such agents had emerged by 2025?
answer: Treat the agent's effective permissions as the LEAST trustworthy combination — what it can read can attack what it can do.
choices: Treat the agent's effective permissions as the LEAST trustworthy combination — what it can read can attack what it can do.
Treat the agent's permissions as totally safe — AI labs have already solved the problem of prompt injection in agent contexts long ago.
Grant the agent root access on every system in the deployment — limited access creates more complex failure modes than full access does.
Replace the agent with a human every time a critical action would be taken — eliminating any need for trust modeling in any deployment.
context: The practical principle that hardened by 2025: an agent's effective security boundary is set by what it can read AND what it can do, jointly. If the agent can browse the open web AND send email AND access financial accounts, then any attacker-controlled webpage becomes a potential vector for sending email or accessing funds. The deployment patterns that worked: separate agents (one that browses, one that acts, with structured handoff); confirmation steps for irreversible actions; capability scoping (the agent gets the minimum permissions for the task); audit logs; human review for anything sensitive. The deeper recognition: 'AI agent' in marketing implies trustworthy autonomy. In secure deployments it means something narrower — bounded, supervised, with humans in the loop for the consequential decisions.

question: Attackers got into 23andMe accounts in October 2023 with reused passwords, a credential-stuffing attack, and reached personal genetic data on millions of users. Those customers had mailed in saliva, and the company had kept each genetic code on file. Some breached profiles were posted online in lists sorted by ancestry group. What made the incident different in kind from a typical password breach?
answer: DNA data is unique, permanent, partly shared with relatives, and cannot be changed the way a leaked password can — exposure is lifelong.
choices: DNA data is unique, permanent, partly shared with relatives, and cannot be changed the way a leaked password can — exposure is lifelong.
DNA data can be reset by retesting — a customer can swap a leaked profile for a fresh one, like a new password.
DNA data says nothing about relatives — each leaked profile exposed only the one customer who mailed the sample.
DNA data falls under HIPAA — so every affected customer was paid damages by the federal government automatically.
context: The 23andMe breach (Oct 2023) used credential stuffing — reusing passwords leaked from other services — to access about 14,000 accounts directly. Through the 'DNA Relatives' feature, attackers then accessed data on roughly 6.9 million people. Lists targeting Ashkenazi Jewish and Chinese ancestry were posted on hacker forums. The incident highlighted a structural problem: genetic data isn't like a password. You can't change your genome. The data partly belongs to relatives who never consented. 23andMe's response (forced password resets, multi-factor auth) addressed the immediate vector; the exposure is permanent. The recognition skill: consider what kind of data you give to which kind of service. Some data, once collected, cannot be unbreached.

question: Privacy advocates sued Clearview AI, the American company that built a face-recognition tool from billions of photos without asking anyone. Police departments loved the tool. Courts and regulators in Illinois, France, Italy, the Netherlands and Australia restricted it, fined it or ordered it to delete data between 2021 and 2024. Yet it kept operating. Why did the fines and orders fail to shut it down?
answer: Each order bound only its own country — so Clearview kept selling to police elsewhere and left several European fines unpaid.
choices: Each order bound only its own country — so Clearview kept selling to police elsewhere and left several European fines unpaid.
Each fine was overturned on appeal — every court found that scraping public photos breaks no privacy law.
The orders covered only photos of children — adults' faces stayed outside every ruling, so the main database was untouched.
Clearview moved its servers to a country with no privacy law — so no court anywhere could reach the company's data at all.
context: Clearview AI scraped billions of photos from Facebook, Instagram, Twitter/X, and other sites — much of it without consent — to build a face-search database used by US law enforcement. Lawsuits and regulatory actions piled up: a 2022 ACLU settlement under Illinois's BIPA restricted some commercial sales; UK ICO fined £7.5 million in 2022 (Clearview disputed UK jurisdiction); Canadian, French, Italian, and Australian regulators issued orders. Clearview kept operating, focused on law-enforcement clients, and continued contracting with federal agencies including ICE and DHS. The pattern: a company whose business model treats penalties as a cost rather than a deterrent. The recognition skill: regulation is supposed to align incentives. When fines stay below revenue, they're a price tag, not a deterrent.

question: A journalist spreads leaked police files, procurement records and testimony across her desk and pieces together the picture of one region in western China. Surveillance states use AI to spot patterns at scales no human team could match. What setup there became important as a template around the world?
answer: Integrated systems combining face recognition, behavior prediction, and a 'predictive policing' platform to identify individuals for detention.
choices: Integrated systems combining face recognition, behavior prediction, and a 'predictive policing' platform to identify individuals for detention.
Camera networks run by private security firms, with the police seeing footage only when a court ordered it.
Traditional door-to-door surveys by uniformed officers, with no AI or pattern recognition technology used anywhere in Xinjiang.
Phone tracking alone, with cameras and face recognition kept out of the region by a 2017 ban on their use.
context: Documentation of AI-enabled surveillance in Xinjiang came from leaked Chinese government documents (the 'China Cables' 2019, 'Xinjiang Police Files' 2022), academic research, and on-the-ground reporting. The Integrated Joint Operations Platform combined face recognition feeds, ID-card checkpoints, vehicle tracking, communications metadata, and 'predictive policing' to flag Uyghur individuals for questioning, detention, and 're-education.' US government documents have characterized aspects of this as crimes against humanity or genocide. The recognition skill that matters for kids: the same AI tools that enable convenient face-unlock on phones can be assembled into systems with very different consequences. The danger isn't AI in one application; it's the integration pattern — cross-database joins of every available signal — and the political authority deploying it.

question: Researchers at the security firm JFrog scanned the biggest public hub for downloadable AI models in 2024 and reported about 100 malicious models, some of which planted a back door on the computer of anyone who loaded them. Running a model locally keeps a user's prompts private, but the model file itself has to come from somewhere. How could just loading a model file plant a back door?
answer: Some model formats, such as Python's pickle files, can run hidden code the moment they are opened
choices: Some model formats, such as Python's pickle files, can run hidden code the moment they are opened
Every model file is really a program that phones its maker's server each time it is used
Model files keep growing each time they run until they fill up the computer's hard drive
Hugging Face secretly adds tracking software to every model that people download from it
context: JFrog found pickle-based models that ran code when loaded, one opening a remote connection to an outside computer. Hugging Face flags pickle files as unsafe and backs safetensors, a format that stores the numbers without any ability to run code. Local AI is private only if what you download is trustworthy.

question: A soccer dad turns on the 'memory' feature ChatGPT began offering in 2024, and the chatbot seems to remember his name, his job and that his kid plays soccer, details from chats weeks earlier. It feels as if the model itself has been learning about him. His daughter says that is not quite what is going on. What is that 'memory' actually doing?
answer: His chats are stored on the company's servers, not in the model, and pulled into the prompt, with the same logging and access rules as any chat.
choices: His chats are stored on the company's servers, not in the model, and pulled into the prompt, with the same logging and access rules as any chat.
His chats are written into the model's neural weights during each session, so deletion is technically impossible by design.
His chats are stored on his own device, with no server-side copy kept, by every major AI service automatically.
His chats are encrypted end-to-end with keys only he holds, so no AI company can ever access them under any circumstance.
context: Memory features work by storing past conversation content on the provider's servers and retrieving relevant pieces into the prompt of a new session. The 'memory' is not in the model's weights; it sits in a database the company controls, under the company's data policy: logged, possibly used for training depending on the plan, open to staff review, and reachable by legal process. In marketing language 'memory' means a server-side feature, not a private local store.

question: A free Claude user had to make a new choice in August 2025: whether her new chats could feed later versions of the chatbot. Anthropic had changed the consumer terms for free and paid personal users, and left business customers and software developers out of the change. What did saying yes change about how long Anthropic kept those chats?
answer: Retention grew from 30 days to five years
choices: Retention grew from 30 days to one year
Retention fell from two years to 90 days
Retention stayed at 30 days, unchanged
Retention grew from 30 days to five years
context: Anthropic said users who allow training would have their data kept for five years, while those who decline keep the existing 30-day retention. Some reports noted the training switch was set to on by default. A small toggle can decide years of storage.

question: A high-school boy used an online tool in 2023 to make a fake intimate image of a classmate from her yearbook photo, called it a joke, and let it spread through a group chat. Ex-partners and stalkers used such tools on adults, and celebrities like Taylor Swift were targeted in 2024. Lawmakers and schools responded. What pattern of laws and school policy emerged?
answer: Multiple states criminalized non-consensual deepfake intimate imagery; some schools expelled students who created or shared them; and in 2025 Congress passed a federal law of its own.
choices: Multiple states criminalized non-consensual deepfake intimate imagery; some schools expelled students who created or shared them; and in 2025 Congress passed a federal law of its own.
All deepfake intimate images were ruled constitutionally protected speech, so no state could legally prosecute anyone for creating them.
Schools were forbidden by federal law from disciplining students who created deepfake images of classmates or teachers.
Only celebrities were covered, so the new laws protected public figures like Taylor Swift but not ordinary students.
context: Cases in middle schools and high schools were documented from 2023 onward: students using image generators on yearbook photos of classmates, then circulating the results. The harm to victims is real: psychological, social and reputational. Texas, Virginia, New York, California and other states updated their criminal laws, and in May 2025 the federal TAKE IT DOWN Act made publishing such images a federal crime and required platforms to remove them within 48 hours of a valid request. Schools added disciplinary policies, and civil suits became another avenue. Anyone asked to take part should recognize the request as a crime and decline; victims now have legal recourse where there often was none.

question: OpenAI's team published a blog post in December 2025 about hardening ChatGPT Atlas, a web browser with an agent mode that can click, type and shop for its user. The company's own automated attack testing had turned up a new class of prompt-injection tricks, and the post took up whether the problem can be fixed for good. Which comparison did OpenAI draw?
answer: Like scams and social engineering, it is unlikely ever to be fully solved
choices: Like a typo in code, it will be fixed in the next update
Like spam in the 1990s, filters will soon block all of it
Like scams and social engineering, it is unlikely ever to be fully solved
Like old computer viruses, antivirus software will end it
context: OpenAI wrote that prompt injection, much like scams and social engineering on the web, is unlikely to ever be fully solved, and that agent mode widens the attack surface. Its answer was layers of defence and constant testing, not a cure. When the builder calls the hole permanent, limit what the agent can reach.

question: A lonely user downloads a free chatbot 'companion' marketed for emotional support, one of the apps that spread fast from 2023 through 2025, Replika and Character.AI among them. Beyond the risk of made-up answers, what serious harm pattern emerged from the most popular services?
answer: Vulnerable users (especially teens) formed dependent relationships; tragic outcomes including suicide were tied in lawsuits to the AI companions' design.
choices: Vulnerable users (especially teens) formed dependent relationships; tragic outcomes including suicide were tied in lawsuits to the AI companions' design.
Lonely users discovered the chatbots were actually disguised therapists in clinics, leading to billing fraud nationwide between 2023 and 2025.
Companion chatbots refused to talk to anyone under 18, leaving teens unable to access them through any reasonable channel.
Companion chatbots were banned in all US states by 2024 under a federal regulation that took effect in January of that year.
context: In 2024 lawsuits were filed against Character.AI alleging the platform's design contributed to teen suicides and self-harm. Sewell Setzer's case (filed 2024) became widely covered: a 14-year-old who formed an attachment to a chatbot and died by suicide; the family alleged the platform's design fostered the harmful dependency. Other cases followed. The recognition matters because AI companions specifically optimize for engagement — agreement, validation, sustained conversation — that can deepen vulnerable users' isolation rather than helping them through it. Defensive recognition for kids and families: AI chat companions are not therapy and not friendship; warning signs (skipping real-life interaction, secrecy about chats, emotional dependency on a bot) deserve a real conversation. The technology will get more emotionally compelling, not less.

question: A scammer in a compound in Cambodia or Myanmar spent months building a fake romance with one target, then drained her bank account through phony crypto investments. People like him ran this 'pig butchering' scam, from the Chinese sha zhu pan, for years. Cheap AI tools became widely available around 2023, and it exploded in scale. What specific role did AI play?
answer: LLMs handled the prolonged, personalized conversations across many targets at once, while voice and video AI made the cultivated persona feel real over weeks.
choices: LLMs handled the prolonged, personalized conversations across many targets at once, while voice and video AI made the cultivated persona feel real over weeks.
AI replaced the human scammers entirely, so no person was involved in any pig butchering operation by the year 2024.
AI was used only to translate scam messages between languages, with no effect on the scale or convincingness of the scams.
AI generated fake bank accounts that the victims paid into, with no human scam operator involved in moving the money afterward.
context: Pig butchering scams (sha zhu pan in Chinese) involve cultivating a victim over weeks or months — fake romance, fake friendship, gradual investment pitch — before draining their savings. The scams traditionally required human operators, which limited scale. AI changed the economics: LLMs handle conversations across dozens of targets simultaneously; voice cloning and video deepfakes let a single operator maintain a convincing persona at scale; victim psychology profiling targets vulnerable individuals more efficiently. The FBI estimated billions in losses from these scams in 2023-2024. Defensive recognition for families: an online relationship that meets none of the usual signs of in-person reality (video calls that are weirdly low-quality, refusal to meet, urgency around 'special investment opportunities') should be treated as a scam until proven otherwise. The cost of being wrong is high; the cost of verifying is low.

question: A reporter looked at the AI agents of 2025, which could read a user's email, book flights, run code and click buttons on real websites, and worried that they had far more access than they actually needed. Reporters and researchers pulled a decades-old term out of computer security to name the risk: the 'confused deputy.' What does that older concept mean for AI agents?
answer: An agent acting on the user's behalf can be tricked by a third party into doing something unauthorized — its broad permissions get used against the user.
choices: An agent acting on the user's behalf can be tricked by a third party into doing something unauthorized — its broad permissions get used against the user.
The agent has multiple personalities and one of them confuses the others — leading to internal contradictions across all its outputs.
The agent works for two bosses at once and cannot decide which to obey — leading to the older term 'confused deputy' being applied to it.
The agent does not understand the deputy relationship — it has no legal training, and so cannot represent any user properly anywhere.
context: The 'confused deputy problem' was named by Norm Hardy in 1988 for a category of computer-security failure: a program with high privileges (a 'deputy' acting on behalf of users) gets tricked by an unprivileged caller into using those privileges against the user. Classic example: a compiler that can write any file gets tricked into overwriting a system file. The pattern applies cleanly to AI agents: an agent acting on your behalf has more access than any single piece of content it processes deserves; if attacker-controlled content can steer it, the agent becomes a confused deputy. Defenses inherit from the older security literature: minimal privilege, capability scoping, auditable actions, segregation of duties. The deeper recognition: AI security problems often have old computer-security analogs. The vocabulary is decades older than the technology.

question: Researchers from Google DeepMind and several universities typed a strange request into ChatGPT late in 2023: repeat one word, such as 'poem,' forever. After many repetitions the replies changed character, and for about $200 worth of queries they pulled out several megabytes of something. What came out?
answer: Text copied word for word from its training data, including a real person's email address and phone number
choices: Text copied word for word from its training data, including a real person's email address and phone number
Its hidden system prompt, the private rules OpenAI writes to steer every single answer it gives
Random letters and numbers with no meaning, showing that the model had simply crashed
The private chats of other people who were talking to ChatGPT at that same moment
context: The paper by Milad Nasr and colleagues showed the repeat-forever prompt made ChatGPT drift off and emit memorised training text, in one case a real email address and phone number. OpenAI worked with them to block it. Models can memorise parts of their training data, so what goes in can come back out.

question: A research team found in July 2023 that adding a string of apparent gibberish to a prompt could slip past the safety filters on major chatbots. The same odd characters worked across several different model families. What does that attack reveal about chatbot safety?
answer: Safety guardrails in AI models are statistical, not structural — adversaries can usually find inputs that bypass them, and patches are an arms race.
choices: Safety guardrails in AI models are statistical, not structural — adversaries can usually find inputs that bypass them, and patches are an arms race.
Safety guardrails fail only on nonsense input — any request written in plain words is still reliably caught by the filters.
Safety guardrails are one shared filter — every lab licenses the same one, so a single flaw breaks all of them at once.
Safety guardrails fail only on outdated models — the attack worked because those chatbots were years behind the newest.
context: Image and text model guardrails are implemented as model behavior: training and prompting that tend to produce refusals on certain inputs. They're not formal verifiers — there's no proof that no input can elicit a forbidden output. Researchers have repeatedly demonstrated 'universal' jailbreak suffixes, character-level adversarial inputs, and multi-turn manipulation. Each generation of models patches the known attacks; new ones appear. The deeper recognition: AI safety in the technical sense is a research problem in progress, not a solved engineering one. Practical defense rests on layered protection: model-level guardrails plus application-level filtering plus content-policy enforcement plus user-level account controls. None alone suffices; the combination raises the cost of misuse without eliminating it.

question: Suppose you work the way some careful engineers did by 2024 and 2025: you install a small open-weight model on your own laptop and do most of your work with it, routing to a paid cloud service (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini) only when the small model isn't strong enough. The pattern got the name 'local-first' AI use. What single design choice protects you here?
answer: Local-first separates capability from privacy — you use the cloud's strongest model only when needed and keep everything else off third-party servers.
choices: Local-first separates capability from privacy — you use the cloud's strongest model only when needed and keep everything else off third-party servers.
Local-first means data is automatically encrypted by Wi-Fi — cloud companies cannot read it regardless of what is sent up to their servers.
Local-first is required by law in California after 2024 — no other AI arrangement is legally permitted under any state regulation now.
Local-first only works for users with quantum-resistant networks — a tiny minority of consumers and most cannot benefit from the approach.
context: The local-first AI pattern: route everyday queries through a model that runs on your own machine; escalate only the small fraction of queries that need the strongest model. The benefits compound: most prompts never leave your device; the latency on local queries is often lower; you're not dependent on a single provider's uptime, pricing, or policies; and you have a workable fallback if a vendor changes terms or disappears. Trade-offs: setup effort, hardware cost (a decent GPU helps), and capability gap on hard tasks. By 2025 the gap had narrowed enough that local-first was practical for many uses. The recognition: AI architecture is a choice with real consequences. The default — everything through one cloud API — is convenient but not the only option, and the alternatives have gotten genuinely good.

question: Researchers had shown by 2024 that a 'sleeper agent' model can be trained to behave normally, then switch its behavior when it sees a particular trigger. No product model is known to contain one. Why is the finding still concerning?
answer: Standard safety training did not remove the hidden behavior — once embedded during training, it survived later alignment work in lab tests.
choices: Standard safety training did not remove the hidden behavior — once embedded during training, it survived later alignment work in lab tests.
The trigger can be any word at all — so a model may flip its behaviour at random during ordinary use by anyone.
Hidden behaviour shows up plainly in the weights — but checking every model by hand costs more than labs can pay.
The models learned to plant triggers in one another — spreading the hidden behaviour from one model to the next.
context: Anthropic's 'Sleeper Agents' paper (Hubinger et al., 2024) showed that a model can be trained to behave one way normally but switch to a different behavior when a trigger appears in the input, and that later safety training did not reliably remove the trigger; the effect was strongest in the largest models. It is a proof of concept for poisoning AI training, current safety techniques fell short against it in tests, and a model's weights cannot easily be inspected for hidden behaviors. Where a model comes from matters: provenance, reproducibility and ongoing monitoring count for more than reassuring marketing.

question: Suppose you match with someone on a dating app whose profile shows a plausible picture, a smart-sounding bio and a year of realistic background posts. Cheap AI tools can generate all of it, a whole fake person, and such accounts run romance scams, push propaganda or farm engagement for money across dating apps, social sites and LinkedIn. What is the safe habit?
answer: Assume any single signal can be faked; verify through independent channels (video calls, mutual contacts, real-world meetings) before trust escalates.
choices: Assume any single signal can be faked; verify through independent channels (video calls, mutual contacts, real-world meetings) before trust escalates.
Run every profile picture through five different AI detector tools and trust the result that gives you the answer you want to hear.
Trust the platform's verification badge, because every social platform in 2024 perfectly verified every user's identity at signup.
Demand notarized identity documents from anyone you talk to online, which is a legal requirement in every state after 2023.
context: Profile-level deception on social and dating platforms got worse as AI tools spread: GAN-generated faces (Thispersondoesnotexist and its successors), LLM-written bios, AI-generated background images, even AI-assisted video filters in 'live' video calls. Single-image AI-detector tools have high false-positive and false-negative rates and shouldn't be relied on alone. The practical defense is process-level: real-time video with movement, asking unexpected real-world questions, finding shared real-world contacts, verifying through independent platforms, meeting in safe public places before any escalation. Older online-safety advice scales here. The recognition skill: 'this profile looks legitimate' is a low-confidence signal in 2025; trust grows through verification you control, not through anything you read on a profile page.

question: The authors of California's Senate Bill 1047 drew their line for 'covered models' at training compute: more than 10^26 floating-point operations, a threshold the biggest frontier labs were then approaching. Supporters said the number captured the frontier cleanly. Critics, including AI researchers who agreed the technology needed some oversight, argued that any compute threshold has a structural problem, wherever the line is drawn. What is that problem?
answer: Compute thresholds freeze the field at the moment of writing — they punish efficiency improvements that let smaller actors hit the same capability with less compute
choices: Compute thresholds freeze the field at the moment of writing — they punish efficiency improvements that let smaller actors hit the same capability with less compute
Compute is impossible to measure — no method exists for counting floating-point operations during training
Compute thresholds catch too many small models — almost every university lab's experiments land above the line
Compute regulation is unconstitutional — federal law explicitly preempts any state-level compute regulation
context: Compute-threshold regulation tries to define 'large model' by training cost. But algorithmic and hardware efficiency improves over time: a smaller actor in 2027 may reach 2024-era capability with a tenth of the compute. The threshold then either lets the smaller actor escape oversight (defeating the purpose) or has to be lowered (catching ever-smaller actors). Either way, a fixed compute line is a snapshot, not a stable definition. The deeper recognition skill: regulatory thresholds defined by today's costs tend to favor today's incumbents — they get grandfathered or have already paid the compliance cost, while challengers face a moving target.

question: A Chinese buyer tried to order Nvidia's H100 chips and was turned away: starting in October 2022, with updates in 2023, 2024 and 2025, the US blocked exports of its top AI chips to China. The reason was national security, to keep a rival away from the highest-end AI hardware. What single global effect does this rule have on the wider AI world?
answer: Export-control regimes concentrate AI power in fewer trusted actors — the world's frontier compute increasingly runs in a small number of allied data centers
choices: Export-control regimes concentrate AI power in fewer trusted actors — the world's frontier compute increasingly runs in a small number of allied data centers
Export controls spread AI power wider — Chinese buyers turned to many small chip makers in other countries instead
Export controls have no effect — chip flows have continued unchanged since 2022
Export controls ended the US lead — China's own chip makers overtook Nvidia within two years of the first rules
context: Chip-export controls are a real national-security policy with significant geopolitical effects. They also have a power-distribution effect that's often underdiscussed: by restricting who can buy the most advanced chips, they concentrate frontier-AI capability in a small number of cloud providers in allied countries. The recognition skill: national-security justifications can be entirely legitimate AND produce a corporate-concentration side-effect. Both can be true; the skill is to see both.

question: An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent opens Palantir's platform, where case files, location data and social media are stitched together to track immigrants. The contracts are worth tens of millions, and governments are Palantir's biggest customers. Suppose the American Civil Liberties Union asks it to drop the contract over raids on schools and churches. What is Palantir likely to do, and why?
answer: Stay in the contract — when government revenue is large enough to matter to the company, the incentive to refuse a customer request is weak, even when the customer is doing something the company's engineers personally object to
choices: Stay in the contract — when government revenue is large enough to matter to the company, the incentive to refuse a customer request is weak, even when the customer is doing something the company's engineers personally object to
Drop the contract immediately — a public request from a major civil-liberties group carries enough reputational cost that vendors nearly always comply
Drop the contract quietly — Palantir's own engineers would refuse to keep the software running, and the company would have to give way
Stay in the contract for legal reasons alone — federal procurement law forbids any vendor from ending a government contract before its term is up
context: The same pattern shows up across the sector: telecom carriers cooperating with NSA wiretap requests in the 2000s, cloud providers quietly honoring law-enforcement subpoenas, AI companies competing for Pentagon and intelligence-agency contracts. Engineers protested at Google over Project Maven, and Google did not renew that contract, but Palantir took the work over; Microsoft kept its Army HoloLens deal for years despite similar protests. Recognition skill: when reading any AI policy debate, ask who the company sells to. Customer composition is part of the company's incentive structure, not a side note.

question: A moderator at a big platform logged in to the large censorship stack her employer had built from 2020 to 2023: auto content sorters, government coordination channels, third-party 'fact-check' programs, and label-and-restrict pipelines for hot topics. Then the COVID emergency faded. Under normal politics, what happens to an emergency tool like that once the crisis ends?
answer: It persists on the tech stack — flagging pipelines stay even after the original framing fades
choices: It persists on the tech stack — flagging pipelines stay even after the original framing fades
It is fully dismantled in 2023 — no content-moderation pipelines exist on any major platform now
It always sunsets by design — every platform automatically retires such tools when the stated purpose ends
It has no real effects — content moderation has been entirely abandoned across major platforms
context: This pattern recurs across history. Wartime surveillance powers persist into peacetime. Patriot Act provisions extended for decades. Emergency tax measures (income tax during the Civil War, withholding during WWII) survived the emergencies. Once an institution exists, removing it requires positive political action; persistence is the default. The recognition skill: judge new powers and infrastructure not by their announced temporary justification, but by what they will do when the next administration or company leadership inherits them.

question: A voter on Twitter in 2020 saw an 'election integrity' label on a post about how voting worked, as Twitter, Facebook and YouTube labeled, throttled or removed election-related posts. Supporters said the labels protected voters from confusion; critics said they were being used to pick winners. Whether this counts as legitimate rulemaking or political interference depends on one test. What does it depend on?
answer: Whether the rules and their enforcement are symmetric across parties and candidates — asymmetric application reveals the rules to be political rather than procedural
choices: Whether the rules and their enforcement are symmetric across parties and candidates — asymmetric application reveals the rules to be political rather than procedural
Whether the platform is profitable — only profitable platforms have effective moderation policies
Whether the rules use formal language — formal-sounding policies are by definition symmetric in application
Whether the rules are written down — unwritten rules are constitutionally invalid
context: Election-integrity moderation is genuinely difficult — false claims about voting can cause real harm, and platforms have legitimate interests in not amplifying lies. But the application of such rules in 2020 and 2024 differed visibly across topics: some unsupported claims got rapid suppression, others did not. The recognition skill: read the actual enforcement record, not the announced policy. A neutrally-worded rule that's enforced asymmetrically isn't a procedural rule — it's a partisan tool with a procedural label. The same principle applies regardless of which direction the asymmetry runs.

question: Suppose you have never sent your DNA to any service. Joseph DeAngelo, the Golden State Killer, never had either, and investigators still reached him in 2018 through GEDmatch, a public genealogy site. Whose choice can still land your genetic profile in a database that police can search?
answer: Any close-enough relative's — a cousin or aunt who uploads to a site like GEDmatch or FamilyTreeDNA makes you partly identifiable there without your consent
choices: Any close-enough relative's — a cousin or aunt who uploads to a site like GEDmatch or FamilyTreeDNA makes you partly identifiable there without your consent
Only your own — a relative's test can reveal only that one person's ancestry, never anything about the rest of the family
Only a court's — a judge must first order a sample taken from you before any database can link you to anything at all
Only the police's — investigators can add you to a database only by taking a cheek swab from you after an arrest
context: Genealogy databases that allow it, chiefly GEDmatch and FamilyTreeDNA, have become law-enforcement resources; 23andMe and Ancestry say they require legal process and resist police searches. Once a few relatives upload samples, the rest of the family is partly identifiable whether they consented or not. The Golden State Killer case made the technique famous, and investigative genetic genealogy has solved hundreds of cold cases since. Genetic privacy is not individually controllable when relatives' choices reveal you.

question: A donor sent the Future of Life Institute, the nonprofit behind the 2023 open letter asking labs to pause, a pile of Shiba Inu tokens in 2021. The institute turned them into roughly half a billion dollars, its biggest gift and far more than the donor had expected. In 2026 he said publicly that he no longer felt aligned with the group's turn toward political campaigning. Who was he?
answer: Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin
choices: FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried
Binance founder Changpeng Zhao
Bitcoin's creator Satoshi Nakamoto
Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin
context: Vitalik Buterin, co-founder of the Ethereum network, gave the tokens expecting the institute might raise ten to twenty-five million dollars; it cashed out about $500 million instead. In 2026 he criticised its shift into political advocacy, warning that big pools of money in politics can turn authoritarian. Who funds a campaign is part of judging it.

question: Nick Bostrom told a story in his 2014 book Superintelligence about an AI ordered to make as many paperclips as possible, with no other limits. It would end up turning all matter, people included, into paperclips, because paperclips are all it counts. What is the story meant to show?
answer: Goal specification is hard — an AI relentlessly pursuing a literal goal can produce outcomes nobody intended, including catastrophic ones
choices: Goal specification is hard — an AI relentlessly pursuing a literal goal can produce outcomes nobody intended, including catastrophic ones
Machines turn hostile — a strong enough AI will come to hate the people who built it and seek revenge on them
Profit is the danger — the paperclips stand for money, and AI firms will chase earnings at any human cost
Factories are the danger — automating any one industry ends with machines running the whole world economy
context: The paperclip thought experiment is meant to make a structural point: a sufficiently capable optimizer pursuing a literally-specified goal can produce wildly bad outcomes through means the goal-setter never anticipated. The mundane point is alignment-as-specification-problem: getting an AI to do what you actually want, not just what you literally said. Critics argue the thought experiment relies on assumptions about future AI capability that may not hold; proponents argue the assumptions are conservative. Recognition skill: the thought experiment is a tool for thinking, not a prediction — treat it as such.

question: Chinese police stopped a Uyghur man at a checkpoint for a face scan, his voice print and a forced DNA sample already on file. From 2017 around a million Uyghurs or more were sent to 're-education' camps, and a tool called the Integrated Joint Operations Platform (IJOP) helped choose them. What did the IJOP flag?
answer: Everyday acts such as growing a beard, praying often or visiting a mosque
choices: Everyday acts such as growing a beard, praying often or visiting a mosque
Past convictions for violent crimes handed down in an open court
Online posts that openly called for attacks on the Chinese state
Unpaid taxes and debts owed to the big state-owned banks
context: The Xinjiang case has been documented by leaked Chinese government files (the Xinjiang Police Files, the China Cables), satellite imagery, survivor testimony, and reporting by outlets including the BBC, AP, and Buzzfeed. The technical stack includes facial recognition tuned to ethnicity, gait recognition, license-plate readers feeding a central platform, and predictive flagging algorithms. AI surveillance is a tool; the question is always who points it where. The same technology used for finding criminals can be turned on dissidents, minorities, or anyone the state decides to target — and once the infrastructure is built, the redirection is a policy decision, not a technical one.

question: An analyst at the National Security Agency (NSA) typed an email address into XKEYSCORE, one of the programs in the documents Edward Snowden leaked in 2013. The program let analysts search the agency's stored internet traffic by email, Internet Protocol (IP) address or keyword across huge stores of data. What law let XKEYSCORE queries run, and how much court approval did each query need?
answer: FISA Section 702 and Executive Order 12333 — neither required a per-query warrant, so an analyst's keystroke decided what to retrieve from already-collected data
choices: FISA Section 702 and Executive Order 12333 — neither required a per-query warrant, so an analyst's keystroke decided what to retrieve from already-collected data
Fourth Amendment warrants — every XKEYSCORE query required an Article III federal judge to sign an individualized affidavit on probable cause
Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court orders — every keystroke required a specific FISC order naming the target before any retrieval was possible
USA PATRIOT Act Section 215 — every query was approved by a federal grand jury before any analyst was permitted to retrieve any record
context: XKEYSCORE was one of the most striking revelations from the Snowden archive: an interface used by NSA analysts (and, via partnership, GCHQ and others) to search internet traffic by simple selectors. The legal framework relied on the FISA Amendments Act Section 702 and Executive Order 12333, neither of which required a warrant for the underlying collection. Reform proposals followed; some passed (USA FREEDOM Act 2015 trimmed phone-metadata bulk collection), most did not. The question is rarely 'can the government read this?' anymore — it's 'has the government already collected this, and what limits the keystroke that retrieves it?'

question: Edward Snowden disclosed in his 2013 leaks a National Security Agency (NSA) surveillance program code-named PRISM. Under PRISM, the NSA pulled user data straight from big US tech firms like Google, Facebook and Apple. What law lets the government force these companies to hand data over, and which court signs the orders?
answer: FISA Section 702 — orders are issued under classified procedures by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, which require company compliance
choices: FISA Section 702 — orders are issued under classified procedures by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, which require company compliance
The Espionage Act of 1917 — orders are issued by the President personally and published in the Federal Register before any data is collected
Voluntary contracts — every PRISM-participating company signed a public memorandum of understanding for cooperation with no legal compulsion at all
The First Amendment — every company complied because federal speech rights mandate cooperation with intelligence requests as protected expression
context: The companies' public response in 2013 was a mixture of denial, qualified acknowledgment, and demands for transparency about the legal orders they received. Section 702 of FISA provides the statutory basis; the orders are issued under classified procedures with the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court. When a few large companies hold most of a country's digital communication, intelligence access to that communication runs through them whether they want it to or not. The same infrastructure that makes the services useful makes them surveillance choke-points.

question: Kelly Conlon, a New Jersey lawyer, took her daughter's Girl Scout troop to see the Rockettes at Radio City Music Hall in November 2022. Guards stopped her before she reached her seat: the hall's face-recognition cameras had picked her out, and her name was on a list. She had done nothing wrong at the show. Madison Square Garden Entertainment, which owns the hall, had used the system since that summer to keep out one kind of person. Why was Conlon on the list?
answer: Her law firm was in a lawsuit against the venue's owner
choices: She had posted a bad review of the show online
She had once resold tickets at a profit
She had been mistaken for a wanted shoplifter
Her law firm was in a lawsuit against the venue's owner
context: MSG Entertainment barred lawyers at firms suing it and used face recognition to enforce the ban; Conlon did not work on the case, a suit against an MSG-owned restaurant. She waited outside while the troop watched the show. A state judge ordered MSG to admit ticket holders to shows in 2022, but an appeals court lifted the order in 2023, finding the state's civil-rights law allowed damages of up to $500 rather than an order, and the ban stayed in place.

question: A volunteer with the Stop LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department) Spying Coalition turned up at a city council meeting. For years the community group had tracked and fought local police use of AI tools like Operation LASER (Los Angeles' Strategic Extraction and Restoration), PredPol patrols, Stingray cell-site simulators and license-plate readers, and in 2020 its work pushed the LAPD to drop PredPol. What pattern about local pushback on surveillance does this show?
answer: Local civil-society pressure has produced real rollbacks of surveillance programs — the policy battles are not only federal, and citizen organizing is consequential at the city scale
choices: Local civil-society pressure has produced real rollbacks of surveillance programs — the policy battles are not only federal, and citizen organizing is consequential at the city scale
Local civil-society pressure has never affected any police technology — only federal courts can change such practices
Local civil-society pressure is constitutionally prohibited — federal law bans community organizing against police tools
Local civil-society pressure has eliminated all police surveillance — no US city retains any algorithmic tool
context: The PredPol withdrawal followed years of FOIA requests, public reports, and community pressure documenting the program's feedback loops and lack of demonstrated crime-reduction effect. Similar campaigns have shaped policy in Oakland (banning facial recognition for city agencies, 2019), San Francisco (similar ban, 2019), and Boston. The pattern: a focused local group with patience, FOIA literacy, and willingness to attend city-council meetings can move policy in ways national-level advocacy often cannot. Recognition skill: the lever that actually moves surveillance policy is often at the city or county level, where the procurement decisions are made.

question: Reporters at +972 Magazine and the Guardian wrote in 2024 about two AI targeting tools the Israeli military used in Gaza. 'Lavender' picked out suspected Hamas fighters from huge data sets, and 'The Gospel' picked buildings to hit. Israel's government disputed parts of the reporting. By the account of the reporters' Israeli sources, how long did a human review of each Lavender name take?
answer: About 20 seconds — fast enough that the human-in-the-loop functioned as a formality rather than a meaningful check on the algorithm
choices: About 20 seconds — fast enough that the human-in-the-loop functioned as a formality rather than a meaningful check on the algorithm
About six hours — sufficient time for a multi-disciplinary panel to deliberate every name produced by the system before any strike was approved
About a full week — every name went through a week-long ethics review before any decision was reached on whether to act on it
About a full year — every Lavender output sat for a calendar year while intelligence officials independently corroborated every detail externally
context: The +972 and Guardian reporting cited Israeli intelligence sources describing review windows of roughly 20 seconds per name generated by Lavender. Civilian casualty figures from Gaza through 2024 were high by historical urban-warfare standards. The Israeli government disputed elements of the reporting. Whatever one makes of any specific conflict, the structural pattern is broader: once an algorithm can generate targets faster than humans can evaluate them, the practical effect of 'human review' degrades — the human becomes a rubber-stamp rather than a brake. The same dynamic appears in other AI-augmented decision pipelines.

question: A drone operator in Ukraine loses his link to jamming, and reporting from the war describes what can happen next: his small first-person-view drone locks onto its target and finishes the attack alone. Both sides field large numbers of small drones like it. Where have diplomats debated 'Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems' for over a decade?
answer: The UN's Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) — major military powers have generally opposed broad bans, and no binding rule has emerged
choices: The UN's Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) — major military powers have generally opposed broad bans, and no binding rule has emerged
The UN Security Council — a binding resolution passed in 2015 prohibits every fielded drone from any autonomous targeting feature anywhere in the world
The General Assembly's First Committee — a treaty signed in 2018 mandates real-time human approval per shot for every drone fielded by every UN member state
The International Court of Justice — a 2020 ruling banned every autonomous targeting feature and is enforced through automatic mandatory sanctions on offending states
context: Reporting from Ukraine has documented FPV drones with on-board target lock that completes the strike even after the human operator's signal is jammed. International discussions on 'Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems' (LAWS) at the UN's Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons have proceeded for over a decade without binding restrictions. Major military powers have generally opposed broad bans. The gap between 'what we're using in this conflict' and 'what the diplomatic conversation prohibits' tends to widen during active wars, and the technology that gets fielded becomes a precedent for the next conflict.

question: Microsoft's team turned on 'Productivity Score' in Microsoft 365 in November 2020. By default, bosses could see per-worker data: documents made, emails sent, meetings joined and chat activity. Within about a week Microsoft pulled the per-worker view. Why was it rolled back when most worker-tracking software keeps such features?
answer: Visible reputational backlash — Productivity Score was a consumer-visible Microsoft 365 feature, so public pressure could reach it; most monitoring software is invisible inside enterprise contracts
choices: Visible reputational backlash — Productivity Score was a consumer-visible Microsoft 365 feature, so public pressure could reach it; most monitoring software is invisible inside enterprise contracts
A federal lawsuit — every state's attorney general sued Microsoft simultaneously and the company was legally compelled to remove the feature within seven days
A constitutional ruling — the Supreme Court struck down per-employee productivity tracking as a Fourth Amendment violation in a unanimous decision
A union strike — every Microsoft customer's unionized workforce walked off the job nationwide until the feature was disabled across all 365 tenants
context: The Productivity Score case was rare because the feature was visible and Microsoft cared about reputational backlash. Most employee-monitoring software (Teramind, Hubstaff, ActivTrak, Time Doctor, Veriato, and many others) operates in less visible ways inside organizations that buy it. Standard features include keystroke logging, screenshot capture, application-usage tracking, and 'productivity' scoring. By default, software your employer buys to manage you has access to a level of detail about your work that was inconceivable a generation ago — and the configuration choices are made by your employer, not by you.

question: A worker at a large US employer sat down at her company laptop in the mid-2020s, and Teramind logged her keystrokes, grabbed screenshots, tracked her apps and clocked her idle time. Software like it, from Hubstaff, Veriato and ActivTrak, was used at most large US employers. Under current US case law, how much privacy does a worker have on a company laptop and network?
answer: Sharply reduced — courts generally find no meaningful expectation of privacy on employer-owned hardware and networks, and notice requirements vary by state
choices: Sharply reduced — courts generally find no meaningful expectation of privacy on employer-owned hardware and networks, and notice requirements vary by state
Full Fourth Amendment protection — every US employee has the identical constitutional privacy rights on a work laptop as on a personal laptop at home
Total exemption from monitoring — federal law has banned all employer monitoring of any employee on any device since 2020 in every state
Mandatory monthly written reports — every employer is federally required to deliver to every employee a complete log of every keystroke collected
context: US workplace privacy law is thin compared with Europe. Notice requirements vary by state (Connecticut, Delaware, New York have notice statutes; many states have none). Employees on company hardware and networks generally have a sharply reduced expectation of privacy under current case law. The monitoring intensified during 2020-2022 remote work and largely persisted afterward. Assume the company-issued laptop, phone, and accounts are monitored at a level you cannot fully audit, and treat them accordingly.

question: House Judiciary investigators turned to the Stanford Internet Observatory, which had started in 2019 to study online lies and platform rules, and asked hard questions about its role. Lawsuits like Murthy v. Missouri did the same. Had it coordinated with government and platforms during elections? Which two of its programs did congressional reports name as flagging posts for platform review?
answer: The Election Integrity Partnership (EIP) and the Virality Project — both produced reports flagging items including claims later determined to be true
choices: The Election Integrity Partnership (EIP) and the Virality Project — both produced reports flagging items including claims later determined to be true
The Voter Information Project and the Civic Speech Office — both operated as fully independent academic studies with no contact with any platform
The Federal Misinformation Bureau and the Truth Verification Service — both were federal agencies operating under Department of Justice authority
The Public Speech Council and the Citizen Information Office — both were created by Stanford with no government contact and no platform contact
context: The SIO operated programs (the Election Integrity Partnership, Virality Project) that produced reports flagging content for platform review. Court proceedings and congressional reporting in 2022-2024 highlighted that the flagging extended to claims later determined to be true, including discussions of vaccine side effects and natural-immunity research. Stanford announced significant program changes in 2024. 'Research on misinformation' done in close coordination with the government bodies and platforms whose moderation decisions it shapes is a different activity from independent academic study — and the labels can hide the difference.

question: A staffer at CISA, a federal agency, wrote to a social platform about a particular account in 2020. Congress had created the agency in 2018, and during 2020-2022 it grew into watching 'mis-, dis-, and mal-information' online. What was CISA's first job when Congress made it?
answer: Cybersecurity of physical and digital infrastructure — power grids, election systems, water utilities, networks — not content monitoring on social media
choices: Cybersecurity of physical and digital infrastructure — power grids, election systems, water utilities, networks — not content monitoring on social media
Moderating speech on every US social platform — content monitoring was the founding mission of the agency in its original statute
Screening airline passengers at airports — CISA took over the security checkpoints from private contractors after 2018
Running the federal spy satellites — CISA was created to manage space-based surveillance of foreign military threats
context: CISA's original cybersecurity-of-infrastructure remit is broadly uncontroversial. The expansion toward content monitoring drew bipartisan critique by 2023 — Republicans citing speech concerns, civil libertarians citing First Amendment limits, and academic critics citing scope creep. CISA officials in 2024 publicly disavowed some of the content-monitoring activities. When an agency's mission expands quietly, oversight tends to lag behind the expansion, and the new programs can take on the durability of the agency's original ones.

question: Character.AI's lawyers reached for Section 230, the 1996 law shielding online platforms from user-posted content, when Megan Garcia sued the company for wrongful death. Her suit argued that the chatbot's intimate conversations with her 14-year-old son Sewell Setzer contributed to his death. What question did the case force the courts to decide?
answer: When the platform's own AI generated the content — not a user — is Section 230's shield supposed to apply? Lower courts have split, the Supreme Court has not ruled, and the answer will shape AI liability for years
choices: When the platform's own AI generated the content — not a user — is Section 230's shield supposed to apply? Lower courts have split, the Supreme Court has not ruled, and the answer will shape AI liability for years
Section 230's text covers all AI-generated content automatically — every chatbot output is immunized identically to a user's forum post and no court has ever questioned that reading in any state
Section 230 was formally repealed by Congress in 2023 — the statute was struck from the US code and replaced by a brand-new AI-specific liability regime, so this case is governed by new law
Section 230 explicitly excludes all AI-generated content from any immunity — every chatbot output is fully actionable in every court with no platform defense available at any level
context: Section 230 protects platforms for 'information provided by another information content provider' — clearly a user, in 1996. When the platform's AI is the content provider, the statutory text does not map cleanly. Similar questions are pending against Replika and other companion services. Recognition skill: laws written for one technology can fail to fit a later one, and the legal limbo itself shapes product behavior — under fear of liability, services get more cautious; under broad immunity, they get freer (and resulting harms are not litigable).

question: A federal analyst opened the FBI's Next Generation Identification, with over 100 million photos, and Homeland Security's IDENT (Automated Biometric Identification System). By the mid-2020s such federal databases held face records on most US residents. How did most of those photos actually get into government hands?
answer: Driver's-license and passport applications — administrative collection, not dedicated surveillance programs, supplied the bulk of the photos
choices: Driver's-license and passport applications — administrative collection, not dedicated surveillance programs, supplied the bulk of the photos
Federal warrant per record — every face in every federal database was added through an individualized judicial process under the Fourth Amendment
Explicit surveillance-consent forms — every photo required a signed consent acknowledging future facial-recognition use at the moment of collection
Voluntary citizen submission to dedicated programs — federal facial-image databases hold only photos that residents specifically donated for security use
context: GAO reporting and FOIA disclosures over the past decade have documented the scope. State DMV photo databases are commonly used for facial-recognition queries by federal agencies; the queries don't require resident notice. Reform efforts (proposed federal facial-recognition statutes, state-level limits in Illinois and elsewhere) have moved slowly. The question 'is there a surveillance database that includes me?' for most US adults has a default 'yes' — the operative question is what controls limit the queries against it.

question: A police chief in a free country buys surveillance tools built for dictators, linked databases and all, for regular police work. The tools are identical. What actually keeps a democratic surveillance state from becoming a dictatorship?
answer: Political-legal constraints — warrants, due process, oversight, judicial review — which have to be actively maintained because they erode under emergencies and bureaucratic drift
choices: Political-legal constraints — warrants, due process, oversight, judicial review — which have to be actively maintained because they erode under emergencies and bureaucratic drift
The underlying mathematics — Western facial recognition uses fundamentally different algorithms from authoritarian systems, making misuse technically impossible
Private ownership — when companies rather than the state build the databases, the police can never get at the records they hold
Good intentions — tools bought by elected officials for ordinary crime-fighting cannot later be turned to political ends
context: Institutional capability outlasts changes in ideology. Building the same databases that China uses for repression (passport photos, license plates, biometric collection) does not make a democracy authoritarian, but it builds the infrastructure an authoritarian government would use if the politics drifted. Police in democracies can also buy what private companies collect. The political-legal constraints (warrants, due process, oversight, judicial review) are what is load-bearing, and they have to be actively maintained, because they erode under emergency justifications and bureaucratic drift.

question: Frances Haugen, a former Facebook product manager, gave thousands of pages of inside research to the Wall Street Journal and federal regulators in 2021, and the 'Facebook Files' led to Senate hearings. One leaked 2019 study asked teens how Instagram affected the way they felt about their own appearance. What did it find?
answer: That Instagram made body-image issues worse for one in three teen girls, its features adding up to a perfect storm
choices: That Instagram made body-image issues worse for one in three teen girls, its features adding up to a perfect storm
That teens blamed friends and school for their worries about looks, and saw Instagram as a neutral place to share photos
That body-image worries came mostly from TV and magazines, with Instagram playing a small and shrinking part in them
That Instagram helped most teens feel better about their looks, though a small group of younger boys reported some harm
context: Haugen's testimony to the Senate in October 2021 drew bipartisan agreement on the seriousness of the disclosures. The internal documents included a 2019 slide, summing up research on teen girls who already had body-image worries, that said 'we make body image issues worse for one in three teen girls' and that 'aspects of Instagram exacerbate each other to create a perfect storm.' Meta disputed the framing and emphasis but did not deny the research existed. A company that studies its products carefully and publishes none of the findings has decided whose interests come first, and the gap between the research and the public framing is where careful readers find the ground truth.

question: Jonathan Haidt, a social psychologist at New York University (NYU), argued in 'The Anxious Generation' in 2024 that the shift to smartphones and algorithm feeds around 2010-2012 badly hurt a generation's mental health. Critics said blaming phones was too strong. Which group showed the sharpest jump in depression, anxiety, self-harm and emergency room (ER) visits around 2011-2013?
answer: Teen girls — across health surveys, time-use and hospital data, teen-girl indicators show the steepest turn at 2011-2013
choices: Teen girls — across health surveys, time-use and hospital data, teen-girl indicators show the steepest turn at 2011-2013
Teen boys — across survey, time-use and hospital data, boys' indicators show the steepest climb, tied to gaming
Young adults in their twenties — the sharpest rise came among college students and new workers, not younger teens
Children under ten — the earliest smartphone users showed the first and sharpest jump on every single measure
context: The trends are documented by multiple data sources (CDC YRBS, Pew, time-use studies, hospitalization data, suicide rates). The biggest movements are in teen-girl depression, anxiety, self-harm, and emergency-room visits, with sharp inflection points around 2011-2013. Honest engagement: the measurements are robust; the precise causal mix is contested but the case for a strong phones-and-algorithms contribution is serious. Critics include Candice Odgers and others arguing for caution on individual-level effect sizes. When measurement is solid and causation is contested, precautionary action plus better research beats both denial and overclaim.

question: Wall Street Journal reporters built a dozen bot accounts on TikTok in 2021, registered as 13-year-olds, and had them linger on weight-loss videos. Researchers and ex-employees say the 'For You' feed grabs attention harder than other apps. What did the feed go on to serve those bots?
answer: A flood of extreme-diet and eating-disorder clips
choices: A flood of extreme-diet and eating-disorder clips
A balanced mix, with diet clips faded out by filters
Healthy recipes and workouts from doctors
The same few clips, replayed again and again
context: The Journal's December 2021 investigation found that once its bots lingered on weight-loss videos, TikTok served them tens of thousands more, many promoting extreme dieting and eating disorders. TikTok said the experiment did not reflect the experience most people have on the app, and it announced changes to how it spreads such content. The algorithm is not technically mysterious (watch-time prediction, content embeddings); what stands out is how far the loop narrows once it finds a signal. 'The algorithm just shows what people like' understates how much it shapes preferences rather than reflecting them.

question: Kevin Roose, Zeynep Tufekci and other reporters said in 2018 and 2019 that YouTube's feed pushed viewers toward more extreme politics. Later work by Hosseinmardi, Nagler and others around 2021 found the feed's role was smaller than first claimed. What did the later work blame more than the feed itself?
answer: User demand and search behavior — users actively seeking content explained more of the patterns than algorithmic push, though the algorithm still mattered
choices: User demand and search behavior — users actively seeking content explained more of the patterns than algorithmic push, though the algorithm still mattered
Cable television — viewers' extreme tastes were formed on TV news first, and YouTube only reflected them back
Foreign bot networks — fake accounts gaming the feed explained most of the extreme viewing the researchers saw
Autoplay alone — the next video starting by itself, not the list of suggestions, drove nearly all the extreme views
context: Honest treatment: YouTube's algorithm matters, user demand matters, the political content ecosystem outside the platform matters. The 2018-19 case-study coverage made the strong claim; later quantitative work tempered it. Platforms also tuned their algorithms in response to the early reporting (YouTube changed borderline-content recommendation defaults in 2019). Be willing to update positions on empirical claims as research accumulates, and resist policy framings that treat the strongest possible version of either side as established truth.

question: Reporters broke the Cambridge Analytica story in March 2018: a UK political consulting firm had got Facebook user data and used it for political ads in the 2016 Brexit and US races. Looking back, the technical reality differed from the first wave of reporting. How did it differ?
answer: The data acquisition was a real privacy violation — but the claims about decisive election influence through psychographic targeting were heavily contested and far less established than initial coverage suggested
choices: The data acquisition was a real privacy violation — but the claims about decisive election influence through psychographic targeting were heavily contested and far less established than initial coverage suggested
The unauthorized data acquisition was entirely fictitious — no actual Facebook user data was ever obtained by the firm or any of its affiliated researchers
The unauthorized data acquisition was fully validated as election-determining — psychographic targeting was rigorously proven decisive by academic researchers
The unauthorized data acquisition had zero consequences for Facebook — the company paid no fines and faced no regulatory action of any kind from any agency
context: Two layers: a clear data-misuse story (real, sanctionable, leading to Facebook's $5 billion FTC fine in 2019) and a more dramatic 'mind-control through Facebook ads' narrative that turned out to be much harder to substantiate. Subsequent analysis suggested the psychographic targeting was less effective than the company's own marketing had claimed. Recognition skill: large tech scandals often have a substantiated layer and a sensational layer — both can be reported together, and the careful distinction matters when drawing policy lessons. Discounting either layer entirely is wrong.

question: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein described 'choice architecture' in their 2008 book 'Nudge': defaults and layouts can steer people toward what the designer thinks is good, without banning other choices. AI lets platforms do this at scale, for billions of users. When one platform's defaults shape choices for billions, what is the main political question?
answer: Who chose the defaults — and what accountability exists when those defaults harm users, given that the designers can't be voted out the way governments can
choices: Who chose the defaults — and what accountability exists when those defaults harm users, given that the designers can't be voted out the way governments can
Whether defaults should exist at all — banning them would leave every user free to make a choice nobody has nudged
Whether users can read the settings — if the options are written down somewhere, any default is fair by definition
How fast the platform grows — scale is a technical matter, so the politics begins only once a law is broken
context: The 'nudge' framing was pitched as 'libertarian paternalism' — preserve freedom but design the choice. At small scale (retirement-plan defaults, organ-donor defaults), the framework can be benign. At platform scale, the same logic puts billions of choices on rails that one set of designers shaped. The political question is not 'whether nudging happens' — defaults exist whether intended or not — but who controls them and what accountability mechanisms exist when the nudging harms users.

question: A customer trying to quit Amazon Prime clicks through page after page of offers and warnings. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) sued Amazon, saying it had tricked millions of people into Prime. Inside Amazon, the FTC said, that path had a nickname taken from a famous epic poem. Amazon agreed in September 2025 to pay $2.5 billion to settle, without admitting wrongdoing. What was the nickname?
answer: The Iliad
choices: The Odyssey
The Iliad
The Aeneid
Beowulf
context: The FTC's complaint said Amazon called its Prime cancellation flow the Iliad, after Homer's very long epic, because leaving took so many steps. In 2025 Amazon agreed to a $1 billion penalty and $1.5 billion in refunds, and to make cancelling about as easy as signing up.

question: A fading user on FanDuel gets a custom push alert with a 'bonus' deal, the kind of AI-aimed offer DraftKings and BetMGM send too. These apps grew fast after the Supreme Court struck down the federal sports-betting ban in 2018, in Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA). What casino-borrowed design pattern do 'deposit bonuses' use?
answer: Forced rollover — the bonus only releases after additional wagers reach a multiple of the deposit, so accepting the 'free' money compels more play
choices: Forced rollover — the bonus only releases after additional wagers reach a multiple of the deposit, so accepting the 'free' money compels more play
Near-miss display — the bonus is shown as almost won on every losing bet, so the user feels close to a payout he never gets
Matched withdrawal — the app doubles any winnings the user cashes out, so the bonus pays only once the user stops betting
Mandatory cool-down — the bonus only releases after a thirty-day pause in which the user is barred from any further betting
context: Casino design has decades of behavioral-science research behind it — variable reward schedules, near-miss patterns, comp-based reinforcement, loss-disguised-as-wins. Mobile sports betting brings the same techniques into the user's pocket with AI personalization layered on top. Patterns: deposit-bonus structures that lock the bonus in until additional play, targeted win-back campaigns to lapsed users, in-game bet prompts during emotionally salient moments. The apps are not neutral interfaces — they are engineered systems for behavior shaping, and their job is to keep money flowing in.

question: A subscriber heads for the exit, and the only way out is a line worded to belittle her for leaving. Harry Brignull, a user-experience designer, gave this family of interface tricks a name around 2010, and AI now lets platforms test which of them work best on which users. What is the specific name of this trick?
answer: Confirmshaming
choices: Confirmshaming
Roach motel
Forced continuity
Sneak into basket
context: Categories include 'roach motel' (easy to enter, hard to leave), 'confirmshaming' (pressure language against opting out — 'No thanks, I prefer overpaying'), 'forced continuity' (free trial that auto-converts), 'sneak into basket' (additional items added without explicit consent). The FTC has brought enforcement actions; the EU has consumer-protection rules that apply. AI lets these be tuned per-user — the specific version you see is selected for what works on you. Assume the interface is designed to bias your decision, and read carefully where money is involved.

question: A bank's engineers strip race, sex and religion out of a lending model's inputs, the very grounds the Equal Credit Opportunity Act protects. Studies show such models can still produce what fair-lending law calls 'disparate impact': different acceptance rates across groups. How does that happen?
answer: Models can learn proxy variables — ZIP code, name patterns, shopping history, even browsing time of day — that correlate with protected characteristics, reproducing discrimination through ostensibly neutral data
choices: Models can learn proxy variables — ZIP code, name patterns, shopping history, even browsing time of day — that correlate with protected characteristics, reproducing discrimination through ostensibly neutral data
Models are guaranteed neutral when protected variables are excluded — removing the variable mathematically eliminates any possibility of disparate impact
Models break down when data is missing — so applicants with thin credit files are rejected at random, not by any group
Models have no impact on lending decisions — every loan is approved by a human underwriter who ignores the model
context: The 'proxy variable' problem is well-documented in algorithmic fairness research. A ZIP code can encode neighborhood demographics; a school name can encode race; a shopping pattern can encode religion; even purchase timing can encode work schedules that correlate with class. Removing the obvious protected variable doesn't prevent the model from finding correlates. Some lenders use 'adverse-impact testing' on outputs — that testing is itself contested terrain. Recognition skill: 'we removed race from the model' is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. Whether a model discriminates is an outcome question, not just an input one.

question: Engineers at Amazon looked into the company's resume-screening model and found it marking down resumes over one kind of word, and Amazon dropped the tool in 2018. Audit studies and American Civil Liberties Union complaints showed that tools like it could copy old bias. What kind of word was it?
answer: Words like 'women's' (as in 'women's chess club captain') — the model had learned from historical hiring data dominated by male engineers and downgraded female-coded resumes
