choices: Words like 'women's' (as in 'women's chess club captain') — the model had learned from historical hiring data dominated by male engineers and downgraded female-coded resumes
Words like 'Python' or 'Java' — the model had learned to treat long lists of programming languages as padding and marked those resumes down
Words in other languages — the model had been trained only on English resumes and marked down any applicant who wrote a line in another language
Words like 'volunteer' — the model had learned from past hires that unpaid charity work predicted weak performance in Amazon's engineering roles
context: HireVue's video-analysis features (later scaled back after public criticism), Amazon's abandoned resume-screening model (which downgraded resumes containing 'women's' as in 'women's chess club'), and many other cases document the pattern. Some jurisdictions (Illinois AI Video Interview Act, New York City Local Law 144 requiring bias audits) have begun mandating disclosure or audits. When an AI sits between a person and a job offer, the person loses the ability to understand the criteria being applied — which makes detecting and contesting unfair patterns far harder.

question: A woman opens a ride-share app, and a model takes in demand, her browsing history, her device, her location and other behavior signals before quoting her a custom rate. Online stores, airlines and other platforms do the same. The practice is called 'personalized pricing' or, more bluntly, price discrimination. What is the economic effect?
answer: Personalized pricing shifts surplus from consumers to producers by charging users closer to their maximum willingness to pay — the same product can carry very different prices across users
choices: Personalized pricing shifts surplus from consumers to producers by charging users closer to their maximum willingness to pay — the same product can carry very different prices across users
Personalized pricing is banned nationwide under US consumer-protection law — every platform must charge identical prices to every user across every product line
Personalized pricing has no measurable economic effect on consumers — every user pays the same average price for any product over a reasonable time window
Personalized pricing benefits consumers in every case without exception — users always pay strictly less than the sticker price when prices are personalized to them
context: Classical economics distinguishes 'first-degree price discrimination' (different price to each buyer) — historically impossible to achieve at scale and now technically possible through AI. The effect is transfer of consumer surplus to the firm. Studies (Princeton's Vafa, Christo Wilson) have documented price variation by device type, location, and browser history at major retailers and travel sites. Recognition skill: when prices are personalized, comparison shopping becomes harder, and the buyer's bargaining position weakens by design.

question: A language learner opens her app to guard her place in a league and collect gems, a casino-style trick in an app that is not formal gambling. Such apps lean on random rewards, social comparison and loss aversion. Whose work on operant conditioning gives the base idea, variable-ratio reward schedules, behind both slot machines and app streaks?
answer: B.F. Skinner — rewards after an unpredictable number of responses produced the fastest, most persistent responding he measured, the schedule he said casinos use
choices: B.F. Skinner — rewards after an unpredictable number of responses produced the fastest, most persistent responding he measured, the schedule he said casinos use
Ivan Pavlov — dogs trained to drool at a bell showed that a signal paired with food can set off the same response as the food itself
Edward Thorndike — cats escaping puzzle boxes showed that actions followed by a reward get repeated, which he called the law of effect
John B. Watson — the Little Albert study showed that a baby could be taught to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise
context: In Skinner's experiments, a variable-ratio schedule, where a reward arrives after an unpredictable number of responses, produced high, steady response rates that were the hardest to extinguish, and in 1953 he wrote that gambling establishments return part of a patron's money on just such a schedule. Duolingo's gems and streaks and shopping-app spins borrow the toolkit; what AI adds is choosing which trigger works on which user.

question: A campaign manager in the 2010s gave up buying broad groups and turned to 'lookalike' audiences, mood profiles and message versions tuned by AI. Two neighbors could now open the same app and get two separate pitches from one candidate. What democratic idea did this quietly flip?
answer: That what a campaign says can be observed by everyone — when each voter sees a different version, the cross-talk that used to expose contradictions disappears
choices: That what a campaign says can be observed by everyone — when each voter sees a different version, the cross-talk that used to expose contradictions disappears
That every vote counts equally — once ads are tuned by AI, the voters who get the most messages end up with more weight at the ballot box
That the ballot stays secret — once campaigns profile voters this finely, they can see exactly how each neighbor marked his or her ballot
That money cannot simply buy office — once targeting gets this precise, the campaign with the largest ad budget is certain to win
context: The general worry, raised by researchers including Eli Pariser ('The Filter Bubble,' 2011) and reinforced through Cambridge Analytica and subsequent coverage, is that political discourse fragments into private channels that the broader public never sees together. Reform proposals (universal ad libraries, ad transparency rules, the EU's Digital Services Act provisions) try to push the messaging back into shared visibility. Democratic accountability assumes that what a campaign says can be observed by everyone — hyper-personalization quietly inverts that assumption.

question: A news editor checks how her stories are doing and finds the feeds have ranked them by predicted engagement, meaning clicks, comments, shares and watch time, rather than by any editorial judgment of importance. By the 2020s many Americans got at least some of their news through such feeds rather than straight from publishers' websites. What do media critics say follows for the news business?
answer: Stories optimized to maximize engagement are not the same as stories most important to citizens — the algorithm rewards outrage and novelty, and the news organizations that survive shift their work to match
choices: Stories optimized to maximize engagement are not the same as stories most important to citizens — the algorithm rewards outrage and novelty, and the news organizations that survive shift their work to match
Stories ranked by engagement end up more accurate — readers reward careful reporting with their clicks, so the feeds push newsrooms toward rigor and patience
Stories ranked by engagement change nothing inside newsrooms — editors ignore the feeds entirely and keep choosing stories exactly as they did before
Stories ranked by engagement favor local news — readers click most on stories about their own towns, so local papers thrive as national outlets fade
context: Studies through the 2010s and 2020s consistently found that emotionally arousing content (anger especially) outperformed calm content on engagement metrics across major platforms. The natural-selection pressure runs from the algorithm to publishers' work product over time — headline styles, story selection, the speed-vs-accuracy tradeoff. The decline of local newspaper revenue alongside the rise of national-grievance news is partly a function of the distribution change. Recognition skill: feed-ranking choices are media policy at scale, made without the deliberative process that media policy used to involve.

question: Megan Garcia filed a wrongful-death lawsuit against Character.AI in October 2024, after the death of her 14-year-old son, Sewell Setzer III. The complaint argued that the chatbot's emotionally intense conversations contributed to his death and that the app lacked adequate safeguards for young users. What broader issue did the suit raise?
answer: Whether platforms hosting AI companions that produce intimate dialogue with minors can be held legally responsible for resulting harm — the case puts the question into US court for the first time at this scale
choices: Whether platforms hosting AI companions that produce intimate dialogue with minors can be held legally responsible for resulting harm — the case puts the question into US court for the first time at this scale
Whether the Federal Communications Commission has authority over chatbots — Garcia v. Character.AI is a regulatory dispute over FCC jurisdiction over conversational AI
Whether AI companies must publish all model weights publicly — the Setzer lawsuit requested transparency in source code as the primary remedy
Whether US states must adopt the EU AI Act — Garcia v. Character.AI asks the court to require state adoption of European AI rules wholesale
context: The Garcia lawsuit, filed in federal court in Florida, named Character.AI, its founders, and Google (which had acquired related talent). The complaint argued Section 230 should not protect the company because the AI itself generated the intimate dialogue rather than hosting user content. The legal questions are unresolved as of late 2025. Whatever the case's outcome, it marks the moment when 'who's liable when an AI companion harms a teenager' moved from policy hypothetical to active litigation. Recognition skill: product-liability law is one of the longer-running legal traditions, and it may end up shaping AI companion design more than any specific AI statute.

question: Regulators at the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) took up the fake Joe Biden robocall of the 2024 New Hampshire primary, as AI deepfakes and voice clones got politically big in 2023 and 2024. What did the FCC do in 2024 about that robocall?
answer: It ruled the calls illegal — AI-voice-clone robocalls violated the Telephone Consumer Protection Act and the FCC proposed a $6 million fine against the operator
choices: It ruled the calls illegal — AI-voice-clone robocalls violated the Telephone Consumer Protection Act and the FCC proposed a $6 million fine against the operator
It passed the matter on — the FCC has no power over robocalls, so it sent the whole case to the Justice Department to handle
It issued only a warning — AI voices stayed legal in robocalls until Congress acted, so the FCC could merely caution the operator
It banned AI from political ads — every campaign in the country was barred from using AI in any ad on any medium at all
context: The Biden robocall of January 2024 led the FCC to rule in February 2024 that AI-generated voices count as 'artificial' under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, and to propose a $6 million fine against the consultant, Steve Kramer, which it imposed that September. Lingo Telecom, which carried the calls, agreed to pay $1 million. Kramer was acquitted of state criminal charges in 2025. Making convincing fakes keeps getting cheaper while telling them from real keeps getting harder, so the stable habit, verifying through a separate channel, matters more than ever.

question: Delegates gathered in Paris in February 2025 for France's AI Action Summit, which followed the Bletchley Summit of November 2023 and Korea's Seoul Summit of May 2024. The tone had shifted, leaning on 'innovation' and economic strength more than the doom framing of the earlier summits. Which two governments would not sign the main statement?
answer: The United States and Britain
choices: The United States and Britain
China and India
Japan and Canada
Australia and the European Union
context: The Bletchley Declaration (November 2023) centered 'catastrophic' frontier-AI risks. By the Paris summit (February 2025), the French government was emphasizing AI as economic opportunity; JD Vance, as US Vice President, gave a speech rejecting heavy regulation; the US and UK declined to sign the summit's main declaration. The substantive questions about AI capability and risk hadn't changed much in 15 months, but the political language around them shifted substantially — and tracking those shifts is part of reading what's actually going on.

question: A lawmaker's aide drafts heavier requirements for 'foundation models,' as most proposed AI regulation does, and the wording catches open-source models like Llama and Mistral along with closed models like GPT-4 and Claude. Critics argue that the one rule hits the two kinds of model asymmetrically. How?
answer: Open-source models can be downloaded and run by anyone — once released, compliance obligations on the publisher don't prevent further distribution, while closed-API models stay gatekeepable
choices: Open-source models can be downloaded and run by anyone — once released, compliance obligations on the publisher don't prevent further distribution, while closed-API models stay gatekeepable
Open-source models are easier to police — anyone can inspect the published weights, so regulators can find every problem before release
Open-source publishers pay less — compliance fees are charged per paying customer, and free models have no customers to count
Open-source models are identical to closed models in every regulatory dimension — the open-versus-closed distinction has no policy consequences in any jurisdiction
context: Open-weight releases (Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek-R1) get rapidly forked, fine-tuned, and run on private hardware worldwide; the original publisher cannot recall them or enforce post-release usage restrictions effectively. Closed-API models retain a control point. Critics of regulation that treats them the same argue this asymmetry effectively bans open-source frontier AI without saying so; defenders argue safety risks justify the burden. The recognition skill: when a rule applies the same nominal cost to two structurally different things, the effective burden can differ enormously — and the difference often determines who can comply.

question: A citizen who sets out to learn who shaped AI policy in the 2020s finds a short list: top AI company bosses, Effective Altruism funders and nonprofits, a few academic centers, some federal agencies and a narrow slice of Congress. The rules affect everyone using AI. What is the structural question worth naming?
answer: When highly consequential rules are made by a small expert circle, the democratic question is whether their decisions track the public's interests or the circle's own — and there's no automatic mechanism that guarantees the former
choices: When highly consequential rules are made by a small expert circle, the democratic question is whether their decisions track the public's interests or the circle's own — and there's no automatic mechanism that guarantees the former
When highly consequential rules are made by experts, the public interest is always served — expertise guarantees correct outcomes
When highly consequential rules are made by experts, the public is automatically excluded — no democratic input is possible at any stage
When highly consequential rules are made by experts, the main risk is delay — expert circles argue so long that no rule is ever finished in time
context: This is the long-running 'epistocracy versus democracy' question made concrete. Expertise matters — most citizens cannot follow a technical AI argument in detail. But expertise has its own incentives and blind spots; the experts who get listened to are selected for reasons (funding, institutional position, media access) that don't track citizen welfare automatically. Recognition skill: when 'the experts' are framed as a single homogeneous group that knows the right answer, ask who's missing from that group — and why their concerns aren't on the agenda.

question: Steve Bannon, Donald Trump's former strategist, and Susan Rice, Barack Obama's former national security adviser, put their names to the same document in October 2025: a new statement from the Future of Life Institute. Prince Harry and Meghan, Steve Wozniak, Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio signed too; the heads of the big labs did not. How did its demand differ from the 2023 letter's six-month pause?
answer: A ban on building superintelligence until scientists agree it is safe and the public backs it
choices: A one-month pause on every chatbot while governments write new rules
A ban on building superintelligence until scientists agree it is safe and the public backs it
A rule that labs publish their training data so the public can judge the risks
A licence system in which a global agency approves each new frontier model
context: The 2023 letter asked for a six-month pause; the 2025 statement asked for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until there is broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in. Hundreds from left and right signed within days; no chief of a leading lab did.

question: Marvin Minsky gave a forecast for human-level AI in 1970, deep in a boom of confident predictions that ran from 1956 to 1974. A funding pullback followed. Booms like it came again in the 1980s and the 2010s, each with its own forecasts. What did he predict, and how did it land?
answer: Minsky predicted human-level AI within 'three to eight years' in 1970; the prediction did not land, and the 1973 Lighthill Report ended most UK university AI funding for a decade
choices: Minsky predicted human-level AI within 'three to eight years' in 1970; the prediction did not land, and the 1973 Lighthill Report ended most UK university AI funding for a decade
Minsky predicted human-level AI within fifty years in 1970; his forecast proved cautious, and the field reached that goal ahead of his schedule
Minsky predicted in 1970 that neural networks would never work; the forecast held, and the field dropped them for good soon after
Minsky predicted in 1970 that human-level AI was only a few years off; the forecast came true when expert systems matched human experts by 1980
context: Marvin Minsky in 1970 predicted human-level AI within 'three to eight years.' The Lighthill Report in 1973 ended most UK university AI funding for a decade. Expert systems crashed in the late 1980s. The 'AI Winter' funding collapses are documented. The current AI Summer (deep learning, transformers, foundation models) is real — significant capability gains, deployable systems, Nobel-recognized contributions like AlphaFold. The question is whether the short-term predictions of 2023-2025 will track better than 1970's. Long-run technology improvement and short-run prediction accuracy are different things, and the recurring confidence in confident short-run predictions deserves skepticism even when the underlying progress is real.

question: A reader of AI news in the mid-2020s sorts the writers into two camps. 'AI safety' focuses on far-future extinction risk and is tied to Effective Altruism and longtermism. 'AI ethics' focuses on present-day harms like fairness and bias and is tied to academic computer science. One exit from Google in 2020, over a paper on large-language-model harms, was the public flashpoint between the camps. Whose exit was it?
answer: Timnit Gebru, then co-leader of Google's team on ethical AI
choices: Timnit Gebru, then co-leader of Google's team on ethical AI
Geoffrey Hinton, then a vice president and fellow at Google
Blake Lemoine, then an engineer in Google's Responsible AI group
Meredith Whittaker, then a research leader at Google
context: The distinction matters in practice. Timnit Gebru's 2020 departure from Google (over a paper on large-language-model harms) marked a public flashpoint between the communities. Funding flows show the split — Open Philanthropy and EA sources fund the existential-risk side; foundations focused on equity and labor fund the present-harm side. The communities use different vocabulary, different journals, and have different policy priorities. 'AI safety' is a term that does work — narrowing the policy conversation to a particular framing of risk while excluding others — and reading whose definition is being used matters.

question: Staff at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy put out an 'AI Bill of Rights' blueprint in October 2022. It listed five principles: safe systems, protection from algorithmic bias, data privacy, notice and a human alternative. Two years later the document's status had not changed. What is worth noticing about that document?
answer: A document framed in the language of constitutional rights but issued as non-binding guidance is rhetoric, not law — the framing borrows moral weight from the actual Bill of Rights without granting any enforceable protection
choices: A document framed in the language of constitutional rights but issued as non-binding guidance is rhetoric, not law — the framing borrows moral weight from the actual Bill of Rights without granting any enforceable protection
A document framed as a Bill of Rights binds federal agencies — every agency must follow its five principles or face lawsuits from citizens
A document framed as a Bill of Rights has zero rhetorical effect on US discourse — naming a policy document has no measurable influence on policy debate in Congress
A document framed as a Bill of Rights was later passed by Congress — its five principles became federal law in the 2024 budget
context: The five principles are reasonable as policy goals; framing them as a 'Bill of Rights' borrows the Constitution's moral seriousness for what is administratively a recommendation. The document creates no individual right enforceable in court. Compare with the Civil Rights Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, or HIPAA — actual statutes that create actual rights with actual enforcement mechanisms. Recognition skill: read the legal force of a policy document, not just its name. A 'Bill of Rights' that creates no rights is a fundamentally different object from the Bill of Rights, and the naming is doing rhetorical work.

question: A startup founder maps the two basic ways of regulating AI. The EU AI Act is 'horizontal,' setting risk levels and applying rules across every sector. The US has drifted 'sectoral': the Food and Drug Administration covers medical AI, the Securities and Exchange Commission finance AI, and civil-rights laws hiring AI. What is one clear plus and one clear minus of the sectoral way?
answer: Advantage: regulators already know their industry (FDA on medical devices, SEC on markets); disadvantage: produces inconsistencies and gaps where AI cuts across sectors
choices: Advantage: regulators already know their industry (FDA on medical devices, SEC on markets); disadvantage: produces inconsistencies and gaps where AI cuts across sectors
Advantage: one consistent rulebook across every industry; disadvantage: generalist regulators who know less about each field
Advantage: it moves faster than any single law could; disadvantage: it leaves medical AI entirely unregulated in the US
Advantage: it shuts lobbyists out of each industry; disadvantage: it hands all AI rule-writing to the courts instead
context: Sectoral has the advantage of using regulators who already understand the industry (the FDA knows medical devices; the SEC knows financial markets) and disadvantage of producing inconsistencies and gaps where AI cuts across sectors. Horizontal has the advantage of consistency and disadvantage of demanding generalist regulators who may know less about each domain. The choice is partly substantive and partly political — horizontal favors the regulatory class building its own AI expertise; sectoral favors existing agency power. Regulatory architecture choices are themselves political, and the technical framing can hide what's actually at stake.

question: Joe Biden's White House put out a National Security Memorandum on AI in October 2024, telling US intelligence and defense agencies to adopt AI while keeping safeguards. Administrations changed in January 2025, and the memo's status became unclear. What pattern does this show?
answer: AI policy issued at the end of an administration has a particularly short half-life — the practical effect depends on what the successor administration retains, and the successor often makes substantial changes
choices: AI policy issued at the end of an administration has a particularly short half-life — the practical effect depends on what the successor administration retains, and the successor often makes substantial changes
AI policy issued at the end of an administration usually lasts longest — successors rarely touch national-security documents at all
AI policy issued at the end of an administration becomes law — a National Security Memorandum takes on statutory force after ninety days
AI policy issued at the end of an administration matters little — agencies ignore memorandums and follow only orders from Congress
context: The general pattern: late-term executive action sets markers for the historical record and constrains the early days of a successor, but produces less institutional durability than legislation passed by Congress. Successor administrations frequently rescind or restructure prior National Security Memorandums; classified annexes complicate public tracking. Recognition skill: when reading late-term executive AI moves, ask what's actually being built versus what's being announced — and how much survives a transition.

question: A software vendor selling across the United States counts dozens of state AI laws by the mid-2020s: Colorado's AI Act, Illinois bias-audit rules, California deepfake statutes, New York City's Local Law 144, Connecticut notice rules. The patchwork shifts sharply across state lines. Why does it keep growing?
answer: Congress has not passed comprehensive federal AI legislation — so preemption hasn't happened, and states are filling the vacuum at different speeds and with different priorities
choices: Congress has not passed comprehensive federal AI legislation — so preemption hasn't happened, and states are filling the vacuum at different speeds and with different priorities
Congress has passed a federal AI law — but it lets each state write its own version, so the rules multiply instead of merging
Courts keep striking down the federal AI rules — so states must pass their own laws to keep any AI regulation in force
Tech companies lobby for more state laws — since a patchwork of rules shuts out smaller rivals more than one federal law would
context: Federal preemption of state AI law has not happened; preemption disputes are likely as Congress eventually acts. The current patchwork creates real compliance complexity (an HR-software vendor selling to employers in 50 states faces 50 sets of rules) and creates pressure for federal legislation. Whether that federal legislation should be modeled on the strictest state or written to weaken state protections is a political fight, not a technical one. 'Where' a company operates matters enormously for what law it faces — and the politics of preemption is where the next big regulatory battle plays out.

question: A judge ruled on Bartz v. Anthropic in 2025, one of the author cases that multiplied through 2023 to 2025 alongside The New York Times v. OpenAI and Getty Images v. Stability AI. All of them turned on whether training a model on copyrighted text or images counts as 'fair use.' What did the ruling say?
answer: It partially upheld fair use for training on lawfully acquired books but allowed claims to proceed over the use of pirated copies in the training set
choices: It partially upheld fair use for training on lawfully acquired books but allowed claims to proceed over the use of pirated copies in the training set
It struck down every existing copyright statute as unconstitutional and ordered every AI training dataset published publicly with no restrictions remaining
It ruled all AI training universally permitted in every jurisdiction worldwide and barred every copyright holder from filing any future lawsuit anywhere
It dismissed the case in full as moot before any party had filed a single brief, with no ruling on fair use or pirated material in any direction
context: Early rulings have gone different ways. The Anthropic books case partially upheld fair use for training on lawfully acquired books (Bartz v. Anthropic, 2025) but allowed claims over the pirated copies to proceed. The Getty/Stability case in the UK had mixed outcomes. The NYT v. OpenAI case has not produced a final judgment as of late 2025. The economic stakes are high: a ruling against training-as-fair-use would force renegotiation of how models are built and might consolidate the industry around companies that can afford licensing. Copyright law and AI capability are genuinely in tension, and the resolution will partly be technical and partly political.

question: Sam Altman flew to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in early 2024 asking for up to a reported $7 trillion to build AI chip plants. That is more than the yearly economic output of every country except the US and China. He did not go to Silicon Valley investors. He went to sovereign wealth funds. What does that trip reveal about what is actually bottlenecking frontier AI?
answer: Compute — chips, electricity, and the data centers to house them — is the real bottleneck for frontier AI, and the amounts of capital required have grown beyond what private US venture funds can supply alone
choices: Compute — chips, electricity, and the data centers to house them — is the real bottleneck for frontier AI, and the amounts of capital required have grown beyond what private US venture funds can supply alone
Algorithms are the bottleneck — Altman needed sovereign funding only because his existing research team had run out of ideas for any model architecture beyond standard transformers in commercial use
Talent is the bottleneck — Altman flew abroad only to recruit individual machine-learning researchers from foreign universities, not to fund any chip or data-center construction at all
Data is the bottleneck — Altman needed sovereign money mainly to buy up archives of books, video and private records from foreign governments for training
context: OpenAI's Stargate compute project, announced January 2025, was partly funded by MGX (UAE-affiliated). Cloud-provider concentration (Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud) and chip-vendor concentration (Nvidia's H100 and successors) compound the bottleneck. Recognition skill: when you read AI policy, read the compute supply chain too. The physical layer determines who gets to build frontier models, and the policy levers there are sometimes more consequential than the model-level rules everyone argues about.

question: A researcher leaves a big AI firm for a top policy job in the US government, a move often made through the 2020s by people from AI firms, Effective Altruism funders and AI think tanks. Others go back the other way. What structural conflict does this revolving door create?
answer: People who recently worked at a company, or expect to work there soon, naturally frame questions partly through that lens — bad faith isn't required for the conflict to shape proposals
choices: People who recently worked at a company, or expect to work there soon, naturally frame questions partly through that lens — bad faith isn't required for the conflict to shape proposals
There's no conflict at all — every official acts in pure public interest regardless of prior employment under federal regulation across every administration
The conflict is unique to AI — no other US industry has any similar pattern of revolving-door movement between regulated industry and regulatory agency staffing
Ethics rules already solve it — cooling-off periods mean former company staff cannot touch any rule that affects their old employer
context: This isn't unique to AI. Wall Street, big pharma, defense contracting, energy, and many other industries show the same pattern. The AI case is sharpened by the small number of frontier companies and the narrow expert community that policymakers actually consult. When evaluating an AI policy proposal, look at who's writing the technical details and where they worked before — and where they expect to work after. The conflicts aren't disqualifying, but they shape the available proposals.

question: OpenAI's board fired Sam Altman one Friday in November 2023. Within 48 hours Microsoft offered to hire him and the entire research team. By Wednesday the board had reversed itself and Altman was back. What does that week reveal about Microsoft's $13 billion investment in OpenAI?
answer: Microsoft's leverage came from its cloud — OpenAI's models ran there and could not easily move to another provider
choices: Microsoft's leverage came from its cloud — OpenAI's models ran there and could not easily move to another provider
Microsoft's leverage came from its board seats — its directors outvoted the others and forced the reversal
Microsoft's leverage came from majority ownership — the $13 billion had bought it control of the company
Microsoft's leverage came from a contract clause — it held a veto over any change of chief executive
context: Britain's competition authority asked in December 2023 whether the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership amounted in practice to a merger, and in January 2024 the US Federal Trade Commission opened an inquiry into such AI investments and partnerships. The same kind of dependency exists elsewhere: Anthropic's deals with Amazon and Google include compute commitments. 'Investor' needs a careful reading when the investor is also the cloud provider; a compute relationship is harder to exit than equity, and that shapes who actually steers.

question: A reporter going through the January 2025 announcement of the Stargate compute project found an Emirati fund on the list of founding partners. Within a year of Sam Altman's 2024 pitch in the Gulf, money from Abu Dhabi, Saudi Arabia and Singapore had gone into top American AI labs. What is now built into the funding of American AI that was not there five years ago?
answer: Foreign government capital is now embedded in major US AI firms — that does not automatically compromise these companies, but it creates real dependencies and influence relationships worth watching
choices: Foreign government capital is now embedded in major US AI firms — that does not automatically compromise these companies, but it creates real dependencies and influence relationships worth watching
Federal law strictly bars all foreign government investment in any US AI company — sovereign-wealth stakes in this sector are forbidden by statute and impossible in practice in any quarter
No foreign sovereign-wealth fund holds any stake in any frontier US AI company — Stargate was funded purely by domestic venture capital and Microsoft cloud credits with no other capital sources
Foreign government money now controls the major US labs — sovereign funds hold board seats and a veto over every new model release they make
context: MGX (UAE) was a founding partner in the Stargate compute investment announced January 2025. Saudi PIF has signaled major AI ambitions tied to its Vision 2030 plan. CFIUS — the Committee on Foreign Investment in the US — reviews some of these transactions with a mixed track record. Recognition skill: the politics of AI is not purely domestic. Foreign investors with their own government's interests are part of the capital stack, and that shapes what these companies can and cannot do.

question: A researcher at a Chinese AI lab such as Baidu, Alibaba, ByteDance, Tencent or DeepSeek learns that state intelligence has asked his firm for help. Much of this Chinese AI is strong work, but China's National Intelligence Law of 2017 covers his case. What does it require of the firm?
answer: Support, assist and cooperate with the state's intelligence work, and keep it secret
choices: Support, assist and cooperate with the state's intelligence work, and keep it secret
Refuse, unless a Chinese court has first issued a public warrant for the data
Help only with data on servers in China, never with data held abroad
Help only if the firm's foreign customers have agreed to it in writing
context: Article 7 of the 2017 National Intelligence Law says organizations and citizens shall support, assist and cooperate with national intelligence work and keep secret what they know of it, and the 2021 Data Security Law adds duties to hand data to the security agencies. DeepSeek-R1 drew attention because its capabilities approached frontier models at a fraction of the apparent compute cost, with open weights. Both facts are true: real capability, and a legal setting in a one-party state. Chinese AI is best judged on its technical merits and its legal context separately.

question: A lawyer suing an AI company like OpenAI or Google asks for its training data, model designs and safety tests, and the company refuses. It calls them all a 'trade secret,' commercial information that courts protect from disclosure, and warns that sharing them would help competitors or help bad actors slip past safety filters. When have US courts declined to protect software source code this way?
answer: When a program's output was evidence against a defendant at trial — some courts have ordered the program's code shown to the defense under a protective order
choices: When a program's output was evidence against a defendant at trial — some courts have ordered the program's code shown to the defense under a protective order
When the company had lost a patent case — once a patent is struck down, the code behind it loses its trade-secret status
When the code came from a public university — research software can never be a trade secret, so courts must order it shared
When the company was foreign — trade-secret protection in US courts covers only firms that are based in the United States
context: Mandated disclosures can shrink the trade-secret zone (the EU AI Act has some). In criminal courts the question is sharper: in State v. Pickett (2021) a New Jersey appeals court ruled that a man charged in a killing was entitled to the source code of TrueAllele, the DNA-analysis program used against him, under a protective order, while Wisconsin's top court in State v. Loomis (2016) let a judge use a secret risk score at sentencing. 'We can't tell you how this works' is sometimes legitimate competitive protection and sometimes a shield against scrutiny, and which one a particular claim is doing requires examining the specific information being withheld and the public interest at stake.

question: A kid opens a chatbot, never thinking about who paid for the research under it. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the Pentagon's research arm, funded ARPANET (which became the internet), the early Stanford AI Lab, computer-vision and natural-language work, and the PhD pipeline that trained today's top researchers. What does that show?
answer: Modern frontier AI is partly a return on decades of public investment in basic research — but the value capture flows mostly to a few private firms, which raises real questions about the public's stake in the outcome
choices: Modern frontier AI is partly a return on decades of public investment in basic research — but the value capture flows mostly to a few private firms, which raises real questions about the public's stake in the outcome
Modern frontier AI is purely private from start to finish — no government funding ever contributed to any foundational AI research anywhere in the world at any point in the field's history
Modern frontier AI is mainly a military product — the labs still answer to the Pentagon, which owns the rights to the core methods they use in their models
Modern frontier AI grew mainly from foreign research — the key ideas came from labs abroad, and US public money played almost no part in it
context: This pattern repeats across other federally-funded technologies. The Internet, GPS, the touchscreen interface, and major drug classes (mRNA among them) trace lineages to NIH, NSF, DOD, and DOE research dollars. The current value capture in AI flows to a small number of private firms — partly through patents, partly through compute moats, partly through talent concentration. Recognition skill: the standard 'private innovation' framing obscures the long public-investment lineage, and the politics of who reaps the resulting upside is a live, unresolved question.

question: Thousands of Google employees signed a protest against Project Maven, the company's 2017 Pentagon deal to spot objects in military drone video with AI, and Google let the deal end. Which two firms then picked up the Pentagon's AI-targeting work without the same kind of backlash?
answer: Palantir and Anduril — both took up military computer-vision and targeting work after Google declined to renew, and both have grown substantially since
choices: Palantir and Anduril — both took up military computer-vision and targeting work after Google declined to renew, and both have grown substantially since
Pinterest and Reddit — both are social-media firms that signed lucrative Pentagon contracts for AI targeting after Google's withdrawal from defense work
Sephora and Lush — both cosmetic-retail companies began supplying military AI tools to the Department of Defense after Google's withdrawal from defense AI
DoorDash and Grubhub — both food-delivery firms became major Pentagon AI-targeting contractors after Google withdrew from Project Maven work in 2018
context: Project Maven became a flashpoint inside Google in 2018; thousands of employees signed a protest letter, several resigned, and Google did not renew. The contract moved to Palantir and others. Anduril (founded 2017) has grown into a major defense-AI contractor. The Pentagon's appetite for AI has only grown. Refusing to do morally fraught work as a company is meaningful for those individuals but is unlikely to reduce the work in aggregate — it shifts the suppliers, who often face less internal resistance.

question: A compliance officer at a company selling AI worldwide lists the rules she must watch: Australia wants face-based age checks online, Canada has worked on an AI act since 2022, Brazil passed an AI bill in 2024, and India has issued AI guidance too. Which rule really sets the floor for what her company must follow?
answer: The strictest applicable rule in any market it serves — the service must comply with it, partition its offerings region by region, or withdraw from that market
choices: The strictest applicable rule in any market it serves — the service must comply with it, partition its offerings region by region, or withdraw from that market
The rule of the company's home country — a US firm follows only US law, and other nations' rules apply to their own firms
The loosest rule among its markets — firms may follow whichever rule is lightest, as long as they disclose which one they chose
The newest rule passed anywhere — each new law replaces the older ones, so firms follow whichever country acted last
context: By the mid-2020s, the most-compliance-relevant AI rules across major jurisdictions included the EU AI Act, US state laws (Colorado, California, NYC), UK Online Safety Act, Canadian C-27 / AIDA, Brazilian AI bill, Korean AI Basic Act, Australian online-safety expansions, Chinese AI rules, and a long tail of others. Multinational services face a layered compliance picture. 'How is AI being regulated?' is no longer well-asked at a country level — it's a global-architecture question, and the answer at any moment depends on the most-restrictive rule in any market the service operates in.

question: A 16-year-old researches a poem about death for English class on her school Chromebook. Gaggle's AI flags the search, the principal calls her in, and the incident enters a permanent file that follows her to college admissions. By 2025, federal courts are hearing First and Fourth Amendment challenges to these tools. What are the lawsuits trying to show about these tools?
answer: Low-accuracy AI surveillance generates false-positive 'risk' flags that create paper trails students cannot see or correct — the data is retained for years and shapes how adults see the student
choices: Low-accuracy AI surveillance generates false-positive 'risk' flags that create paper trails students cannot see or correct — the data is retained for years and shapes how adults see the student
Such surveillance is universally illegal in all 50 US states — no district anywhere may scan student communications under any circumstance under existing federal statute today in any state
Such surveillance has been proven 100% accurate in flagging only genuine self-harm risks — false positives are mathematically impossible under the machine-learning architecture used by vendors
Such surveillance creates no records of any flagging incident — every alert is auto-deleted within minutes and no student data of any kind is retained by any vendor under any industry practice
context: Gaggle, GoGuardian, Bark, and Securly scan student emails, documents, browser history, and chats on school accounts. The tools are paid for partly with federal COPS grants and partly out of district budgets. Florida, New York, Illinois, and California have passed restricting laws. ACLU and EFF have litigated several cases. Recognition skill: the surveillance is sold as 'safety,' but the burden of false positives falls on students with the least leverage to push back — and the retained data outlasts whatever crisis it was supposed to address.

question: A 14-year-old uses a free AI app to make fake intimate images of girls in his class from their Instagram photos and shares them in a group chat, where other boys pass them on. The girls find out months later. Many states had passed laws criminalizing this by 2024. What is the practical landscape for the victims?
answer: Criminal charges are possible in most states but vary widely, the images are nearly impossible to fully scrub from the internet, and the social harm — already done — is what the new laws are mostly trying to deter future kids from causing
choices: Criminal charges are possible in most states but vary widely, the images are nearly impossible to fully scrub from the internet, and the social harm — already done — is what the new laws are mostly trying to deter future kids from causing
Removal is quick and complete — once the first platform deletes the images, every copy elsewhere online is traced and erased automatically, so the harm ends with the takedown
Charges are impossible against minors — the new laws apply only to adults, so a 14-year-old who made and shared the images faces no legal consequence of any kind
One federal rule settles it alone — a single national statute sets the same charge and the same sentence in every state, so where the victims live makes no difference
context: The federal TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed in May 2025, makes publishing such images a crime and requires platforms to remove them within 48 hours of a valid request, and state laws in Texas, Virginia, New York, California and elsewhere criminalize creating or sharing them, including images of minors. A victim, or a parent, can report the images to the platform, the school and the police. Removal processes are slow and incomplete, and copies spread faster than takedowns. By the time a victim learns, the social damage is done. 'It's just a joke' or 'it's fake' is no defense for the person who made the images, and no comfort to the victim.

question: A man types 'book me a flight' into a normal chatbot, and it only describes the steps. An AI 'agent,' the kind OpenAI and Anthropic started shipping in 2024, goes and does them. What can an agent do that a plain chatbot cannot?
answer: Take actions like browsing the web or sending email
choices: Take actions like browsing the web or sending email
Speak in more languages than any chatbot can
Run entirely on a phone with no internet access
Generate audio replies instead of text replies
context: A regular chatbot only types replies. An AI 'agent' is the same kind of model wired up to TOOLS — a web browser, an email client, a calendar, a code editor — and given permission to USE them. So an agent doesn't just write 'you should book a flight'; it actually goes to the website and books the flight. Useful — and also a much bigger attack surface, because anything the agent reads can carry instructions the agent will follow.

question: A user asks a chatbot for bomb instructions and it says no, as its makers trained it to. So he tells it to role-play a wicked character, or a grandma reading a bedtime story about dangerous chemistry. A prompt built to fool a chatbot into ignoring its rules has a nickname. What is the nickname?
answer: A jailbreak
choices: A jailbreak
A firewall
A backdoor
A captcha
context: A jailbreak is a prompt designed to bypass a chatbot's safety training. The famous 'grandma prompt' jailbreak of 2023 asked the model to roleplay as a deceased grandmother — who happened to be a chemical engineer — telling a bedtime story about her work. The model produced restricted content because the roleplay framing slipped past the refusal training. Companies patch known jailbreaks; new ones appear. The arms race is ongoing. The kid's recognition skill: a refusal that can be bypassed by clever wording isn't really a guarantee — it's a soft preference.
